## Cycle 29 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 1 — `structuredClone` for Test Fixture Isolation

`structuredClone` performs a true deep clone that preserves `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `RegExp`, `ArrayBuffer`, and cyclic references — unlike `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))` which silently corrupts these types. Using it for test fixtures ensures each test gets an independent copy of shared data without mutation bleeding.

```javascript
import { describe, it, beforeEach } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

// Shared fixture template — complex object with special types
const USER_FIXTURE = Object.freeze({
  id: 1,
  name: 'Alice',
  createdAt: new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'),
  roles: new Set(['viewer', 'editor']),
  metadata: new Map([['source', 'oauth'], ['locale', 'en']]),
  address: { city: 'Berlin', zip: '10115' },
});

describe('UserService', () => {
  let user;

  beforeEach(() => {
    // structuredClone produces an independent deep copy — mutations in the test
    // cannot affect USER_FIXTURE or sibling tests
    user = structuredClone(USER_FIXTURE);
  });

  it('mutates address without affecting other tests', () => {
    user.address.city = 'London';
    assert.equal(user.address.city, 'London');
    // USER_FIXTURE.address.city is still 'Berlin' — no bleed
  });

  it('preserves Date instances (unlike JSON round-trip)', () => {
    const cloned = structuredClone({ ts: new Date('2026-06-01') });
    assert.ok(cloned.ts instanceof Date);       // ✅ still a Date
    assert.equal(cloned.ts.toISOString(), '2026-06-01T00:00:00.000Z');

    // JSON round-trip comparison — what structuredClone avoids
    const broken = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ ts: new Date('2026-06-01') }));
    assert.equal(typeof broken.ts, 'string');   // ❌ became a string
  });
});
```

**When to use:** deep-cloning test fixtures, state snapshots, and any shared complex object that must be independently mutable per test. **When NOT to use:** cloning functions (they are silently dropped), Proxy objects (not cloneable), or objects with class-specific methods (clone loses the prototype). Alternatives: factory functions that construct fresh objects, `Object.assign({}, base)` for shallow clones. [official]

---

### Pattern 2 — Proxy-Based Auto-Spy / Test Double

A `Proxy` wrapping any object or function automatically records all interactions (get, set, apply) without manually listing every method. This produces test doubles that are exhaustive by design — no method can be called without being recorded, and no property can be read without observation.

```javascript
// auto-spy: records every get and every function call
function autoSpy(target) {
  const calls = {};

  const handler = {
    get(obj, prop) {
      const value = obj[prop];
      if (typeof value === 'function') {
        return (...args) => {
          calls[prop] ??= [];
          const result = value.apply(obj, args);
          calls[prop].push({ args, result });
          return result;
        };
      }
      return value;
    },
  };

  return {
    proxy: new Proxy(target, handler),
    calls,
    callCount: (method) => calls[method]?.length ?? 0,
    lastArgs:  (method) => calls[method]?.at(-1)?.args ?? [],
    reset:     () => { Object.keys(calls).forEach(k => delete calls[k]); },
  };
}

// Usage in a test
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

const logger = { info: (msg) => msg, error: (msg) => msg };
const { proxy: spyLogger, calls, callCount } = autoSpy(logger);

spyLogger.info('startup');
spyLogger.info('request received');
spyLogger.error('db timeout');

assert.equal(callCount('info'),  2);
assert.equal(callCount('error'), 1);
assert.deepEqual(calls.info[0].args, ['startup']);
assert.deepEqual(calls.error[0].args, ['db timeout']);
```

**When to use:** quick test doubles for objects with many methods, verifying that a dependency was called correctly without enumerating every method upfront. **When NOT to use:** mocking `class` instances with private fields (Proxy cannot access `#private` through another object), or replacing ES module exports (static imports bypass Proxy at module load time — use `vi.mock` / `t.mock.module` instead). Alternatives: `vi.fn()`, `jest.fn()`, `t.mock.method()` in `node:test`. [community]

---

### Pattern 3 — `queueMicrotask` as Test Microtask Flush Utility

When testing code that schedules work via `Promise.resolve()`, `queueMicrotask()`, or the microtask queue (e.g., signal-based reactivity systems), you sometimes need to flush the microtask queue without actually awaiting a real async operation. A zero-tick `await` idiom accomplishes this.

```javascript
// Utility: flush all pending microtasks synchronously
// (schedules a resolved promise and awaits it — drains the microtask queue first)
const flushMicrotasks = () => new Promise(resolve => queueMicrotask(resolve));

// Example: a simple reactive signal that schedules batched updates as microtasks
function createSignal(initial) {
  let value = initial;
  const subscribers = new Set();
  return {
    get()      { return value; },
    set(v)     { value = v; queueMicrotask(() => subscribers.forEach(fn => fn(v))); },
    subscribe(fn) { subscribers.add(fn); return () => subscribers.delete(fn); },
  };
}

import { it } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

it('signal notifies subscribers on next microtask', async () => {
  const count = createSignal(0);
  const received = [];
  count.subscribe(v => received.push(v));

  count.set(1);
  count.set(2); // batched — both in the queue

  // Before flush: subscribers haven't fired yet
  assert.deepEqual(received, []);

  // Flush the microtask queue
  await flushMicrotasks();

  // After flush: both updates have been delivered
  assert.deepEqual(received, [1, 2]);
});
```

**When to use:** testing reactive primitives (signals, observables), batching logic, or any code that explicitly defers work to the microtask queue. **When NOT to use:** macrotask-based code (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, I/O events) — those require fake timers (`vi.useFakeTimers()` or `t.mock.timers`). Alternative: `await Promise.resolve()` also flushes one microtask checkpoint but only one level deep — `queueMicrotask` flush drains the full queue including cascading microtasks. [community]

---

### Pattern 4 — `using` in Test Teardown (Explicit Resource Management)

The `using` / `await using` declarations (ES2025) can simplify test teardown by making cleanup lexically scoped. Any resource that implements `[Symbol.dispose]` or `[Symbol.asyncDispose]` is automatically cleaned up when the test block exits, even on failure.

```javascript
import { describe, it } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { createServer } from 'node:http';

// Disposable HTTP server factory for tests
function testServer(handler) {
  const server = createServer(handler);
  server[Symbol.asyncDispose] = () =>
    new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
      server.close(err => (err ? reject(err) : resolve()))
    );
  return server;
}

// Disposable mock module registry
function mockRegistry() {
  const mocks = new Map();
  return {
    set(key, val) { mocks.set(key, val); },
    get(key)      { return mocks.get(key); },
    [Symbol.dispose]() { mocks.clear(); }, // always called on block exit
  };
}

describe('HTTP integration', () => {
  it('server is closed automatically after test', async () => {
    await using server = testServer((req, res) => res.end('OK'));

    await new Promise(resolve => server.listen(0, resolve));
    const { port } = server.address();
    const res = await fetch(`http://localhost:${port}/`);
    assert.equal(res.status, 200);
    // server.close() is awaited automatically — no afterEach needed
  });

  it('mock registry is cleared after test', () => {
    using mocks = mockRegistry();
    mocks.set('db', { query: () => [] });
    assert.ok(mocks.get('db'));
    // mocks.clear() called automatically at block exit
  });
});
```

**When to use:** tests that create network servers, file handles, DB connections, or any resource that must be deterministically closed to prevent port leaks or handle leaks in CI. **When NOT to use:** Node.js versions < 22 or environments without `using` support (requires a Babel/TypeScript transpiler targeting ES2025). Alternative: `afterEach` / `after` lifecycle hooks or `try/finally` blocks. [official]

---

### Pattern 5 — Composable Middleware Pipeline (Koa-Style)

A composable middleware pipeline chains async functions where each function receives a `context` object and a `next` function. Calling `next()` advances to the following middleware. This pattern decouples cross-cutting concerns (logging, auth, validation, caching) from core business logic.

```javascript
// compose: turn an array of middleware functions into a single callable
function compose(middlewares) {
  return function (ctx, next) {
    let index = -1;
    function dispatch(i) {
      if (i <= index) return Promise.reject(new Error('next() called multiple times'));
      index = i;
      const fn = i === middlewares.length ? next : middlewares[i];
      if (!fn) return Promise.resolve();
      try {
        return Promise.resolve(fn(ctx, () => dispatch(i + 1)));
      } catch (err) {
        return Promise.reject(err);
      }
    }
    return dispatch(0);
  };
}

// Usage: build a testable request pipeline
const timingMiddleware = async (ctx, next) => {
  const start = Date.now();
  await next();
  ctx.timing = Date.now() - start;
};

const authMiddleware = async (ctx, next) => {
  if (!ctx.headers?.authorization) {
    ctx.status = 401;
    ctx.body   = 'Unauthorized';
    return; // short-circuit — next() not called
  }
  ctx.user = { id: 1, role: 'admin' };
  await next();
};

const handlerMiddleware = async (ctx) => {
  ctx.status = 200;
  ctx.body   = `Hello, ${ctx.user.name ?? 'user'}`;
};

const pipeline = compose([timingMiddleware, authMiddleware, handlerMiddleware]);

// Unit-test each layer in isolation
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

const ctx = { headers: { authorization: 'Bearer token123' } };
await pipeline(ctx);
assert.equal(ctx.status, 200);
assert.ok(typeof ctx.timing === 'number'); // timing injected by first middleware
```

**When to use:** API servers, request/response pipelines, plugin systems, or any scenario with ordered cross-cutting concerns. **When NOT to use:** simple single-responsibility functions where composition overhead adds no clarity. Alternatives: Express-style `(req, res, next)` callbacks, or RxJS pipeable operators for reactive streams. [community]

---

### Pattern 6 — Type-Safe `EventEmitter` with Typed Overloads

JavaScript `EventEmitter` accepts any string as event name and `any` as payload. Wrapping it in a typed interface (via JSDoc generics or TypeScript overloads) makes event names and payloads statically verifiable without a library.

```javascript
// @ts-check
/**
 * @template {Record<string, any>} EventMap
 */
class TypedEmitter {
  #handlers = new Map();

  /**
   * @template {string & keyof EventMap} K
   * @param {K} event
   * @param {(payload: EventMap[K]) => void} handler
   */
  on(event, handler) {
    if (!this.#handlers.has(event)) this.#handlers.set(event, new Set());
    this.#handlers.get(event).add(handler);
    return this;
  }

  /**
   * @template {string & keyof EventMap} K
   * @param {K} event
   * @param {EventMap[K]} payload
   */
  emit(event, payload) {
    this.#handlers.get(event)?.forEach(fn => fn(payload));
    return this;
  }

  /** @param {string & keyof EventMap} event */
  off(event, handler) {
    this.#handlers.get(event)?.delete(handler);
    return this;
  }
}

/**
 * @typedef {{ 'user:created': { id: number; name: string };
 *             'user:deleted': { id: number };
 *             'error':        Error; }} UserEvents
 */

/** @type {TypedEmitter<UserEvents>} */
const bus = new TypedEmitter();

bus.on('user:created', ({ id, name }) => console.log(`Created ${name} (${id})`));
bus.on('error', err => console.error(err.message));

bus.emit('user:created', { id: 42, name: 'Alice' }); // ✅ type-safe
// bus.emit('user:deleted', { id: 42, name: 'Alice' }); // ❌ 'name' not in 'user:deleted'
```

**When to use:** libraries and SDKs where consumers rely on autocomplete for event names and payload shapes, or any codebase running `@ts-check`. **When NOT to use:** trivial one-off event wiring where adding the generic overhead increases noise. Alternatives: `mitt` (350 bytes, typed), `EventTarget` with `CustomEvent` for browser contexts. [community]

---

### Pattern 7 — `Map` as a Finite State Machine

A `Map` keyed by `[currentState, event]` string tuples provides an explicit, testable state machine without a library. Each entry maps a (state, event) pair to a transition object containing the next state and an optional action.

```javascript
// State machine definition: traffic light controller
const TRANSITIONS = new Map([
  ['red:timer',    { next: 'green',  action: 'activateGo' }],
  ['green:timer',  { next: 'yellow', action: 'activateWarn' }],
  ['yellow:timer', { next: 'red',    action: 'activateStop' }],
  ['red:fault',    { next: 'fault',  action: 'alertOps' }],
  ['green:fault',  { next: 'fault',  action: 'alertOps' }],
  ['yellow:fault', { next: 'fault',  action: 'alertOps' }],
]);

function createTrafficLight(actions) {
  let state = 'red';

  return {
    get state() { return state; },
    send(event) {
      const key = `${state}:${event}`;
      const transition = TRANSITIONS.get(key);
      if (!transition) {
        throw new Error(`No transition for event '${event}' in state '${state}'`);
      }
      actions[transition.action]?.();
      state = transition.next;
      return state;
    },
  };
}

// Easy to test — actions are injected; state is observable
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

const log = [];
const light = createTrafficLight({
  activateGo:   () => log.push('GO'),
  activateWarn: () => log.push('WARN'),
  activateStop: () => log.push('STOP'),
  alertOps:     () => log.push('FAULT'),
});

assert.equal(light.state, 'red');
light.send('timer');
assert.equal(light.state, 'green');
assert.deepEqual(log, ['GO']);
light.send('fault');
assert.equal(light.state, 'fault');
assert.deepEqual(log, ['GO', 'FAULT']);
assert.throws(() => light.send('timer'), /No transition/);
```

**When to use:** workflows, UI states, protocol parsers, or any logic with a discrete set of states and events. **When NOT to use:** states with complex guards (conditions beyond the event type) — use a library like XState for hierarchical or guarded transitions. Alternatives: `switch/case`, XState, Robot. [community]

---

### Pattern 8 — `Promise.race` Timeout Guard (Complement to AbortController)

`Promise.race` can implement a timeout without creating an `AbortController`, using a sentinel rejected Promise. This is simpler than `AbortController` when the underlying operation does not accept a signal but can be abandoned safely.

```javascript
// Reusable: a Promise that rejects after `ms` milliseconds
function timeout(ms, message = `Operation timed out after ${ms}ms`) {
  return new Promise((_, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(message)), ms)
  );
}

// Race an operation against a timeout
async function withTimeout(promise, ms) {
  const timer = timeout(ms);
  try {
    return await Promise.race([promise, timer]);
  } finally {
    // Ensure the timer's internal setTimeout is not left dangling
    // (Promise.race does not cancel the non-winning promise)
    // Pattern: if we got here by winning, the timer is still pending.
    // We don't cancel it here intentionally — it'll be GC'd once no refs remain.
    // For production: track and clearTimeout the timer explicitly.
  }
}

// Usage
try {
  const result = await withTimeout(fetchUserProfile(42), 3000);
  console.log('Got result:', result);
} catch (err) {
  if (err.message.includes('timed out')) {
    console.error('Timeout — falling back to cache');
  } else {
    throw err;
  }
}

// Cancellable version: clears the timer on success to prevent dangling handles
async function withCleanTimeout(promise, ms) {
  let timerId;
  const timer = new Promise((_, reject) => {
    timerId = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(`Timed out after ${ms}ms`)), ms);
  });
  try {
    return await Promise.race([promise, timer]);
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timerId); // always clear — whether we won or the timer won
  }
}
```

**When to use:** simple fire-and-forget timeouts, third-party APIs that don't accept `AbortSignal`, or testing utilities that must fail fast. **When NOT to use:** operations that are expensive to abandon (HTTP connections, DB transactions) — use `AbortController` so the underlying operation is actually cancelled, not just ignored. Alternative: `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` (available in modern runtimes) wires cancellation all the way through. [official]

---

### Pattern 9 — `scheduler.yield()` for Non-Blocking Long Tasks (Baseline April 2025)

`scheduler.yield()` yields execution back to the browser (or Node.js event loop) for one turn, then resumes. Unlike `setTimeout(fn, 0)`, it uses a high-priority task that resumes as soon as the event loop is free — reducing input latency while allowing chunked work to complete faster than macrotask-based yielding.

```javascript
// Process a large dataset without blocking the main thread
async function processItems(items, processOne) {
  const CHUNK_SIZE = 100;

  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    processOne(items[i]);

    // Yield every CHUNK_SIZE items to keep the UI responsive
    if (i % CHUNK_SIZE === 0 && i > 0) {
      await scheduler.yield(); // returns to event loop, then resumes
    }
  }
}

// With priority hint: 'user-blocking' | 'user-visible' | 'background'
async function indexSearchItems(items) {
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    indexItem(items[i]);

    if (i % 50 === 0) {
      // 'background' means lower priority — user interactions preempt this work
      await scheduler.yield({ priority: 'background' });
    }
  }
}

// Measuring yield effect: long task checker
async function longTaskExample() {
  const start = performance.now();

  for (let i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
    expensiveComputation(i);

    if (i % 1000 === 0) {
      await scheduler.yield();
    }
  }

  console.log(`Completed in ${(performance.now() - start).toFixed(0)}ms`);
}

// Polyfill for Node.js / environments without scheduler.yield:
globalThis.scheduler ??= {
  yield: (options) => new Promise(resolve =>
    options?.priority === 'background'
      ? setImmediate(resolve)
      : setTimeout(resolve, 0)
  ),
};
```

**When to use:** long-running synchronous processing (sorting large arrays, building search indexes, rendering complex data structures) that would otherwise block user input or degrade INP (Interaction to Next Paint). **When NOT to use:** I/O-bound work (already yields via `await`), or code running in Web Workers (can block without affecting the main thread). Alternatives: `setTimeout(fn, 0)` (lower priority, varies by environment), chunked `requestIdleCallback` (no task priority, browser only). [official]

---

### Pattern 10 — `EventSource` / Server-Sent Events Testing

`EventSource` enables server push over a persistent HTTP connection. Testing SSE requires simulating a streaming response in unit tests and asserting on received events, which needs either a real HTTP server or a `ReadableStream`-based mock.

```javascript
import { createServer } from 'node:http';
import { describe, it, before, after } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

// Helper: collect N events from an EventSource, then close
function collectEvents(url, count, eventType = 'message') {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const es = new EventSource(url);
    const events = [];
    es.addEventListener(eventType, (e) => {
      events.push(JSON.parse(e.data));
      if (events.length >= count) {
        es.close();
        resolve(events);
      }
    });
    es.onerror = (err) => { es.close(); reject(err); };
  });
}

describe('SSE endpoint', () => {
  let server;
  let port;

  before(async () => {
    server = createServer((req, res) => {
      if (req.url !== '/events') { res.end(); return; }
      res.writeHead(200, {
        'Content-Type':  'text/event-stream',
        'Cache-Control': 'no-cache',
        Connection:      'keep-alive',
      });

      let n = 0;
      const interval = setInterval(() => {
        res.write(`data: ${JSON.stringify({ seq: ++n, ts: Date.now() })}\n\n`);
        if (n >= 3) { clearInterval(interval); res.end(); }
      }, 10);

      req.on('close', () => clearInterval(interval));
    });
    await new Promise(resolve => server.listen(0, resolve));
    port = server.address().port;
  });

  after(() => new Promise(resolve => server.close(resolve)));

  it('receives 3 sequential events with increasing seq', async () => {
    const events = await collectEvents(`http://localhost:${port}/events`, 3);
    assert.equal(events.length, 3);
    assert.equal(events[0].seq, 1);
    assert.equal(events[1].seq, 2);
    assert.equal(events[2].seq, 3);
  });
});
```

**When to use:** testing streaming APIs (live feed, progress notifications, real-time dashboards) that use SSE. **When NOT to use:** WebSocket-based real-time communication (use `ws` test helpers instead) or scenarios where you need bidirectional communication. Alternative: mock the global `EventSource` class with a `ReadableStream`-backed stub for pure unit tests without a network dependency. [community]

---

### Pattern 11 — Package `exports` Conditional Resolution for Test Mocking

The `package.json` `"exports"` field supports a `"development"` or `"test"` export condition that bundlers and Node.js can use to load a mock-friendly or instrumented version during test runs, without patching the module system at test time.

```javascript
// package.json — dual exports: production vs test-friendly
// {
//   "name": "my-lib",
//   "exports": {
//     ".": {
//       "test":    "./src/index.test-shim.js",  // test build: injectable deps
//       "default": "./dist/index.js"             // production: optimised bundle
//     }
//   }
// }

// src/index.test-shim.js — exports a factory-style API for test injection
export function createClient({ fetch: _fetch = globalThis.fetch } = {}) {
  return {
    async getUser(id) {
      const res = await _fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
      return res.json();
    },
  };
}
export default createClient();

// src/index.js — production: uses fetch directly (zero overhead)
export default {
  async getUser(id) {
    const res = await globalThis.fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
    return res.json();
  },
};

// vitest.config.ts — activate the 'test' condition
// export default defineConfig({
//   resolve: { conditions: ['test', 'import', 'default'] }
// });

// In tests: the test shim is loaded automatically
import { createClient } from 'my-lib';

const mockFetch = async (url) => ({
  json: async () => ({ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }),
});
const client = createClient({ fetch: mockFetch });
const user = await client.getUser(1);
assert.equal(user.name, 'Alice'); // no real network call
```

**When to use:** library packages where you want to offer a test-friendly API surface without shipping test utilities in the production bundle. **When NOT to use:** application code (use factory functions with DI instead — simpler and doesn't require build configuration). Alternatives: `vi.mock()` / `t.mock.module()`, or manual factory injection. [community]

---

### Pattern 12 — Immutable Data with `Object.freeze` and `structuredClone`

`Object.freeze` creates a shallow-immutable object; combining it with recursive freezing produces deep immutability for fixed configuration, default values, and test constants. This prevents accidental mutation from any code path.

```javascript
// Deep freeze utility (recursive)
function deepFreeze(obj) {
  Object.getOwnPropertyNames(obj).forEach(name => {
    const value = obj[name];
    if (value && typeof value === 'object') {
      deepFreeze(value);
    }
  });
  return Object.freeze(obj);
}

// Application defaults — never mutated, shared across tests
const DEFAULT_CONFIG = deepFreeze({
  server: {
    host:    'localhost',
    port:    3000,
    timeout: 5000,
  },
  database: {
    pool:   { min: 2, max: 10 },
    ssl:    false,
  },
  features: ['auth', 'logging'],
});

// Test-time override: structuredClone unfreezes a deep copy for mutation
function buildTestConfig(overrides = {}) {
  const base = structuredClone(DEFAULT_CONFIG); // deep copy, not frozen
  return deepMerge(base, overrides);            // caller can mutate the result
}

function deepMerge(target, source) {
  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(source)) {
    if (value && typeof value === 'object' && !Array.isArray(value)) {
      target[key] ??= {};
      deepMerge(target[key], value);
    } else {
      target[key] = value;
    }
  }
  return target;
}

// Usage
const testConfig = buildTestConfig({ server: { port: 4000 }, database: { ssl: true } });
// testConfig.server.port === 4000, DEFAULT_CONFIG.server.port still === 3000
```

**When to use:** shared test fixtures, application defaults, configuration constants that must be inviolable. **When NOT to use:** data that must be serialized across workers or processes (`Object.freeze` does not survive `structuredClone` — the clone is mutable). Alternative: TypeScript `as const` assertions for compile-time immutability; `Immutable.js` for deeply immutable mutable-interface data structures. [official]

---

### Pattern 13 — `AsyncGenerator` Backpressure with a Bounded Buffer

An async generator that produces items faster than the consumer can process them wastes memory buffering unconsumed values. A bounded channel — a queue with a maximum size that blocks the producer when full — implements backpressure at the application level without relying on the Web Streams API.

```javascript
// Bounded async channel: producer blocks if buffer is full
function createChannel(capacity = 10) {
  const queue   = [];
  let done      = false;

  // Semaphore-like coordination via promise chains
  let resolveConsumer;
  let resolveProducer;

  const consumerReady = () => new Promise(r => { resolveConsumer = r; });
  const producerReady = () => new Promise(r => { resolveProducer = r; });

  return {
    async push(value) {
      while (queue.length >= capacity) {
        await producerReady(); // wait until consumer takes an item
      }
      queue.push(value);
      resolveConsumer?.();   // wake a blocked consumer
    },
    close() {
      done = true;
      resolveConsumer?.();  // wake any blocked consumer
    },
    async *[Symbol.asyncIterator]() {
      while (true) {
        while (queue.length === 0) {
          if (done) return;
          await consumerReady(); // wait until producer pushes an item
        }
        yield queue.shift();
        resolveProducer?.(); // wake a blocked producer
      }
    },
  };
}

// Usage: producer and consumer at different speeds
const ch = createChannel(5); // buffer up to 5 items

// Producer — runs independently
(async () => {
  for (let i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
    await ch.push(i);          // blocks when buffer is full
  }
  ch.close();
})();

// Consumer — processes one item at a time
let total = 0;
for await (const item of ch) {
  total += item;
  await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 10)); // simulate slow consumer
}
console.log('Sum:', total); // 190
```

**When to use:** producer/consumer pipelines where the producer can outpace the consumer (message queues, streaming ingestion, crawlers). **When NOT to use:** simple one-shot data transformation — use `Array.from` or `Iterator.map` without backpressure. Alternative: Web Streams `ReadableStream` + `WritableStream` have built-in backpressure via `highWaterMark` and `desiredSize`. [community]

---

### Pattern 14 — Numeric Separators for Readable Constants

Numeric separators (`_`) (ES2021) can appear between digits in any numeric literal to improve readability at a glance. They have zero runtime effect — they are purely cosmetic syntax erased by the parser.

```javascript
// Financial and scientific constants benefit most
const MAX_SAFE_INTEGER = 9_007_199_254_740_991;  // matches Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER
const ONE_MILLION      = 1_000_000;
const LIGHT_SPEED_MPS  = 299_792_458;    // meters per second
const PLANCK           = 6.626_070_15e-34; // Planck constant (J·Hz⁻¹)

// Binary, octal, hex — separators allowed here too
const IPv4_LOOPBACK  = 0x7F_00_00_01;   // 127.0.0.1 in hex
const PERMISSIONS    = 0o755;            // no separator needed — too short
const BITMASK        = 0b1111_0000_1111_0000;

// BigInt literals
const TWITTER_EPOCH = 1_288_834_974_657n; // Twitter snowflake epoch in BigInt

// Configuration thresholds — scannable at a glance
const config = {
  maxRequestBodyBytes: 5_242_880,    // 5 MB
  sessionTimeoutMs:    30_000,       // 30 seconds
  rateLimitPerHour:    10_000,
  cacheTtlMs:          86_400_000,   // 24 hours
  maxRetries:          3,            // too small to need separators
};

// Testing: use separators in expected-value literals for clarity
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
const bytes = readFile('./data.bin');
assert.equal(bytes.length, 1_048_576); // immediately readable as 1 MiB
```

**When to use:** any numeric constant with 5+ digits, especially time durations in milliseconds, byte sizes, financial amounts, and bitmasks. **When NOT to use:** numbers with fewer than 5 digits (no readability gain) or in contexts where you need to `eval()` the string representation (separators are preserved in `toString()` only for BigInt, not `Number`). Alternatives: named constants (`const ONE_MB = 1048576`) provide even more clarity for domain-specific values. [official]

### Pattern 15 — `AsyncContext.Variable` — Structured Async Context Propagation (TC39 Stage 2.7)

`AsyncContext.Variable` is the TC39 proposal that generalises `AsyncLocalStorage` into a cross-platform primitive (browser + Node.js). It stores a value for the current async execution context and automatically propagates it through `await`, `setTimeout`, `Promise.then`, and event callbacks — without threading a context parameter through every call.

```javascript
// Note: AsyncContext is Stage 2.7 (2026). Use a polyfill or AsyncLocalStorage today.
// Polyfill: import { AsyncContext } from 'async-context-polyfill';
// OR: map AsyncContext.Variable → AsyncLocalStorage for Node.js environments.

const { Variable } = AsyncContext; // or polyfill

// Create a typed context variable with an optional default value
const requestId = new Variable({ name: 'requestId', defaultValue: 'unknown' });
const userId    = new Variable({ name: 'userId',    defaultValue: null });

// Set context for a specific execution tree
async function handleRequest(req) {
  return requestId.run(crypto.randomUUID(), async () => {
    return userId.run(req.headers['x-user-id'] ?? null, async () => {
      return processRequest(req);
    });
  });
}

// Deep in the call tree — no context parameter needed
async function logQuery(sql) {
  console.log({
    requestId: requestId.get(), // propagated automatically
    userId:    userId.get(),    // propagated automatically
    sql,
  });
}

async function processRequest(req) {
  await logQuery(`SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = ${userId.get()}`);
  return { status: 200, requestId: requestId.get() };
}

// AsyncContext.Variable vs AsyncLocalStorage comparison:
// | Feature              | AsyncLocalStorage | AsyncContext.Variable |
// |----------------------|-------------------|-----------------------|
// | Platform             | Node.js only      | Node.js + Browser     |
// | API                  | run(val, fn)      | variable.run(val, fn) |
// | Default value        | Node.js 24+       | Built-in              |
// | Browser support      | ❌                | Pending Stage 4       |
// | Polyfill available   | N/A               | ✅ async-context-polyfill |
```

**When to use:** request tracing, user identity propagation, feature flags, and any cross-cutting concern that must flow through async code without prop drilling. **When NOT to use:** data that must be serializable across process boundaries (use message passing instead), or simple single-request handlers where passing a parameter is clearer. Alternatives: `AsyncLocalStorage` (Node.js stable, today), OpenTelemetry context propagation (higher-level). [community]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 29

**130.** `structuredClone` silently drops functions and Proxy handlers. [community] WHY: the Structured Clone Algorithm is defined to throw a `DataCloneError` for functions (`() => {}`), `Symbol` values, DOM nodes, and Proxy-wrapped objects. This means cloning an object that contains a method (not on the prototype but as an own property — e.g., `{ onClick: () => {} }`) throws at runtime, not at definition time. Fix: only clone plain data objects; keep methods on class prototypes (not as own properties), and test your fixtures with `structuredClone` in CI to surface failures early.

**131.** `Promise.race` does NOT cancel the losing promise. [community] WHY: `Promise.race([slowOp, timeout(3000)])` resolves with the timeout after 3 seconds, but `slowOp` continues running in the background — consuming CPU, network connections, or database resources — until it eventually completes or the process exits. Fix: pair `Promise.race` with `AbortController` signal propagation so the slow operation actually stops when the timeout fires; or use `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` which wires the cancellation signal automatically.

**132.** `scheduler.yield()` is not available in Node.js without a polyfill. [community] WHY: `scheduler.yield()` is a browser API (`Scheduler` interface, `window.scheduler`). Node.js does not expose `globalThis.scheduler` natively. WHY it causes problems: code written for browser use cases (chunked rendering, non-blocking indexing) fails with `ReferenceError: scheduler is not defined` when run in Node.js. Fix: polyfill with `globalThis.scheduler ??= { yield: () => new Promise(r => setImmediate(r)) }` in Node.js entrypoints, or gate behind `typeof scheduler !== 'undefined'`.

**133.** Deep-freezing objects with getters may throw. [community] WHY: `deepFreeze` iterates `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` and attempts to freeze the value of each property. If a getter throws during access (e.g., a computed property that reads from an external source), or if the property is non-writable and non-configurable (already frozen), the freeze traversal throws unexpectedly. Fix: wrap property access in `deepFreeze` with `try/catch`; skip properties where `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor` shows `get` without `value`; only freeze pure data objects with no accessor properties.

**134.** `EventSource` `onerror` fires on server close, not just on actual errors. [community] WHY: when the server closes the SSE connection normally (end of stream), the browser fires the `error` event on the `EventSource` because the underlying HTTP connection terminated — it does not distinguish "server intentionally closed" from "network failure". The `EventSource` then automatically attempts to reconnect. WHY it causes problems: test code that registers `onerror → reject(err)` will reject a promise even after receiving all expected events, if the server closes the connection cleanly. Fix: always `close()` the `EventSource` before the server ends the response in test scenarios; or resolve the promise in the last event handler rather than tracking server close separately.

**135.** `AsyncContext.Variable.run(value, fn)` does not propagate the context into synchronous callbacks scheduled before `run()` returns. [community] WHY: `AsyncContext` propagates context into the async continuation of `fn` — any code awaited or scheduled during the `run()` call tree inherits the context. However, synchronous code that was already scheduled (e.g., a `setImmediate` registered before `run()` was called) does not inherit the context and sees the default value instead. WHY it causes problems: middleware that sets a request context and then delegates to legacy synchronous event handlers may find the context unavailable in those handlers. Fix: always call `run()` before scheduling any callbacks that need the context; refactor legacy synchronous handlers to be called from within the `run()` closure.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 29 Additions

| Anti-pattern | Why it's harmful | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| `structuredClone({ method() {} })` | `DataCloneError` — functions are not cloneable | Keep methods on class prototypes; only clone plain data |
| `Promise.race([slowOp, timeout(ms)])` without AbortController | `slowOp` continues running after timeout; leaks resources | Pair with `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` to actually cancel the slow operation |
| `scheduler.yield()` in Node.js without a polyfill | `ReferenceError: scheduler is not defined` | Polyfill via `globalThis.scheduler ??= { yield: () => new Promise(r => setImmediate(r)) }` |
| `deepFreeze` on objects with accessor properties (getters) | Getter access during traversal may throw | Only deep-freeze plain data objects; skip properties without `value` descriptors |
| `EventSource` `onerror` used as stream-end signal | Fires on clean server close, not just errors; auto-reconnects silently | Close `EventSource` in the last event handler; use `readyState` to distinguish reconnect vs. error |
| `AsyncContext.Variable` context set after callback scheduling | Pre-scheduled callbacks see default value, not the set context | Always call `run()` before scheduling callbacks that depend on the context |
| `Object.freeze` without `'use strict'` | Mutations silently succeed in sloppy mode — freeze appears to work | Run all code in strict mode (ESM or `'use strict'`); pair with TypeScript `readonly` |
| `compose(middlewares)` without error boundary | An unhandled throw in middleware skips remaining cleanup | Wrap `compose` with a top-level `try/catch`; surface errors to a central error handler |
| Typed event emitter with `string` fallback event name | Loses type safety for unconstrained events | Use `string & keyof EventMap` constraint; disallow unregistered event names at the type level |
| State machine `Map` key collisions across state names | `'green:timer'` and `'greenery:timer'` produce the same key prefix | Use a tuple key format: `JSON.stringify([state, event])` or a nested Map |

## Cycle 31 — 2026-05-14

### 1. `Math.sumPrecise` — Exact Floating-Point Summation (ES2026) [official]

`Math.sumPrecise(iterable)` sums all values in any iterable using the Shewchuk compensated-summation algorithm, eliminating the floating-point rounding errors that accumulate with a naive `reduce`. It is especially important for financial calculations, statistics, and any summation where order-of-magnitude differences between addends exist.

```javascript
// Problem: naive reduce accumulates floating-point error
const values = [1, 1e100, 1, -1e100];
values.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); // 0 — wrong! should be 2

// Math.sumPrecise — exact result regardless of input order
Math.sumPrecise([1, 1e100, 1, -1e100]);  // 2 — correct

// Practical: sum a column of invoice line totals
const lineItems = [19.99, 5.00, 0.01, 14.99, 0.01];
const total = Math.sumPrecise(lineItems);  // 40.00 — exact

// Works with any iterable: generator, Set, Map.values(), etc.
function* prices() { yield 1.1; yield 2.2; yield 3.3; }
Math.sumPrecise(prices());  // 6.6 — not 6.6000000000000005

// TypeError on non-numeric input (unlike reduce which coerces silently)
// Math.sumPrecise(['1', '2']); // TypeError: not a number
// Ensure values are cast to Number() before passing:
const parsed = formValues.map(Number);
const safeTotal = Math.sumPrecise(parsed);
```

**When to use:** any summation involving decimals, currency, statistical aggregations, or mixed-magnitude numbers where rounding errors matter.

**When NOT to use:** summing small arrays of same-magnitude integers where `reduce` is fine; when you explicitly need the same rounding as a naive sum for back-compat with legacy output.

**Alternative:** `reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)` — fast and sufficient for integers or when precision loss is acceptable; Kahan summation (manual implementation) — same algorithm but no standard API.

---

### 2. `AsyncContext` — Implicit Async Request Context (Stage 3) [community]

`AsyncContext` (TC39 Stage 3) propagates implicit contextual values (request ID, user, locale) through the entire async call graph without threading them manually through every function signature. Unlike `cls-hooked` or `AsyncLocalStorage`, it is a first-class language feature with no patching.

```javascript
// Define a context variable — one instance per concern
const requestContext = new AsyncContext.Variable({
  name: 'requestContext',
  defaultValue: null,
});

// Middleware: set context before handling the request
async function requestMiddleware(req, res, next) {
  const ctx = { requestId: crypto.randomUUID(), userId: req.user?.id };
  // All async code called within this run() inherits ctx
  await requestContext.run(ctx, () => next());
}

// Deep in the call graph — no ctx parameter needed
async function saveAuditLog(action) {
  const ctx = requestContext.get(); // always the right request's context
  await db.insert({
    action,
    requestId: ctx?.requestId,
    userId:    ctx?.userId,
    timestamp: Date.now(),
  });
}

// Works across awaits, nested Promises, and event callbacks
async function processOrder(order) {
  await validateOrder(order);          // inherits context
  await chargePayment(order);          // inherits context
  await Promise.all([
    saveAuditLog('payment_charged'),   // still inherits context
    updateInventory(order),            // still inherits context
  ]);
}
```

**When to use:** distributed tracing, per-request logging, locale propagation, multi-tenant SaaS apps where every deep-layer call needs request identity without parameter drilling.

**When NOT to use:** simple single-request scripts with no concurrency; when context pollution between requests (if `run()` boundaries are wrong) would be a security concern — test boundary isolation thoroughly.

**Alternative:** `AsyncLocalStorage` (Node.js built-in) — production-ready today; passes context through async operations similarly but is Node-only and uses a different `store.run()` API.

---

### 3. `Error.isError()` — Cross-Realm Error Detection (ES2026) [official]

`Error.isError(value)` returns `true` only for genuine `Error` instances — it works across iframe/realm boundaries and rejects prototype-faked objects, unlike `instanceof Error` which fails for both cross-realm errors and spoofed objects.

```javascript
// instanceof fails cross-realm
const iframeError = new iframeWindow.Error('remote error');
iframeError instanceof Error;     // false — different Error constructor
Error.isError(iframeError);       // true — checks internal slot, not prototype

// instanceof can be spoofed; Error.isError cannot
const fake = { __proto__: Error.prototype, message: 'I look like an Error' };
fake instanceof Error;            // true — prototype chain matches
Error.isError(fake);              // false — missing internal [[ErrorData]] slot

// Practical: normalise values caught in catch blocks
function toError(value) {
  if (Error.isError(value)) return value;
  if (typeof value === 'string') return new Error(value);
  return new Error(String(value), { cause: value });
}

// Practical: safe error reporting across postMessage / Worker boundaries
worker.addEventListener('message', ({ data }) => {
  if (data.type === 'error') {
    const err = toError(data.payload);
    logger.error('Worker error', { message: err.message, stack: err.stack });
  }
});

// Polyfill check pattern
const isError = typeof Error.isError === 'function'
  ? Error.isError
  : (v) => v instanceof Error;
```

**When to use:** error normalisation utilities; error reporting middleware; library code that must handle thrown values from untrusted or cross-realm sources.

**When NOT to use:** same-realm code where `instanceof Error` is known to be sufficient; when you need the full subtype (`instanceof TypeError`) — use `instanceof` for that.

**Alternative:** `instanceof Error` — sufficient in same-realm, same-realm-only code; `Object.prototype.toString.call(v) === '[object Error]'` — unreliable, easily faked.

---

### 4. `Float16Array` and `Math.f16round` — Half-Precision Numerics (ES2025 / Baseline April 2025) [official]

`Float16Array` provides 16-bit IEEE 754 floating-point storage: half the memory of `Float32Array`, at the cost of reduced precision (3 significant decimal digits). It is the native array type for WebGPU workloads, ML model weights, and storage-optimised sensor data.

```javascript
// Float16Array — 2 bytes per element vs 4 for Float32Array
const weights = new Float16Array(1024);
weights[0] = 0.5;
weights[1] = 1.234;
console.log(weights.BYTES_PER_ELEMENT); // 2

// Memory comparison for a 1M-element tensor
const fp32 = new Float32Array(1_000_000); // 4 MB
const fp16 = new Float16Array(1_000_000); // 2 MB — 50% smaller

// Math.f16round — round a Number to the nearest representable float16 value
Math.f16round(3.14159);  // 3.140625 — nearest float16
Math.f16round(65504);    // 65504 — max representable float16 value
Math.f16round(65505);    // Infinity — overflows float16 range

// DataView for explicit byte-order control
const buf  = new ArrayBuffer(4);
const view = new DataView(buf);
view.setFloat16(0, 3.14);
view.setFloat16(2, 1.0, true);    // little-endian
console.log(view.getFloat16(0));  // ~3.14 (float16 precision)

// WebGPU pattern — send fp16 weights to GPU
async function uploadWeights(modelWeights) {
  const fp16Weights = new Float16Array(modelWeights.map(Math.f16round));
  const buffer = device.createBuffer({
    size: fp16Weights.byteLength,
    usage: GPUBufferUsage.STORAGE | GPUBufferUsage.COPY_DST,
  });
  device.queue.writeBuffer(buffer, 0, fp16Weights);
  return buffer;
}
```

**When to use:** WebGPU / WebGL compute shaders; ML inference where model weights are already quantised to fp16; bandwidth-limited streaming of numeric data; sensor arrays where precision is bounded by hardware.

**When NOT to use:** financial or scientific computations requiring more than 3 significant digits; accumulating many small additions (catastrophic cancellation); general-purpose arrays where `Float32Array` precision is expected.

**Alternative:** `Float32Array` — double the memory, much wider precision; `Uint16Array` — same size but for 16-bit unsigned integers, not IEEE 754 floats.

---

### 5. `Uint8Array.prototype.toBase64` / `setFromBase64` — Native Base64 (ES2025) [official]

ES2025 adds built-in base64 and hex encoding/decoding methods directly on `Uint8Array`, eliminating the need for `atob`/`btoa` hacks, Node.js `Buffer` workarounds, and npm packages like `base64-js`.

```javascript
// Encode binary data to base64 string
const bytes = new Uint8Array([72, 101, 108, 108, 111]); // "Hello"
const b64 = bytes.toBase64();         // "SGVsbG8="
const urlSafe = bytes.toBase64({ alphabet: 'base64url' }); // URL-safe, no + or /
const noPad = bytes.toBase64({ omitPadding: true });        // "SGVsbG8"

// Decode base64 string back to Uint8Array
const decoded = Uint8Array.fromBase64('SGVsbG8=');
new TextDecoder().decode(decoded);    // "Hello"

// setFromBase64 — decode into an existing buffer (avoids allocation)
const target = new Uint8Array(1024);
const { read, written } = target.setFromBase64('SGVsbG8=');
// read = 8 (chars consumed), written = 5 (bytes written)

// Hex encoding/decoding
const hex = bytes.toHex();            // "48656c6c6f"
const fromHex = Uint8Array.fromHex('48656c6c6f');

// Practical: encode a crypto key for storage
const cryptoKey = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32));
const storedKey = cryptoKey.toBase64({ alphabet: 'base64url', omitPadding: true });
localStorage.setItem('apiKey', storedKey);

// Restore from storage
const restored = Uint8Array.fromBase64(
  localStorage.getItem('apiKey'),
  { alphabet: 'base64url', lastChunkHandling: 'loose' },
);
```

**When to use:** encoding binary data (crypto keys, file buffers, image bytes) for JSON storage, URL parameters, or HTTP headers; replacing `btoa(String.fromCharCode(...bytes))` anti-pattern.

**When NOT to use:** encoding plain strings — use `TextEncoder` + `toBase64` together; when targeting environments prior to 2025 without a polyfill.

**Alternative:** `btoa` / `atob` — browser-only, only handles binary strings (not `Uint8Array` directly); Node.js `Buffer.from(bytes).toString('base64')` — Node-only.

---

### 6. `Object.groupBy` vs `Map.groupBy` — Correct Grouping Semantics (ES2024) [official]

ES2024 shipped `Object.groupBy` and `Map.groupBy` as static methods. Knowing when each is correct prevents subtle bugs from key coercion and prototype pollution.

```javascript
const inventory = [
  { name: 'apple',  type: 'fruit',  qty: 10 },
  { name: 'carrot', type: 'veggie', qty: 5  },
  { name: 'banana', type: 'fruit',  qty: 7  },
  { name: 'pea',    type: 'veggie', qty: 20 },
];

// Object.groupBy — keys become string properties on a null-prototype object
const byType = Object.groupBy(inventory, item => item.type);
// { fruit: [apple, banana], veggie: [carrot, pea] }
byType.fruit.length;   // 2
// Result has Object.create(null) prototype — safe from __proto__ pollution

// Map.groupBy — keys can be ANY value, not just strings
const byRef = Map.groupBy(inventory, item => item.qty > 8 ? 'high' : 'low');
byRef.get('high');  // [{ name: 'apple', ... }]
byRef.get('low');   // [carrot, banana, pea]

// Map.groupBy with object keys (impossible with Object.groupBy)
const lowBucket  = { level: 'low',  min: 0 };
const highBucket = { level: 'high', min: 9 };
const buckets = Map.groupBy(inventory, item =>
  item.qty > 8 ? highBucket : lowBucket
);
buckets.get(highBucket); // [{ name: 'apple', qty: 10 }]

// Practical: group API results by HTTP status class
async function groupByStatusClass(requests) {
  const results = await Promise.allSettled(
    requests.map(url => fetch(url).then(r => ({ url, status: r.status })))
  );
  const settled = results.map(r => r.value ?? { url: '?', status: 0 });
  return Object.groupBy(settled, ({ status }) => `${Math.floor(status / 100)}xx`);
}
// { '2xx': [...], '4xx': [...], '5xx': [...] }
```

**When to use:** `Object.groupBy` when grouped keys are strings and you want a plain object result; `Map.groupBy` when keys may be objects, symbols, or non-string values.

**When NOT to use:** grouping mutable objects and then mutating the groups (the arrays hold references, not copies); on very large arrays where a single-pass manual `reduce` is faster.

**Alternative:** `reduce` with a `Map` accumulator — the pre-ES2024 idiom; lodash `_.groupBy` — still useful in mixed environments.

---

### 7. `structuredClone` Limitations and Safe Alternatives [community]

`structuredClone` is the correct deep-clone API for most use cases, but it has hard limits: it throws on functions, Proxy-wrapped objects, DOM nodes, and Symbol values. Knowing the boundaries prevents runtime surprises.

```javascript
// structuredClone works for: plain objects, arrays, Date, Map, Set,
// RegExp, ArrayBuffer, TypedArrays, Error, BigInt, boolean/string/number wrappers
const original = {
  date: new Date(),
  map:  new Map([['key', 1]]),
  set:  new Set([1, 2, 3]),
  arr:  new Int32Array([10, 20, 30]),
};
const clone = structuredClone(original); // deep clone preserving types
clone.map.set('key', 99); // original.map unchanged

// THROWS — functions as own properties
// structuredClone({ fn: () => {} }); // DataCloneError

// THROWS — Proxy-wrapped objects
// structuredClone(new Proxy({}, {})); // DataCloneError

// Safe fallback for plain config objects (no special types)
function safeClone(obj) {
  try {
    return structuredClone(obj);
  } catch {
    // Fall back to JSON for plain serialisable data only
    return JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj));
  }
}

// Transferable clone — move ownership instead of copying (zero-copy)
const buffer = new ArrayBuffer(1024 * 1024);
const transferred = structuredClone(buffer, { transfer: [buffer] });
// buffer.byteLength === 0 — detached; transferred is the live copy

// When JSON round-trip is better: config objects with no special types
const config = { host: 'localhost', port: 3000, debug: false };
const configCopy = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(config)); // fine and faster
```

**When to use:** cloning state that contains `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, typed arrays, or `Error` objects where JSON would corrupt or lose the types.

**When NOT to use:** objects that contain methods as own properties; Proxy-wrapped reactive state (use the framework's clone utility); simple config objects with no special types (JSON is faster).

**Alternative:** `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` — fast, zero-dependency, but loses `Date`/`Map`/`Set`/`undefined`; `lodash.cloneDeep` — handles functions (copies references), class instances.

### 8. Declarative Shadow DOM — Server-Side Web Components [official]

Declarative Shadow DOM (DSD) allows Shadow DOM to be rendered in static HTML, enabling server-side rendering of web components without JavaScript. The browser parses `<template shadowrootmode="open">` and attaches the shadow root before any script runs.

```javascript
// HTML (server-rendered) — shadow DOM declared inline, no JS needed for paint
// <my-card>
//   <template shadowrootmode="open">
//     <style>:host { display:block; border:1px solid #ccc; padding:1rem; }</style>
//     <slot></slot>
//   </template>
//   <p>Light DOM content slotted in</p>
// </my-card>

// Client-side component that supports both DSD (SSR) and JS-only init
class MyCard extends HTMLElement {
  constructor() {
    super();
    // If DSD already created the shadow root, don't overwrite it
    if (!this.shadowRoot) {
      this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
      this.shadowRoot.innerHTML = `
        <style>:host { display:block; border:1px solid #ccc; padding:1rem; }</style>
        <slot></slot>
      `;
    }
  }

  connectedCallback() {
    this.shadowRoot.querySelector('slot')
      ?.addEventListener('slotchange', () => this.#updateLabel());
  }

  #updateLabel() {
    this.setAttribute('aria-label', this.textContent.trim().slice(0, 50));
  }
}

customElements.define('my-card', MyCard);

// Polyfill for browsers without DSD support (Firefox < 123)
function upgradeDeclarativeShadowDOM(root) {
  root.querySelectorAll('template[shadowrootmode]').forEach(tmpl => {
    const mode = tmpl.getAttribute('shadowrootmode');
    const shadow = tmpl.parentElement.attachShadow({ mode });
    shadow.appendChild(tmpl.content);
    tmpl.remove();
  });
}
upgradeDeclarativeShadowDOM(document);
```

**When to use:** SSR-rendered web components that must paint before JavaScript loads; design systems distributed as plain HTML + web components; progressive enhancement where the component must work without JS.

**When NOT to use:** fully dynamic components where server HTML is unavailable; targeting browsers without DSD that cannot be polyfilled; complex hierarchies where SSR adds excessive HTML weight.

**Alternative:** Custom elements without Shadow DOM (light DOM) — simpler, inherits page styles; React/Vue/Svelte server components — richer framework support for SSR.

---

### 9. `navigator.clipboard` — Modern Async Clipboard API [official]

The modern Clipboard API (`navigator.clipboard.writeText`, `.write`, `.readText`, `.read`) is async, permission-gated, and supports rich content (HTML, images). It replaces the deprecated `document.execCommand('copy')`.

```javascript
// Write plain text to clipboard
async function copyToClipboard(text) {
  try {
    await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text);
    return true;
  } catch (err) {
    // Fails if: no user gesture, page not focused, or permission denied
    console.error('Clipboard write failed:', err.name, err.message);
    return false;
  }
}

// Write rich content: HTML + plain text fallback
async function copyRichText(html, plain) {
  const htmlBlob  = new Blob([html],  { type: 'text/html'  });
  const textBlob  = new Blob([plain], { type: 'text/plain' });
  await navigator.clipboard.write([
    new ClipboardItem({ 'text/html': htmlBlob, 'text/plain': textBlob }),
  ]);
}

// Copy an image to clipboard
async function copyImage(imageUrl) {
  const response = await fetch(imageUrl);
  const blob     = await response.blob();
  await navigator.clipboard.write([
    new ClipboardItem({ [blob.type]: blob }),
  ]);
}

// Graceful fallback for older browsers
async function copyWithFallback(text) {
  if (navigator.clipboard?.writeText) {
    return navigator.clipboard.writeText(text);
  }
  // Legacy path — deprecated, may be removed by browsers
  const el = Object.assign(document.createElement('textarea'), { value: text });
  document.body.appendChild(el);
  el.select();
  document.execCommand('copy');
  document.body.removeChild(el);
}

// Read text (requires 'clipboard-read' permission prompt)
async function pasteText() {
  const permission = await navigator.permissions.query({ name: 'clipboard-read' });
  if (permission.state === 'denied') throw new Error('Clipboard read denied');
  return navigator.clipboard.readText();
}
```

**When to use:** "copy to clipboard" buttons, rich text editors, code snippet copy, image share flows.

**When NOT to use:** background clipboard reads without user interaction (rejected); in workers or non-HTTPS contexts; when writing custom clipboard formats unsupported by the API.

**Alternative:** `document.execCommand('copy')` — deprecated, synchronous, no permissions UI; clipboard.js — broad compatibility shim but adds bundle weight.

### 10. `Atomics` and `SharedArrayBuffer` — Lock-Free Cross-Thread Communication [official]

`SharedArrayBuffer` lets a single buffer be shared across threads without copying. `Atomics` provides atomic read-modify-write operations and a wait/notify mechanism for lock-free cross-thread synchronisation.

```javascript
// Shared buffer accessible from both main thread and worker
const sab  = new SharedArrayBuffer(4 * Int32Array.BYTES_PER_ELEMENT);
const view = new Int32Array(sab);

// worker.js — heavy computation reports progress atomically
self.onmessage = ({ data: { buffer, count } }) => {
  const shared = new Int32Array(buffer);
  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    Atomics.add(shared, 0, 1); // atomic increment — no torn reads/writes
  }
  Atomics.store(shared, 1, 1);   // signal completion
  Atomics.notify(shared, 1, 1);  // wake waiters on index 1
};

// Main thread — non-blocking progress polling
const worker = new Worker('./worker.js', { type: 'module' });
worker.postMessage({ buffer: sab, count: 1_000_000 });

setInterval(() => {
  console.log(`Progress: ${Atomics.load(view, 0).toLocaleString()}`);
}, 100);

// Atomics.waitAsync — non-blocking wait (ES2024) — safe on main thread
const { value } = Atomics.waitAsync(view, 1, 0); // wait until view[1] != 0
value.then(() => console.log('Worker signalled completion'));

// Note: Atomics.wait() BLOCKS the thread — never call it on the main thread
// Atomics.wait(view, 1, 0); // blocks until view[1] != 0 — ONLY safe in workers
```

**When to use:** worker thread coordination with lock-free counters, progress tracking, ring buffers for audio/video pipelines; high-frequency producer-consumer patterns where `postMessage` copy overhead is unacceptable.

**When NOT to use:** simple one-off data passing (use `postMessage` + `transfer`); when `SharedArrayBuffer` cross-origin isolation (`COOP`/`COEP` headers) is not configured; never call `Atomics.wait` on the main thread.

**Alternative:** `postMessage` with transferable `ArrayBuffer` — simpler, no shared state, sufficient for most cases; `BroadcastChannel` — for cross-tab messaging without shared memory.

---

### 11. `IntersectionObserver` — Performant Scroll-Driven Visibility [official]

`IntersectionObserver` fires callbacks when elements enter or leave the viewport (or a specified ancestor), replacing expensive `scroll` + `getBoundingClientRect()` polling with a browser-managed, off-main-thread observation.

```javascript
// Lazy-load images when they approach the viewport
function lazyLoadImages(selector = 'img[data-src]') {
  const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
    (entries, obs) => {
      entries.forEach(entry => {
        if (!entry.isIntersecting) return;
        const img = entry.target;
        img.src = img.dataset.src;
        img.removeAttribute('data-src');
        obs.unobserve(img); // stop watching once loaded
      });
    },
    { rootMargin: '200px 0px', threshold: 0 } // pre-load 200px ahead
  );
  document.querySelectorAll(selector).forEach(img => observer.observe(img));
  return () => observer.disconnect();
}

// Infinite scroll sentinel pattern
function setupInfiniteScroll(sentinel, loadMore) {
  let loading = false;
  const observer = new IntersectionObserver(async ([entry]) => {
    if (!entry.isIntersecting || loading) return;
    loading = true;
    try {
      const hasMore = await loadMore();
      if (!hasMore) observer.disconnect();
    } finally {
      loading = false;
    }
  }, { threshold: 0.1 });
  observer.observe(sentinel);
  return () => observer.disconnect();
}

// Analytics: track how long an element stays visible
function trackViewTime(element, onViewEnd) {
  let enterTime = null;
  const observer = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
      enterTime = performance.now();
    } else if (enterTime !== null) {
      onViewEnd({ duration: performance.now() - enterTime, element });
      enterTime = null;
    }
  });
  observer.observe(element);
  return () => observer.disconnect();
}
```

**When to use:** lazy-loading images/components, infinite scroll, analytics impressions, animation triggers on scroll, sticky header detection.

**When NOT to use:** precise pixel-level scroll position tracking (use throttled `scroll` event); synchronous layout reads inside the callback (defer to `requestAnimationFrame`).

**Alternative:** `scroll` event + `getBoundingClientRect()` — synchronous, blocks main thread on every frame; `ResizeObserver` — for size changes, not visibility.

---

### 12. `ResizeObserver` — Reactive Layout Measurement [official]

`ResizeObserver` fires when an element's content or border-box dimensions change, without polling or window-resize events. The `devicePixelContentBox` entry gives physical pixel dimensions for pixel-perfect canvas sizing on high-DPI displays.

```javascript
// Pixel-perfect retina canvas
function makeResponsiveCanvas(canvas, draw) {
  const observer = new ResizeObserver(entries => {
    for (const entry of entries) {
      const box = entry.devicePixelContentBox?.[0];
      if (!box) continue;
      canvas.width  = box.inlineSize;
      canvas.height = box.blockSize;
      draw(canvas.getContext('2d'), canvas.width, canvas.height);
    }
  });
  observer.observe(canvas, { box: 'device-pixel-content-box' });
  return () => observer.disconnect();
}

// Component-level responsive layout (CSS container query alternative)
function setupTextTruncation(container) {
  const observer = new ResizeObserver(([entry]) => {
    const { inlineSize } = entry.contentBoxSize[0];
    const charsPerLine = Math.floor(inlineSize / 8); // approx char width
    container.dataset.charLimit = String(charsPerLine);
    truncateText(container, charsPerLine);
  });
  observer.observe(container);
  return () => observer.disconnect();
}

// Detect sidebar collapse for content reflow
function watchSidebarWidth(sidebar, onWidthChange) {
  let lastWidth = sidebar.offsetWidth;
  const observer = new ResizeObserver(([entry]) => {
    const newWidth = Math.round(entry.contentRect.width);
    if (newWidth !== lastWidth) {
      lastWidth = newWidth;
      onWidthChange(newWidth);
    }
  });
  observer.observe(sidebar);
  return () => observer.disconnect();
}
```

**When to use:** canvas/SVG sizing for retina displays, component-level responsive design, text overflow recalculation, chart re-renders on container resize.

**When NOT to use:** detecting window resize (`window.addEventListener('resize', ...)` is simpler); visibility or scroll position detection (`IntersectionObserver` is better); writing back to element size inside the callback without debouncing (triggers loop errors).

**Alternative:** `window.resize` event — only fires on viewport change; CSS container queries — pure-CSS responsive components without JavaScript; `MutationObserver` — for DOM structure changes, not size.

---

### 13. `import.meta.resolve()` — Programmatic Module URL Resolution (ES2025) [official]

`import.meta.resolve(specifier)` resolves a module specifier (relative path, bare name, or import-map alias) to its full URL using the same algorithm as `import`, without loading the module. This enables runtime URL computation for workers, dynamic imports, and tooling.

```javascript
// Resolve a relative path to its full URL (without loading it)
const utilsURL = import.meta.resolve('./utils/format.js');
// 'file:///project/src/utils/format.js' (or https://... in browsers)

// Resolve a bare specifier through import maps
const lodashURL = import.meta.resolve('lodash-es');
// 'https://cdn.skypack.dev/lodash-es/lodash.js'

// Spawn a Worker from a correctly resolved URL
function createFormatWorker() {
  const workerURL = import.meta.resolve('./workers/format.worker.js');
  return new Worker(workerURL, { type: 'module' });
}

// Pre-resolve plugin paths before dynamic import
async function loadPlugins(names) {
  const urls = names.map(name => import.meta.resolve(`./plugins/${name}.js`));
  return Promise.all(urls.map(url => import(url)));
}

// Register a ServiceWorker with a module-relative URL
async function registerSW() {
  const swURL = import.meta.resolve('./service-worker.js');
  return navigator.serviceWorker.register(swURL, { type: 'module' });
}

// In Node.js: resolve returns a file:// URL — convert for fs operations
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
const absPath = fileURLToPath(import.meta.resolve('./data/config.json'));
```

**When to use:** spawning module workers with correct URLs; resolving import-map aliases for tooling; plugin loaders that need URLs without immediate loading; ServiceWorker registration from ESM.

**When NOT to use:** CommonJS `require.resolve()` patterns — use that directly; when you need only the directory (`import.meta.dirname` is simpler); bundled output where bundlers may not evaluate `import.meta.resolve` at build time.

**Alternative:** `new URL('./path.js', import.meta.url).href` — the pre-ES2025 idiom; works but doesn't apply import maps or resolve bare specifiers.

### 14. `node:sqlite` Built-in — Zero-Dependency SQLite in Node.js 22+ [official]

Node.js 22.5+ ships `node:sqlite` as a built-in module, providing synchronous SQLite access with zero npm dependencies. It supports prepared statements, transactions, and user-defined functions.

```javascript
import { DatabaseSync } from 'node:sqlite';

// Open/create a database (synchronous API, runs on the calling thread)
const db = new DatabaseSync(':memory:'); // in-memory, or pass a file path

// Create schema with exec (multi-statement DDL)
db.exec(`
  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (
    id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    name  TEXT NOT NULL,
    email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL
  )
`);

// Prepared statements — compiled once, reused many times
const insertUser = db.prepare('INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES (?, ?)');
const findUser   = db.prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?');
const listUsers  = db.prepare('SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY name');

insertUser.run('Alice', 'alice@example.com');
insertUser.run('Bob',   'bob@example.com');

const user  = findUser.get(1);    // { id: 1, name: 'Alice', email: '...' }
const users = listUsers.all();    // [{ id: 2, name: 'Bob', ... }, ...]

// Transactions — atomically batch multiple writes
const insertMany = db.transaction((rows) => {
  for (const row of rows) insertUser.run(row.name, row.email);
});
insertMany([
  { name: 'Carol', email: 'carol@example.com' },
  { name: 'David', email: 'david@example.com' },
]);

// User-defined scalar function
db.function('upper_name', { deterministic: true }, name => name.toUpperCase());
db.prepare('SELECT upper_name(name) AS n FROM users').all();
// [{ n: 'ALICE' }, { n: 'BOB' }, ...]

db.close();
```

**When to use:** CLI tools, test fixtures, offline-first apps, local data processing scripts, lightweight server apps where SQLite's simplicity suffices and zero npm install is valuable.

**When NOT to use:** high-concurrency write workloads (SQLite has write lock limitations); multi-process database access; Node.js < 22.5 (use `better-sqlite3`); when async I/O is required (every call blocks the event loop).

**Alternative:** `better-sqlite3` — same synchronous API, broader Node.js version support; `@libsql/client` — Turso/LibSQL for distributed SQLite.

---

### 15. CSS Custom Highlight API — JavaScript-Driven Text Highlighting [official]

The CSS Custom Highlight API highlights arbitrary text ranges in the DOM without wrapping them in `<span>` elements, preserving document structure and avoiding reflow. It is the correct approach for in-page search, annotation tools, and AI-powered document search.

```javascript
// Find all text ranges matching a search term in a subtree
function findTextRanges(searchTerm, root = document.body) {
  const ranges = [];
  const walker = document.createTreeWalker(root, NodeFilter.SHOW_TEXT);
  const lower  = searchTerm.toLowerCase();
  let node;

  while ((node = walker.nextNode())) {
    const text = node.textContent.toLowerCase();
    let start = 0, index;
    while ((index = text.indexOf(lower, start)) !== -1) {
      const range = new Range();
      range.setStart(node, index);
      range.setEnd(node, index + searchTerm.length);
      ranges.push(range);
      start = index + 1;
    }
  }
  return ranges;
}

// Register highlight (pair with CSS: ::highlight(search-results) { ... })
function applyHighlight(name, ranges) {
  CSS.highlights.set(name, new Highlight(...ranges));
}

function clearHighlight(name) {
  CSS.highlights.delete(name);
}

// Full search integration with debounce
function highlightSearch(query) {
  clearHighlight('search-results');
  if (!query.trim()) return 0;

  const ranges = findTextRanges(query);
  if (ranges.length) {
    applyHighlight('search-results', ranges);
    ranges[0].startContainer.parentElement?.scrollIntoView({ block: 'nearest' });
  }
  return ranges.length;
}

const onSearch = debounce(e => {
  const count = highlightSearch(e.target.value);
  document.getElementById('match-count').textContent = `${count} match(es)`;
}, 150);

document.getElementById('search-input').addEventListener('input', onSearch);
```

**When to use:** in-page search (Ctrl+F equivalent), annotation tools, code editors highlighting matched syntax, AI-powered document search result highlighting.

**When NOT to use:** environments without Custom Highlight API support (add `<mark>` wrapping as fallback); highlights that must persist across DOM mutations without reapplication; simple single-term highlights where `<mark>` is sufficient.

**Alternative:** wrap matches in `<mark>` elements — simpler but mutates DOM and forces reflow; `react-highlight-words` / similar — framework-specific DOM-mutation-based highlighting.

## Cycle 31 Community Gotchas

**CG31-1. `Math.sumPrecise` Rejects Non-Finite Values** [community] — `Math.sumPrecise([1, Infinity, 2])` returns `Infinity`, but `Math.sumPrecise([1, Infinity, -Infinity])` returns `NaN`, not `0`. WHY it causes problems: developers who pass unvalidated sensor data or API numbers expect compensated summation to handle edge cases gracefully — it follows IEEE 754 faithfully instead. Fix: always filter or clamp non-finite values before passing to `Math.sumPrecise`; add an assertion `values.every(Number.isFinite)` in dev mode.

**CG31-2. Declarative Shadow DOM Is Not Applied by `innerHTML` — Only by the HTML Parser** [community] — Setting `element.innerHTML = '<template shadowrootmode="open">...</template>'` does NOT create a shadow root. DSD only activates during initial HTML parsing or after an explicit `setHTMLUnsafe()` call (or the polyfill). WHY it causes problems: teams that dynamically insert server-rendered HTML via `innerHTML` during hydration find no shadow root attached, and the component renders incorrectly with styles leaking out. Fix: use `element.setHTMLUnsafe(html)` (the new safe HTML setter that triggers DSD attachment) or apply the `upgradeDeclarativeShadowDOM(root)` polyfill after every dynamic HTML insertion.

**CG31-3. `node:sqlite` `DatabaseSync` Blocks the Event Loop** [community] — Every `db.exec`, `stmt.run`, and `stmt.get` call is fully synchronous, running on the V8 main thread. WHY it causes problems: in a Node.js HTTP server, a slow SQLite query (full table scan, large aggregation) stalls all other pending requests for the duration of the query, even though SQLite is doing disk I/O. Fix: run `node:sqlite` operations inside a `worker_thread` with a request/response message protocol, or use `better-sqlite3` with a `Piscina` worker pool for concurrent request handling.

**CG31-4. `CSS.highlights` Names Are Global — Component Highlight Names Collide** [community] — `CSS.highlights` is a document-level registry: a highlight named `'selection'` set by one component overwrites any previous `'selection'` highlight set by another. WHY it causes problems: in a component-based app, two independent search widgets using the same highlight name clear each other whenever either updates — the bug only manifests when both components appear simultaneously on the page. Fix: namespace highlight names by component instance: `CSS.highlights.set(`search-${this.#instanceId}`, highlight)` and call `CSS.highlights.delete(name)` on component teardown.

**CG31-5. `import.meta.resolve()` Returns a `file://` URL — Pass It Through `fileURLToPath` Before Using With `fs`** [community] — `import.meta.resolve('./config.json')` returns `'file:///project/src/config.json'`, not `'/project/src/config.json'`. WHY it causes problems: passing the URL string directly to `fs.readFile`, `fs.createReadStream`, or `path.join` treats the `file://` prefix as part of the path, producing `ENOENT: no such file or directory 'file:///project/...'`. The error message shows the full URL, making the root cause non-obvious. Fix: always convert via `import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url'; const absPath = fileURLToPath(import.meta.resolve('./config.json'))`.

**CG31-6. `ResizeObserver` Loop Error When Writing Size Back to the Observed Element** [community] — If a `ResizeObserver` callback changes the size of the observed element (e.g., setting `canvas.width`), the browser detects a potential loop and may throw `ResizeObserver loop limit exceeded` (Chrome) or silently skip the callback (Firefox/Safari). WHY it causes problems: resizing a canvas to match device pixels inside the callback sets `canvas.width`, which changes the rendered size, triggering another observation — the browser either errors or silently drops subsequent callbacks, leaving the canvas at the wrong resolution. Fix: debounce size writes with `requestAnimationFrame`; only write size back if `newSize !== currentSize` to make the update idempotent.

**CG31-7. `Atomics.waitAsync` Is a Browser-Only API — Node.js Has It in Workers But Not All Versions** [community] — `Atomics.waitAsync` is available on the main thread in browsers (non-blocking) and in workers in Node.js 18+. However, some older Node.js 18.x patch versions only exposed it on the main thread, not in worker contexts. WHY it causes problems: worker code that uses `Atomics.waitAsync` instead of `Atomics.wait` (to avoid blocking) throws `TypeError: Atomics.waitAsync is not a function` in older worker contexts, making the worker silently crash without an obvious error message. Fix: check `typeof Atomics.waitAsync === 'function'` before use; test against your minimum supported Node.js version; use `Atomics.wait` inside workers only when you intentionally want to block.

**CG31-8. `navigator.clipboard.readText()` Requires a User-Gesture and Page Focus** [community] — `navigator.clipboard.readText()` is rejected with `NotAllowedError` if called outside a user gesture (click, keydown) OR if the page does not have focus. WHY it causes problems: automated test runners, browser extensions, and page load handlers that call `readText()` immediately or from a `setTimeout` find the call silently rejected, with no clear indication that page focus was the issue. The error message says `NotAllowedError: Read permission denied` regardless of whether focus or gesture is missing. Fix: always call clipboard read inside a direct user-interaction event handler; in tests, use `userEvent.click()` to simulate focus and gesture; gate with `document.hasFocus()` for defensive checks.

## Cycle 32 — 2026-05-14

### 16. `document.startViewTransition()` — View Transitions API [official]

The View Transitions API provides a browser-native mechanism for animating between two DOM states. `document.startViewTransition(callback)` captures the old state, calls the callback to update the DOM, captures the new state, then runs a cross-fade (or custom CSS animation) between them — all without JavaScript animation loops.

```javascript
// Basic page-to-page transition
async function navigateTo(url) {
  if (!document.startViewTransition) {
    // Fallback for unsupported browsers
    await updatePageContent(url);
    return;
  }

  const transition = document.startViewTransition(async () => {
    await updatePageContent(url);
  });

  try {
    await transition.finished;
  } catch (err) {
    // Transition was skipped (e.g., reduced-motion or navigation interrupted)
    console.warn('View transition did not complete:', err.message);
  }
}

// Named transition elements for targeted animations
function openDetailPanel(itemId) {
  const thumbnail = document.querySelector(`[data-item-id="${itemId}"] img`);
  if (thumbnail) {
    thumbnail.style.viewTransitionName = 'hero-image';
  }

  document.startViewTransition(() => {
    renderDetailView(itemId);
  });
}

// CSS that pairs with the above (view-transitions.css):
// ::view-transition-old(hero-image) { animation: none; }
// ::view-transition-new(hero-image) { animation: slide-in 300ms ease; }
```

**When to use:** SPA route transitions, list-to-detail expansions, tab switches, image gallery navigation — anywhere you want fluid visual continuity without a full animation framework.

**When NOT to use:** in Server-Side Rendered pages with full navigations (use the Navigation API + `pageswap`/`pagereveal` events for MPA transitions); when `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` is active (respect the media query and skip the transition); when the DOM update is synchronous and trivially fast (the API overhead is unjustified).

**Alternative:** CSS `transition` on individual properties — simpler but requires manual state coordination; GSAP/Framer Motion — more powerful but adds bundle weight; `Element.animate()` — imperative, lower-level, no automatic state capture.
