### 17. `scheduler.yield()` — Cooperative Main-Thread Concurrency [official]

`scheduler.yield()` is a WICG / Chrome-origin API now at Baseline Interop status that cedes control back to the browser event loop, allowing user interactions, rendering, and other pending microtasks to be processed before resuming a long-running task. It is the priority-aware successor to `await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 0))`.

```javascript
// Process a large array without blocking UI interactions
async function processLargeDataset(items) {
  const results = [];
  const CHUNK_SIZE = 50;

  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    results.push(expensiveTransform(items[i]));

    // Yield to event loop every CHUNK_SIZE items
    if (i % CHUNK_SIZE === 0 && i > 0) {
      if ('scheduler' in globalThis && typeof scheduler.yield === 'function') {
        await scheduler.yield();
      } else {
        // Polyfill: setTimeout(0) yields but loses priority inheritance
        await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 0));
      }
    }
  }

  return results;
}

// Prioritised: scheduler.yield() inherits the task's priority,
// meaning user-visible work is never preempted by background tasks
async function renderWithPriority() {
  await scheduler.postTask(async () => {
    initLayout();
    await scheduler.yield();   // Other 'user-visible' tasks can interleave here
    finaliseRender();
  }, { priority: 'user-visible' });
}
```

**When to use:** long data-processing loops (imports, parsers, formatters) that run on the main thread and would cause input latency; progressive rendering pipelines where partial results should display before the full dataset is processed.

**When NOT to use:** in Web Workers where blocking is acceptable and `scheduler.yield()` is unavailable; trivially short loops where the yield overhead exceeds the computation time; when you can move work off-main-thread entirely (always prefer a Worker if feasible).

**Alternative:** `setTimeout(fn, 0)` — universal but loses task priority; `requestIdleCallback` — only runs during idle periods, unsuitable for latency-sensitive work; Web Workers — best for truly CPU-bound tasks.

---

### 18. `WeakRef` + `FinalizationRegistry` — Observable Weak Caching [official]

`WeakRef` holds a non-owning reference to an object that the garbage collector can reclaim. `FinalizationRegistry` lets you run a cleanup callback after an object is collected. Together they enable observable caches that release entries automatically without a separate `Map` + manual `delete` lifecycle.

```javascript
class WeakCache {
  #cache = new Map();                  // key → WeakRef<value>
  #registry = new FinalizationRegistry(key => {
    // Called AFTER the value is GC'd; safe to remove the stale entry
    const ref = this.#cache.get(key);
    if (ref && ref.deref() === undefined) {
      this.#cache.delete(key);
    }
  });

  set(key, value) {
    this.#cache.set(key, new WeakRef(value));
    this.#registry.register(value, key, value); // third arg = unregister token
  }

  get(key) {
    return this.#cache.get(key)?.deref();       // undefined if GC'd
  }

  delete(key) {
    const ref = this.#cache.get(key);
    if (ref) {
      const value = ref.deref();
      if (value) this.#registry.unregister(value);
      this.#cache.delete(key);
    }
  }

  get size() { return this.#cache.size; }
}

// Usage: cache parsed DOM structures without preventing GC
const domCache = new WeakCache();
domCache.set('template-hero', document.querySelector('#hero').cloneNode(true));
const node = domCache.get('template-hero'); // undefined if GC ran
```

**When to use:** image/template/parsed-AST caches where the cached object is large and expendable; event-listener maps keyed by DOM elements; memoisation of per-instance computed values that should evaporate with the instance.

**When NOT to use:** caches where you need deterministic memory bounds (GC timing is non-deterministic — use a `Map` with explicit LRU eviction); when the referenced objects are primitives or strings (only object references can be held weakly); in hot inner loops (WeakRef deref has GC overhead).

**Alternative:** `Map` with explicit `delete` — deterministic but requires manual lifecycle management; `WeakMap` keyed on the object itself — simpler but inverts key/value relationship; `lru-cache` npm package — deterministic LRU with size limits.

---

### 19. `TypedArray.prototype.transfer()` — Zero-Copy Buffer Ownership Transfer [official]

`ArrayBuffer.prototype.transfer()` (ES2024) and `TypedArray.prototype.transfer()` create a new buffer with the same bytes, detaching the original buffer in a single operation — a memcpy-free ownership hand-off. Essential for passing buffers to Web Workers without duplicating memory.

```javascript
// Hand off a buffer to a worker without copying
function streamChunkToWorker(worker, uint8Chunk) {
  // transfer() detaches `uint8Chunk.buffer` and returns a new Uint8Array
  // backed by the transferred ArrayBuffer — zero copy
  const transferred = uint8Chunk.transfer();
  worker.postMessage({ type: 'chunk', data: transferred }, [transferred.buffer]);
  // uint8Chunk.buffer is now detached; any access throws TypeError
}

// Grow a buffer without copying (resizable ArrayBuffer + transfer)
function growBuffer(existing, newByteLength) {
  return existing.transfer(newByteLength);  // truncates or extends
}

// Safe pattern: always check byteLength before using transferred buffers
self.onmessage = function({ data }) {
  if (data.type === 'chunk') {
    if (data.data.byteLength === 0) return;           // skip empty chunks
    processChunk(data.data);
  }
};

// Detach after use to prevent accidental re-reads of stale data
function consumeAndDetach(buffer) {
  const view = new Uint8Array(buffer);
  const result = computeHash(view);
  buffer.transfer(0);   // detach by transferring to 0-length buffer
  return result;
}
```

**When to use:** Worker message passing of large audio/video/image buffers; streaming parsers that progressively hand off parsed chunks; ring-buffer implementations where ownership passes between producer and consumer.

**When NOT to use:** when you need to retain access to the original data after the transfer (use `slice()` to copy explicitly); buffers smaller than ~1 KB where the function call overhead exceeds the copy cost; when the receiving context cannot accept Transferable objects.

**Alternative:** `ArrayBuffer.prototype.slice()` — copies data, safe but O(n); `SharedArrayBuffer` — shared memory without transfer, but requires COOP/COEP headers and `Atomics` for synchronisation; `structuredClone(buf, { transfer: [buf] })` — equivalent but more verbose.

### 20. `globalThis.reportError()` — Standards-Compliant Unhandled Error Reporting [official]

`globalThis.reportError(error)` (ES2025 / WHATWG) dispatches an `ErrorEvent` on the global object exactly as if the error were unhandled — triggering `window.onerror` / `self.onerror` handlers and the `unhandledrejection`-equivalent plumbing. It is the standards-based replacement for the `throw` hack used to surface errors from deep async contexts.

```javascript
// Surface an error from a disconnected async context
function createSafeEventTarget() {
  const emitter = new EventTarget();

  emitter.addEventListener('data', async (event) => {
    try {
      await processData(event.detail);
    } catch (err) {
      // Don't swallow — report to global error monitoring
      globalThis.reportError(err);
    }
  });

  return emitter;
}

// In a Web Worker: propagate errors to the main thread's onerror handler
self.addEventListener('message', async ({ data }) => {
  try {
    const result = await heavyComputation(data);
    self.postMessage({ ok: true, result });
  } catch (err) {
    // This triggers the worker's error event on the main thread
    globalThis.reportError(err);
  }
});

// Error monitoring integration (main thread)
window.addEventListener('error', (event) => {
  if (event.error) {
    monitoring.captureException(event.error, {
      source: event.filename,
      line: event.lineno,
    });
  }
});
```

**When to use:** inside `addEventListener` callbacks, `setTimeout`/`setInterval` handlers, and Worker message handlers where you cannot propagate errors via return values; when centralising error reporting through `window.onerror` / Sentry-style handlers.

**When NOT to use:** when the caller can `await` your function and handle the rejection directly — prefer rejected Promises over side-channel reporting; do not use to surface expected/recoverable errors; avoid in tight loops (triggers full event dispatch machinery).

**Alternative:** `throw error` at the top level — works in synchronous contexts but causes `Uncaught Error` noise; `console.error` — logs but does not trigger monitoring hooks; `window.dispatchEvent(new ErrorEvent('error', ...))` — equivalent but more verbose and non-standard across environments.

---

### 21. `BroadcastChannel` — Efficient Cross-Tab / Cross-Worker Messaging [official]

`BroadcastChannel` provides a named message bus shared across all browsing contexts (tabs, iframes, workers) of the same origin. Messages are serialised via the structured-clone algorithm, making it ideal for cache invalidation, session sync, and coordinated state without a service worker.

```javascript
// Cache invalidation across tabs
const CACHE_CHANNEL = new BroadcastChannel('app-cache-v1');

// Publisher (e.g., after a successful mutation)
function invalidateCache(entityType, id) {
  CACHE_CHANNEL.postMessage({ type: 'invalidate', entityType, id });
  localCacheStore.delete(`${entityType}:${id}`);
}

// Subscriber (in every tab)
CACHE_CHANNEL.addEventListener('message', (event) => {
  const { type, entityType, id } = event.data;
  if (type === 'invalidate') {
    localCacheStore.delete(`${entityType}:${id}`);
    // Re-fetch if this entity is currently displayed
    if (uiState.activeEntityId === id) {
      refreshUI(entityType, id);
    }
  }
});

// Session coordination: detect logout in another tab
const SESSION_CHANNEL = new BroadcastChannel('session');
SESSION_CHANNEL.addEventListener('message', ({ data }) => {
  if (data.type === 'logout') {
    clearAuthTokens();
    redirectToLogin();
  }
});

// Always close to prevent memory leaks
window.addEventListener('beforeunload', () => {
  CACHE_CHANNEL.close();
  SESSION_CHANNEL.close();
});
```

**When to use:** cache invalidation, session management (login/logout sync), theme/locale preference sync, real-time collaborative-editing coordination where all tabs need identical state.

**When NOT to use:** large binary payloads (structured-clone is CPU-intensive for large `ArrayBuffer`s — prefer `postMessage` with transferables via `SharedWorker` or `ServiceWorker`); cross-origin communication (BroadcastChannel is same-origin only); one-way fire-and-forget metrics (use `navigator.sendBeacon` instead).

**Alternative:** `localStorage` + `storage` event — universal but only fires in *other* tabs, not the sender; `SharedWorker` — supports bidirectional request/response, more complex; `ServiceWorker` as a hub — enables offline support, higher setup cost.

---

### 22. `Intl.DurationFormat` — Locale-Aware Duration Rendering [official]

`Intl.DurationFormat` (ES2025) formats duration objects (`{ hours, minutes, seconds, … }`) into locale-appropriate human-readable strings without manual unit concatenation or third-party i18n libraries.

```javascript
// Basic duration formatting across locales
function formatDuration(durationObj, locale = navigator.language) {
  const formatter = new Intl.DurationFormat(locale, { style: 'long' });
  return formatter.format(durationObj);
}

// "1 hour, 30 minutes, 45 seconds" (en-US)
console.log(formatDuration({ hours: 1, minutes: 30, seconds: 45 }));

// "1 Stunde, 30 Minuten und 45 Sekunden" (de)
console.log(formatDuration({ hours: 1, minutes: 30, seconds: 45 }, 'de'));

// Narrow style for compact UIs (e.g., "1h 30m 45s")
const compact = new Intl.DurationFormat('en', { style: 'narrow' });
console.log(compact.format({ hours: 1, minutes: 30, seconds: 45 }));

// Digital style: "1:30:45"
const digital = new Intl.DurationFormat('en', { style: 'digital' });
console.log(digital.format({ hours: 1, minutes: 30, seconds: 45 }));

// Fractional seconds for performance timers
const precise = new Intl.DurationFormat('en', {
  style: 'narrow',
  fractionalDigits: 3,
});
console.log(precise.format({ seconds: 2, milliseconds: 345 })); // "2s 345ms"

// Integration with Temporal (when available)
function formatElapsed(start, end) {
  const duration = end.since(start);
  return new Intl.DurationFormat('en').format(duration);
}
```

**When to use:** time-tracking UIs, video player duration displays, log timestamps, any user-facing elapsed/remaining time where locale-correct unit ordering and conjunction phrasing matter.

**When NOT to use:** machine-readable output (use ISO 8601 `PT1H30M` format); very old browser targets without `Intl.DurationFormat` support (check `'DurationFormat' in Intl` before use); sub-microsecond precision (use performance.measure formatting instead).

**Alternative:** manual string concatenation with `Intl.NumberFormat` + unit labels — locale-correct but verbose; `date-fns formatDuration` — library dependency, locale data bundled; `humanize-duration` npm — broad locale support but adds ~15 KB to bundle.

---

### 23. View Transition API — Multi-Page Application (MPA) Navigation Transitions [official]

Chrome 126+ (and progressively other engines) support cross-document View Transitions triggered by regular `<a>` link navigations — no JavaScript SPA router required. The `@view-transition` CSS at-rule and `pageswap`/`pagereveal` events enable seamless animations between server-rendered pages.

```javascript
// pageswap fires on the OLD page before it unloads
// pagereveal fires on the NEW page before first render

// old-page.js — capture which element triggered the navigation
document.addEventListener('pageswap', (event) => {
  if (!event.viewTransition) return;

  const clickedCard = document.querySelector('.card.active');
  if (clickedCard) {
    clickedCard.style.viewTransitionName = 'selected-card';
  }
});

// new-page.js — match the element on arrival
document.addEventListener('pagereveal', (event) => {
  if (!event.viewTransition) return;

  const heroEl = document.querySelector('.detail-hero');
  if (heroEl) {
    heroEl.style.viewTransitionName = 'selected-card';
  }
});

// CSS: enable cross-document transitions in BOTH pages
// @view-transition { navigation: auto; }
//
// ::view-transition-group(selected-card) {
//   animation-duration: 400ms;
//   animation-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1);
// }

// Feature-detect before relying on transition
if ('onpagereveal' in window) {
  document.addEventListener('pagereveal', handler);
}
```

**When to use:** MPAs served from the same origin where seamless visual continuity between pages improves perceived performance; e-commerce product lists → detail pages; article cards → full articles; documentation navigation.

**When NOT to use:** cross-origin navigations (blocked by same-origin policy); pages where content shifts dramatically between old and new state (poor visual match = jarring animation); when `prefers-reduced-motion` is enabled (gate with `matchMedia`).

**Alternative:** SPA router with `document.startViewTransition()` — full control, more JavaScript; shared-element transitions via GSAP Flip plugin — cross-browser but pure JS; CSS `fade` transition via Navigation API — simpler, no element matching.

### 24. `IntersectionObserver` v2 with `trackVisibility` — True Visibility Detection [official]

Standard `IntersectionObserver` reports whether an element's bounding box intersects the viewport — but it does NOT detect occlusion by overlapping elements, zero opacity, or CSS transforms that visually hide the element. `IntersectionObserver` v2 adds `trackVisibility: true` which reports `isVisible` only when the element is genuinely visible to the user.

```javascript
// Ad impression tracking that counts only truly visible impressions
function trackAdImpressions(adElements) {
  if (!('IntersectionObserver' in window)) return;

  const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
    (entries) => {
      for (const entry of entries) {
        if (entry.isIntersecting && entry.isVisible) {
          // Element is in viewport AND not occluded/transparent
          reportImpression({
            adId: entry.target.dataset.adId,
            visibleRatio: entry.intersectionRatio,
            timestamp: Date.now(),
          });
          observer.unobserve(entry.target); // Count once
        }
      }
    },
    {
      threshold: 0.5,          // At least 50% in viewport
      trackVisibility: true,   // Enable v2 visibility checks
      delay: 100,              // Required when trackVisibility is true (min 100ms)
    }
  );

  adElements.forEach(el => observer.observe(el));
  return () => observer.disconnect();
}

// Feature detection: fall back gracefully
const supportsVisibility = (() => {
  try {
    new IntersectionObserver(() => {}, { trackVisibility: true, delay: 100 });
    return true;
  } catch { return false; }
})();
```

**When to use:** ad impression billing (MRC/IAB compliance requires genuine visibility); video autoplay eligibility; lazy-loading that should only trigger for unoccluded content; analytics events that must not fire for below-overlay content.

**When NOT to use:** general lazy-loading where occlusion detection is unnecessary (standard `IntersectionObserver` is sufficient and has no `delay` requirement); in performance-sensitive rendering loops (the mandatory 100ms delay means it cannot drive frame-by-frame animations); elements that are intentionally off-screen for accessibility (offscreen-positioned `sr-only` content).

**Alternative:** standard `IntersectionObserver` — faster, universally supported, but no occlusion detection; `getBoundingClientRect` + manual occlusion check — accurate but layout-thrashing; Page Visibility API — page-level, not element-level.

---

### 25. `EventSource` / Server-Sent Events — Efficient Unidirectional Streaming [official]

`EventSource` provides a lightweight, browser-managed HTTP streaming connection for server-push data. Unlike WebSocket, it is unidirectional (server → client), uses standard HTTP, automatically reconnects, and supports named event types — making it ideal for live dashboards, notification feeds, and LLM token streaming.

```javascript
// Basic SSE subscription with named events and reconnect handling
function createEventStream(url, handlers = {}) {
  const source = new EventSource(url, { withCredentials: true });

  source.addEventListener('open', () => {
    console.log('SSE stream connected');
  });

  // Handle named event types from the server
  for (const [eventType, handler] of Object.entries(handlers)) {
    source.addEventListener(eventType, (event) => {
      try {
        handler(JSON.parse(event.data), event.lastEventId);
      } catch (err) {
        console.error(`Failed to parse ${eventType} event:`, err);
      }
    });
  }

  source.addEventListener('error', (event) => {
    if (source.readyState === EventSource.CLOSED) {
      console.warn('SSE stream closed by server');
    }
    // readyState === CONNECTING means browser is auto-reconnecting
  });

  return {
    close: () => source.close(),
    get readyState() { return source.readyState; },
  };
}

// LLM token streaming example
const stream = createEventStream('/api/generate', {
  token: (data) => appendToken(data.text),
  done:  (data) => finaliseResponse(data.fullText),
  error: (data) => showError(data.message),
});
```

**When to use:** real-time notification feeds, live score/dashboard updates, LLM response streaming, log tailing — wherever the server pushes data and the client only reads.

**When NOT to use:** bidirectional communication (use WebSocket); frequent high-throughput binary data (SSE is text-only; binary must be base64-encoded); when HTTP/1.1 with a six-connection-per-origin limit is a constraint (SSE holds one connection per `EventSource` instance).

**Alternative:** WebSocket — bidirectional, binary-capable, more complex; `fetch` with `ReadableStream` — equivalent streaming without auto-reconnect; `long polling` — simpler server, higher latency, higher load.

---

### 26. Web Animations API (`Element.animate()`) — Performant Imperative Animation [official]

The Web Animations API exposes the browser's compositor-thread animation engine to JavaScript without CSS keyframe declarations. `element.animate()` runs transforms and opacity off the main thread, supports `Promise`-based lifecycle (`ready`, `finished`), and plays, pauses, and reverses programmatically.

```javascript
// Entrance animation with Promise lifecycle
async function animateIn(element) {
  const animation = element.animate(
    [
      { opacity: 0, transform: 'translateY(20px)' },
      { opacity: 1, transform: 'translateY(0)' },
    ],
    {
      duration: 250,
      easing: 'cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)',
      fill: 'forwards',
    }
  );

  await animation.finished;  // Resolves when animation completes
  return animation;
}

// Programmatic control: pause and seek
function createProgressBar(element, durationMs) {
  const anim = element.animate(
    [{ width: '0%' }, { width: '100%' }],
    { duration: durationMs, fill: 'forwards', easing: 'linear' }
  );

  return {
    pause:    () => anim.pause(),
    resume:   () => anim.play(),
    setProgress: (pct) => {
      anim.currentTime = (pct / 100) * durationMs;
    },
    finish:   () => anim.finish(),
  };
}

// Respect reduced-motion preference
function motionSafeAnimate(element, keyframes, options) {
  if (window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches) {
    return element.animate(keyframes, { ...options, duration: 0 });
  }
  return element.animate(keyframes, options);
}
```

**When to use:** programmatically triggered animations (toast notifications, modal entry/exit, drag-and-drop feedback); animations that must synchronise with async events (data load complete, WebSocket message); complex sequenced animations where CSS alone lacks the required control.

**When NOT to use:** simple hover or focus animations — CSS `transition` and `@keyframes` are declarative, cacheable, and zero-JS; animations that must degrade in very old browsers without a polyfill; physics-based springs (use CSS `linear()` easing or a library like Motion One).

**Alternative:** CSS `@keyframes` + `animation` — declarative, zero runtime cost; GSAP — extensive sequencing API, ~28 KB min+gzip; Motion One (`motion/dom`) — ~4 KB, Web Animations API wrapper with spring physics.

---

### 27. `crypto.subtle.deriveKey` with PBKDF2 — Client-Side Key Derivation [official]

`SubtleCrypto.deriveKey()` with the PBKDF2 algorithm derives a cryptographic key from a passphrase in a way that is intentionally slow (configurable iteration count), making brute-force attacks computationally expensive. This is the standards-correct approach for encrypting user data with a password in the browser.

```javascript
// Derive an AES-GCM key from a password (PBKDF2)
async function deriveKeyFromPassword(password, salt) {
  const encoder = new TextEncoder();

  // Step 1: import raw password bytes as a PBKDF2 key
  const baseKey = await crypto.subtle.importKey(
    'raw',
    encoder.encode(password),
    'PBKDF2',
    false,          // not extractable
    ['deriveKey']
  );

  // Step 2: derive the AES-GCM key
  return crypto.subtle.deriveKey(
    {
      name: 'PBKDF2',
      salt: encoder.encode(salt),
      iterations: 600_000,   // OWASP 2023 recommendation
      hash: 'SHA-256',
    },
    baseKey,
    { name: 'AES-GCM', length: 256 },
    false,          // not extractable — key stays in the browser's crypto engine
    ['encrypt', 'decrypt']
  );
}

// Encrypt data with the derived key
async function encryptData(key, plaintext) {
  const iv = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(12)); // 96-bit IV for AES-GCM
  const ciphertext = await crypto.subtle.encrypt(
    { name: 'AES-GCM', iv },
    key,
    new TextEncoder().encode(plaintext)
  );
  return { iv, ciphertext };
}
```

**When to use:** encrypting locally-stored user data (notes, credentials, health records) with a user-provided passphrase; generating deterministic keys for end-to-end encrypted sync; any scenario where the key must be derived from human-memorable input.

**When NOT to use:** server-side key derivation (use `node:crypto` `scrypt` or `argon2` — stronger KDFs); when you can avoid client-side encryption entirely (server-side encryption with proper key management is simpler and more auditable); do not use MD5 or SHA-1 as the PBKDF2 hash — always use SHA-256 or SHA-512.

**Alternative:** `crypto.subtle.deriveKey` with HKDF — for deriving multiple keys from a single high-entropy secret (not passwords); `bcrypt.js` / `argon2-browser` — stronger KDFs but large WASM bundles (~500 KB); native `node:crypto.scrypt` (Node.js only) — memory-hard, preferred for server-side.

### 28. `AbortController` Composition — Multi-Source Signal Merging [official]

`AbortController` is well-known for cancelling `fetch()`, but composing multiple abort signals (e.g., user cancellation AND timeout AND component unmount) into a single signal requires `AbortSignal.any()` (ES2024) — which resolves as soon as any of the input signals aborts.

```javascript
// Merge signals: abort when ANY condition fires
function composedFetch(url, options = {}) {
  const timeout = AbortSignal.timeout(5000);          // 5s timeout signal
  const combined = AbortSignal.any([
    timeout,
    options.signal,                                    // caller's signal
  ].filter(Boolean));

  return fetch(url, { ...options, signal: combined });
}

// Component-lifecycle-aware data fetching (e.g., React)
function useAbortableFetch(url) {
  const [data, setData] = React.useState(null);

  React.useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();

    composedFetch(url, { signal: controller.signal })
      .then(r => r.json())
      .then(setData)
      .catch(err => {
        if (err.name !== 'AbortError') throw err;  // Rethrow non-abort errors
      });

    return () => controller.abort('Component unmounted');
  }, [url]);

  return data;
}

// Using AbortSignal.timeout() standalone (ES2022+)
async function fetchWithTimeout(url, ms = 3000) {
  const response = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms) });
  return response.json();
}
```

**When to use:** any `fetch()` that should respect both a global timeout AND a user-initiated cancel; component teardown patterns in React/Vue/Svelte; streaming operations (ReadableStream with abort) that should stop when the consumer disconnects.

**When NOT to use:** `AbortSignal.any()` is not needed when you have only a single abort source — use that signal directly; do not share the same `AbortController` across independent requests (aborting one aborts all); avoid creating new `AbortController` instances inside render functions without memoisation.

**Alternative:** `Promise.race([fetch(...), rejectAfterMs(5000)])` — timeout only, no signal propagation; manual `AbortController` chain (`signal.addEventListener('abort', ...)`) — fine-grained but verbose; RxJS `takeUntil` — declarative, requires Observable adoption.

### 29. `FormData` + `fetch` — Progressive Enhancement File Upload [official]

Uploading files with `fetch()` and `FormData` supports streaming uploads, upload progress via `ReadableStream`, and multipart encoding — replacing `XMLHttpRequest` upload patterns without third-party libraries.

```javascript
// File upload with progress tracking using ReadableStream
async function uploadFileWithProgress(file, url, onProgress) {
  let uploadedBytes = 0;
  const totalBytes = file.size;

  // Create a readable stream that reports progress
  const fileStream = file.stream();
  const progressStream = new TransformStream({
    transform(chunk, controller) {
      uploadedBytes += chunk.byteLength;
      onProgress(uploadedBytes / totalBytes);
      controller.enqueue(chunk);
    },
  });

  const response = await fetch(url, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': file.type,
      'Content-Length': String(totalBytes),
    },
    body: fileStream.pipeThrough(progressStream),
    // duplex: 'half' required for streaming request bodies in Chrome
    duplex: 'half',
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Upload failed: ${response.status}`);
  return response.json();
}

// Multipart form upload (FormData)
async function uploadFormWithFiles(formElement, url) {
  const formData = new FormData(formElement);  // Reads all inputs/files
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    method: 'POST',
    body: formData,
    // Do NOT set Content-Type — browser sets multipart boundary automatically
  });
  return response.json();
}
```

**When to use:** file uploads where you need progress feedback; multipart form submissions to REST APIs; replacing `XMLHttpRequest` upload patterns; chunked/streaming uploads to endpoints that support `Content-Length`-less streaming.

**When NOT to use:** uploading directly to signed cloud storage URLs (S3 PUT, GCS resumable) — use the cloud SDK or a direct `fetch` PUT with the binary body; files >2 GB where resumable upload protocols (TUS, S3 multipart) are required; environments where `ReadableStream` request bodies are unsupported (check `duplex: 'half'` compatibility).

**Alternative:** `XMLHttpRequest` with `xhr.upload.onprogress` — universal, synchronous progress events; `tus-js-client` — resumable uploads over the TUS protocol; Uppy — full-featured upload library with UI components.

---

### 30. `navigator.share()` — Native OS-Level Share Sheet [official]

`navigator.share()` invokes the platform's native share dialog, allowing users to share URLs, text, and files through installed apps (Messages, Mail, social apps) without custom share UI. This is the standards-based approach for "share" affordances in PWAs and mobile-first web apps.

```javascript
// Share a URL with fallback for unsupported environments
async function shareContent(shareData) {
  if (!navigator.share) {
    // Desktop fallback: copy to clipboard
    await navigator.clipboard.writeText(shareData.url ?? shareData.text ?? '');
    showToast('Copied to clipboard');
    return;
  }

  // Validate before calling (prevents silent failures)
  if (!navigator.canShare(shareData)) {
    console.warn('Share data is not shareable:', shareData);
    return;
  }

  try {
    await navigator.share(shareData);
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name === 'AbortError') return;  // User dismissed — not an error
    throw err;
  }
}

// Share a file (e.g., a generated PDF or canvas export)
async function shareGeneratedFile(canvas, filename) {
  const blob = await new Promise(resolve => canvas.toBlob(resolve, 'image/png'));
  const file = new File([blob], filename, { type: 'image/png' });

  await shareContent({
    title: 'My Chart',
    files: [file],
  });
}

// Usage
shareContent({ title: 'Check this out', url: location.href, text: 'Cool article' });
```

**When to use:** mobile web apps and PWAs where users expect native share behaviour; "Share article" / "Share score" / "Export as image" features; when the target audience is primarily on iOS or Android.

**When NOT to use:** desktop-first applications where the native share sheet is unfamiliar or missing (add clipboard fallback); when you need to control the list of share targets (the native sheet shows all installed apps); in iframes (share requires top-level browsing context in most browsers).

**Alternative:** Open Graph + social share links (Twitter intent URLs, etc.) — deterministic targets, no browser API; custom share drawer UI — cross-platform, full design control; `navigator.clipboard.writeText` — clipboard-only, no app targets.

## Cycle 32 Community Gotchas

**CG32-1. `scheduler.yield()` Is Not Available in All Browsers — Silently Falls Back to Undefined** [community] — `scheduler` is on `globalThis` in Chrome/Edge but not in Firefox or Safari as of mid-2026. WHY it causes problems: code that calls `await scheduler.yield()` in Firefox throws `ReferenceError: scheduler is not defined` at runtime (not a type error, not a warning), and the entire long-running loop crashes instead of merely skipping the yield. Fix: always guard with `typeof scheduler !== 'undefined' && typeof scheduler.yield === 'function'`, and fall back to `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0))`.

**CG32-2. `BroadcastChannel` Messages Are Delivered in a Separate Task — Not Synchronously** [community] — Unlike `localStorage` `storage` events (which are dispatched synchronously in the receiving tab during the same event loop tick in some engines), `BroadcastChannel` messages are always delivered as separate tasks. WHY it causes problems: teams that assume BroadcastChannel works like a synchronous inter-tab call find that code immediately after `postMessage` in the receiver's handler can observe stale state — the sender's DOM has not yet updated when the message fires. Fix: treat all BroadcastChannel messages as eventually consistent; never assume ordering guarantees across tabs; use sequence numbers or vector clocks if message ordering is critical.

**CG32-3. `WeakRef.deref()` Can Return `undefined` Between Two Lines of the Same Synchronous Function** [community] — JavaScript engines may run GC between any two allocations, even in the middle of a synchronous function. WHY it causes problems: code that does `const val = ref.deref(); if (val) { processLargeObject(val); }` can have `val` collected before `processLargeObject` completes if `processLargeObject` triggers large allocations internally, causing the passed reference to become invalid mid-call. In V8, this is rare but reproducible under memory pressure. Fix: store the `deref()` result in a local variable and pass that variable — the local binding keeps the object alive for the duration of the call. Never call `ref.deref()` twice expecting the same result.

**CG32-4. `TypedArray.transfer()` Detaches the Original Buffer Immediately — Including Other Views Sharing the Same Buffer** [community] — When multiple `TypedArray` views share an `ArrayBuffer` (e.g., `new Uint8Array(sharedBuf)` and `new Float32Array(sharedBuf)`), calling `.transfer()` on one view detaches the underlying `ArrayBuffer` for ALL views simultaneously. WHY it causes problems: teams that create typed array slices (`subarray()`) over a shared buffer for performance then pass one slice to a worker via `transfer()` find all other slices throw `TypeError: Cannot perform %TypedArray%.prototype.set on a detached ArrayBuffer` on next access — even if they are in the same thread. Fix: only call `transfer()` on a buffer you exclusively own; use `slice()` to copy out a portion before transferring if other views must remain valid.

**CG32-5. `EventSource` Does Not Respect the `Cache-Control` Header — Browsers May Cache the SSE Endpoint** [community] — Some browser/CDN combinations cache the SSE response if the endpoint does not set `Cache-Control: no-cache` explicitly. WHY it causes problems: a CDN edge node caches the first SSE response body and replays it to subsequent clients, meaning all connected clients receive stale or replayed events instead of live server pushes — the connection appears open but no new events arrive. Fix: always set `Cache-Control: no-cache` and `X-Accel-Buffering: no` on SSE responses; also set `Content-Type: text/event-stream` with `charset=utf-8`; for Nginx, add `proxy_buffering off` to prevent buffering of the streaming response.

**CG32-6. `navigator.share()` with `files` Requires Calling `navigator.canShare()` First — Otherwise It Silently No-ops on Some Platforms** [community] — iOS Safari rejects `navigator.share({ files: [...] })` with an unspecified error if any file type in the array is not shareable, rather than falling back to sharing just the URL or text. WHY it causes problems: developers who test file sharing only on Android (where it is permissive) ship to production without realising that iOS silently rejects the entire share operation — including the URL — when an unsupported file type is included. Fix: always call `navigator.canShare({ files })` before including files in the share payload; if it returns `false`, fall back to sharing just `{ url, text }` without files.

**CG32-7. `document.startViewTransition()` Callback Must Be Synchronous or Return a Promise That Resolves Before the Next Frame** [community] — The DOM snapshot for the "new state" is captured by the browser after the callback's returned Promise resolves. WHY it causes problems: if the callback awaits a `fetch()` call to load data before updating the DOM, the transition "new state" snapshot is taken after the network round-trip, which may be hundreds of milliseconds later — the old state is frozen on screen for the entire duration, making the transition feel broken rather than smooth. Fix: update the DOM with placeholder/skeleton content synchronously (or within a single microtask), then fetch and update incrementally; alternatively, pre-fetch data before calling `startViewTransition`.

**CG32-8. `Element.animate()` with `fill: 'forwards'` Holds a Strong Reference to the Element — Prevents GC** [community] — When an animation uses `fill: 'forwards'`, the browser must retain the final keyframe values and continues holding a reference to the animated element and its computed styles. WHY it causes problems: in SPAs that animate elements then remove them from the DOM (toast notifications, modal exit animations), the `fill: 'forwards'` animation keeps the element alive in memory indefinitely because the `Animation` object itself (reachable from `element.getAnimations()` on the detached element) maintains a strong reference chain. Fix: always call `animation.commitStyles()` followed by `animation.cancel()` after the element is removed from the DOM to persist the final styles and release the animation; alternatively use `fill: 'none'` and set final styles manually.

### Pattern 1 — `ReadableStream.from()` for Iterable-to-Stream Conversion [official]

**Description.** `ReadableStream.from(asyncIterable)` (Baseline September 2024) converts any sync or async iterable — arrays, generators, `ReadableStream`s from other APIs — into a `ReadableStream` that can be piped, teed, or consumed with a `for await` loop. It eliminates boilerplate `ReadableStream` constructors with manual `controller.enqueue()` calls. Internally the browser pulls one chunk at a time via the iterable's `next()` method, applying natural backpressure. The resulting stream is a standard `ReadableStream` and participates in the full Streams API surface: `pipeThrough`, `pipeTo`, `tee`.

```js
// Convert an async generator directly to a ReadableStream
async function* generateChunks(data) {
  for (const chunk of data) {
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 10)); // simulate async production
    yield new TextEncoder().encode(chunk);
  }
}

const stream = ReadableStream.from(generateChunks(['hello', ' ', 'world']));
const response = new Response(stream, {
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' }
});
const text = await response.text();
console.log(text); // "hello world"
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** bridging generator-based data pipelines with Fetch API, Service Worker responses, or `pipeTo(WritableStream)` consumers; replacing manual `ReadableStream` constructor boilerplate.
- **Do NOT use when:** the iterable is synchronous and small — a plain `Uint8Array` or string fed directly to `new Response(body)` is simpler and faster; or when you need to cancel the underlying generator on stream cancellation (requires a custom `cancel` method on the `ReadableStream` constructor instead).
- **Alternative:** `new ReadableStream({ start(controller) { ... } })` with manual enqueue/close for full lifecycle control.

### Pattern 2 — `TextDecoderStream` / `TextEncoderStream` as Transform Pipeline Stages [official]

**Description.** `TextDecoderStream` and `TextEncoderStream` implement the `TransformStream` interface, making them composable stages in a `pipeThrough` chain. `TextDecoderStream` converts a binary `ReadableStream<Uint8Array>` into a `ReadableStream<string>`, handling multi-byte UTF-8 sequences that span chunk boundaries automatically. `TextEncoderStream` performs the inverse. Composing them via `pipeThrough` keeps all streaming in a single pipeline without accumulating the full response in memory.

```js
// Stream-decode a large HTTP response without buffering the whole body
async function streamDecodeResponse(url) {
  const response = await fetch(url);
  const reader = response.body
    .pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream())       // Uint8Array → string chunks
    .getReader();

  let result = '';
  while (true) {
    const { done, value } = await reader.read();
    if (done) break;
    result += value; // value is already a decoded string chunk
    process(value);  // process each chunk as it arrives
  }
  return result;
}

function process(chunk) {
  // incremental rendering, parsing, etc.
  console.log('chunk:', chunk.slice(0, 40));
}
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** consuming large streaming text (NDJSON, SSE body, large JSON) where you want to process lines incrementally without `.text()` buffering.
- **Do NOT use when:** the response is known to be small (< 64 KB) and you just need the decoded string — `await response.text()` is clearer and faster for small payloads.
- **Alternative:** `new TextDecoder().decode(chunk, { stream: true })` in a manual loop, but this requires managing the stateful decoder instance yourself across chunks.

### Pattern 3 — `OffscreenCanvas` + `transferControlToOffscreen()` for Worker Rendering [official]

**Description.** `transferControlToOffscreen()` transfers rendering control of a `<canvas>` element to an `OffscreenCanvas` that lives in a Web Worker, allowing GPU-accelerated drawing (2D context, WebGL, WebGPU) without blocking the main thread. The main thread retains a placeholder `<canvas>` in the DOM but the worker owns the drawing context. This is the correct pattern for heavy visualisation (charts, 3D scenes, real-time data plots) in performance-sensitive UIs. Baseline 2023.

```js
// main.js
const canvas = document.getElementById('my-canvas');
const offscreen = canvas.transferControlToOffscreen();
const worker = new Worker('./render-worker.js', { type: 'module' });
worker.postMessage({ canvas: offscreen }, [offscreen]); // transfer ownership

// render-worker.js
self.addEventListener('message', ({ data: { canvas } }) => {
  const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
  let frame = 0;
  function draw() {
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
    ctx.fillStyle = `hsl(${frame % 360}, 70%, 50%)`;
    ctx.fillRect(10, 10, canvas.width - 20, canvas.height - 20);
    frame++;
    self.requestAnimationFrame(draw); // rAF is available in workers
  }
  draw();
});
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** canvas drawing is computationally expensive and causes jank on the main thread; data visualisation dashboards, WebGL scenes, real-time audio waveform renderers.
- **Do NOT use when:** the canvas needs to read DOM layout coordinates synchronously (e.g., drawing tooltips at cursor position derived from `getBoundingClientRect`) — layout queries are not available in workers.
- **Alternative:** `requestIdleCallback` for deferring canvas drawing to idle time on the main thread when offloading to a worker is not feasible.

### Pattern 4 — `MessageChannel` for Decoupled Bidirectional Module Communication [official]

**Description.** `MessageChannel` creates a pair of entangled `MessagePort` objects (`port1`, `port2`) that communicate via `postMessage` without a shared reference to either endpoint. One port is passed to a module, worker, or iframe; the other is kept locally. This enables decoupled request–reply semantics, capability passing, and clean teardown (closing either port silences both). Unlike `window.postMessage`, `MessageChannel` messages are scoped: no other listener can intercept them and origin checks are not required.

```js
// Capability-passing: give a module only the port it needs
function createRpcChannel(handler) {
  const { port1, port2 } = new MessageChannel();
  port1.onmessage = async ({ data }) => {
    const result = await handler(data.method, data.args);
    port1.postMessage({ id: data.id, result });
  };
  return port2; // caller keeps port2
}

// Usage
const workerPort = createRpcChannel(async (method, args) => {
  if (method === 'add') return args[0] + args[1];
  throw new Error(`Unknown method: ${method}`);
});

let pendingId = 0;
const pending = new Map();
workerPort.onmessage = ({ data }) => {
  pending.get(data.id)?.(data.result);
  pending.delete(data.id);
};

function callRpc(method, ...args) {
  return new Promise(resolve => {
    const id = pendingId++;
    pending.set(id, resolve);
    workerPort.postMessage({ id, method, args });
  });
}

callRpc('add', 3, 4).then(console.log); // 7
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** passing communication capability to iframes, workers, or third-party modules without exposing the full `window` or `Worker` reference; implementing lightweight RPC between isolated contexts.
- **Do NOT use when:** you need broadcast semantics to many listeners — `BroadcastChannel` is designed for that; or when the two parties need to exchange `SharedArrayBuffer` regions.
- **Alternative:** `window.postMessage` with origin filtering for simple iframe communication where the port-passing pattern adds unnecessary indirection.

### Pattern 5 — Navigation API `navigate` Event Interception for SPA Routing [official]

**Description.** The Navigation API (`navigation.navigate()`, `navigate` event) replaces the history-hacking pattern (`history.pushState` + `popstate` listener) with a first-class SPA routing primitive. The `navigate` event fires before the navigation commits, exposing `event.intercept({ handler })` which tells the browser to handle scroll restoration, loading indicators, and URL update automatically. Supported in Chrome/Edge 102+; Safari 18+; not yet in Firefox stable as of 2026 (requires feature detection).

```js
// SPA router using Navigation API
if ('navigation' in window) {
  navigation.addEventListener('navigate', (event) => {
    // Only intercept same-origin navigations to our known routes
    if (!event.canIntercept) return;
    const url = new URL(event.destination.url);
    if (!isKnownRoute(url.pathname)) return;

    event.intercept({
      async handler() {
        const content = await loadRoute(url.pathname);
        renderContent(content);          // update DOM
        document.title = content.title;  // update title
      }
    });
  });
}

function isKnownRoute(path) {
  return ['/home', '/about', '/settings'].includes(path);
}
async function loadRoute(path) {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/route${path}`);
  return res.json();
}
function renderContent(content) {
  document.getElementById('app').innerHTML = content.html;
}
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** building SPAs in Chromium-based environments or future cross-browser scenarios; replacing brittle `history.pushState` / `popstate` hacks; benefiting from browser-managed focus/scroll restoration.
- **Do NOT use when:** Firefox support is required without a polyfill — fall back gracefully to `popstate`-based routing; or in SSR frameworks where the router runs on the server.
- **Alternative:** `history.pushState` + `popstate` listener (universal but manual); framework routers (React Router, Vue Router) that abstract over both patterns.

### Pattern 6 — Popover API for Accessible Non-Modal Overlays [official]

**Description.** The Popover API (`popover` attribute, `showPopover()`, `hidePopover()`, `togglePopover()`) provides a browser-native mechanism for tooltips, dropdowns, and non-modal overlays that automatically handles the top-layer stacking context, light-dismiss (click outside / Escape key), and focus management — features that were previously reimplemented in every UI framework. Baseline 2024. The `popover` attribute value is either `"auto"` (light-dismiss, one at a time) or `"manual"` (programmatic control only).

```js
// Declarative popover with JavaScript enhancement
const btn = document.getElementById('info-btn');
const pop = document.getElementById('info-popover');

// Pure HTML wiring: <button popovertarget="info-popover">Info</button>
// <div id="info-popover" popover>Content here</div>

// JS enhancement: position popover relative to button on show
pop.addEventListener('toggle', (event) => {
  if (event.newState !== 'open') return;
  const btnRect = btn.getBoundingClientRect();
  pop.style.top = `${btnRect.bottom + 8}px`;
  pop.style.left = `${btnRect.left}px`;
});

// Programmatic control when needed
document.getElementById('custom-trigger').addEventListener('click', () => {
  pop.showPopover();
});
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** implementing tooltips, context menus, combobox dropdowns, or any UI overlay that should close on outside-click or Escape — offloading accessibility work to the browser.
- **Do NOT use when:** you need a blocking modal dialog that traps focus — use `<dialog>` with `showModal()` instead; or when animation of the popover entry/exit requires coordinating with `@starting-style` CSS (not yet universally supported).
- **Alternative:** `<dialog>` with `show()` (non-modal) for cases that need `::backdrop`; custom `div` + focus-trap library for complex overlay scenarios.

### Pattern 7 — Permissions API Live `PermissionStatus` for Reactive Permission Handling [official]

**Description.** `navigator.permissions.query({ name })` returns a `PermissionStatus` object with a `state` property (`"granted"`, `"denied"`, `"prompt"`) and an `onchange` event that fires when the user revokes or grants a permission outside the page (e.g., via the browser's site settings). This enables reactive UI that accurately reflects the current permission state without polling. Supported in all modern browsers for camera, microphone, geolocation, notifications, and clipboard-read.

```js
async function setupCameraPermissionUI(button, videoEl) {
  const status = await navigator.permissions.query({ name: 'camera' });

  function updateUI() {
    if (status.state === 'granted') {
      button.textContent = 'Camera active';
      button.disabled = false;
    } else if (status.state === 'denied') {
      button.textContent = 'Camera blocked — check site settings';
      button.disabled = true;
    } else {
      button.textContent = 'Enable camera';
      button.disabled = false;
    }
  }

  updateUI();
  status.addEventListener('change', updateUI); // live updates

  button.addEventListener('click', async () => {
    if (status.state === 'prompt') {
      await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ video: true })
        .then(stream => { videoEl.srcObject = stream; })
        .catch(() => {}); // user denied in the prompt
    }
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** building media-access UIs, notification opt-ins, or clipboard operations where users frequently change permissions in browser settings while the page is open.
- **Do NOT use when:** the permission status is only needed once at page load — a single `status.state` check at initialization is sufficient without the overhead of an event listener.
- **Alternative:** request the API directly (e.g., `getUserMedia`) and handle rejection as implicit permission denial, then show a static "blocked" UI message.

### Pattern 8 — `reportError()` for Programmatic Error Dispatch to `window.onerror` [official]

**Description.** `reportError(err)` (Baseline 2022) dispatches an `ErrorEvent` on the global object, triggering `window.onerror` and `window.addEventListener('error', ...)` handlers exactly as if the error were uncaught. It is the correct way to propagate errors from Promise chains, worker message handlers, or async callbacks into the application's centralized error monitoring infrastructure without rethrowing into an outer `try/catch`. Unlike `console.error`, `reportError` is observable by error-tracking SDKs (Sentry, Datadog) that instrument `window.onerror`.

```js
// Centralized error reporting from async contexts
async function processQueue(queue) {
  for (const task of queue) {
    try {
      await task.run();
    } catch (err) {
      // Enrich the error before reporting
      err.taskId = task.id;
      err.queueLength = queue.length;
      // Route to window.onerror / error tracking SDK
      reportError(err);
      // Continue processing remaining tasks
    }
  }
}

// In a Worker — errors must be explicitly routed to main thread
self.addEventListener('message', async ({ data }) => {
  try {
    const result = await heavyComputation(data);
    self.postMessage({ result });
  } catch (err) {
    // Without reportError, this swallows the error silently
    reportError(err); // triggers worker's global error event
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** integrating with third-party error monitoring SDKs; surfacing async errors from queues, schedulers, or message handlers into the application's `onerror` pipeline.
- **Do NOT use when:** you want to display an error to the user directly (use a toast / error boundary); or when the error is expected and recoverable — `reportError` signals an unexpected fault.
- **Alternative:** `throw` in a context where the error will bubble to the unhandled rejection handler; explicit `onerror` callback calls for environments without `reportError` support.

### Pattern 9 — `Symbol.hasInstance` for Custom `instanceof` Behavior [official]

**Description.** Defining `Symbol.hasInstance` on a class or object as a static method overrides what `instanceof` tests. This enables type-checking against duck-typed contracts (interface-like checks), union membership, or versioned class hierarchies where `instanceof` across iframe/module boundaries would fail. The hook receives the candidate value and returns a boolean. It is called by the `instanceof` operator whenever the right-hand side has a `Symbol.hasInstance` method.

```js
// Duck-typed "interface" check with instanceof
class Iterable {
  static [Symbol.hasInstance](instance) {
    return (
      instance != null &&
      typeof instance[Symbol.iterator] === 'function'
    );
  }
}

console.log([] instanceof Iterable);          // true
console.log('hello' instanceof Iterable);     // true
console.log(new Map() instanceof Iterable);   // true
console.log(42 instanceof Iterable);          // false

// Cross-realm class identity check
class SerializableError {
  static [Symbol.hasInstance](value) {
    // Works even when Error comes from another iframe/VM context
    return (
      value !== null &&
      typeof value === 'object' &&
      typeof value.message === 'string' &&
      typeof value.stack === 'string'
    );
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** implementing interface-like contracts, cross-realm type checks (iframes, Node.js `vm.runInNewContext`), or union type membership tests in framework code.
- **Do NOT use when:** you need simple nominal class hierarchy checks — standard `instanceof` is faster and clearer; or when the check is used in tight loops where the extra function call overhead matters.
- **Alternative:** `Array.isArray()`, `typeof`, or explicit `duck` check functions (`isIterable(x)`) are more readable for application code that does not need operator syntax.

### Pattern 10 — Proxy `apply` Trap for Function Instrumentation [official]

**Description.** A Proxy with an `apply` trap wraps any callable value, intercepting every invocation with access to `target` (the original function), `thisArg`, and `argumentsList`. This is the foundation for transparent instrumentation: timing, logging, argument validation, memoization, and RPC stubs — without modifying the original function's source. The Proxy is a drop-in replacement: its `typeof` is `"function"`, it passes `instanceof` checks, and its `name`/`length` reflect the target.

```js
// Generic function instrumentation via Proxy apply trap
function instrument(fn, { name = fn.name, onCall, onReturn, onError } = {}) {
  return new Proxy(fn, {
    apply(target, thisArg, args) {
      onCall?.({ name, args });
      const start = performance.now();
      try {
        const result = Reflect.apply(target, thisArg, args);
        const elapsed = performance.now() - start;
        onReturn?.({ name, result, elapsed });
        return result;
      } catch (err) {
        onError?.({ name, err });
        throw err;
      }
    }
  });
}

const trackedFetch = instrument(fetch, {
  onCall: ({ name, args }) => console.log(`[call] ${name}`, args[0]),
  onReturn: ({ name, elapsed }) =>
    console.log(`[done] ${name} took ${elapsed.toFixed(1)}ms`),
  onError: ({ name, err }) => console.error(`[error] ${name}`, err)
});

// trackedFetch is a drop-in replacement for fetch
const res = await trackedFetch('https://api.example.com/data');
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** building transparent instrumentation layers (APM, logging, argument validation) that must not require callers to change their code; RPC stub generation in test doubles.
- **Do NOT use when:** performance is critical in hot paths — Proxy invocation adds ~10–30% overhead vs direct calls in V8; or for simple decoration of a single function where a wrapper closure is clearer.
- **Alternative:** Higher-order wrapper functions (`function logged(fn) { return (...args) => { ... } }`) are faster and simpler when the full transparency of a Proxy is not required.

---

### Pattern 11 — `navigator.scheduling.isInputPending()` for Cooperative Yielding [official]

**Description.** `navigator.scheduling.isInputPending()` returns `true` if there are unprocessed user input events (pointer, keyboard) waiting in the queue. It enables long-running synchronous work to yield to the browser at the right moment — only when user input is actually pending — rather than yielding on every `setTimeout(0)` tick. This reduces unnecessary yielding while still keeping the UI responsive. Available in Chrome/Edge; not yet in Firefox or Safari (requires feature detection).

```js
// Cooperative task scheduler that yields only when input is pending
async function runWithCooperativeYield(items, processItem) {
  const YIELD_INTERVAL_MS = 50; // fallback: yield every 50ms regardless
  let lastYield = performance.now();

  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    processItem(items[i]);

    const shouldYield =
      (typeof navigator.scheduling?.isInputPending === 'function' &&
        navigator.scheduling.isInputPending()) ||
      performance.now() - lastYield > YIELD_INTERVAL_MS;

    if (shouldYield) {
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0));
      lastYield = performance.now();
    }
  }
}

// Usage: process 10,000 records without blocking input
await runWithCooperativeYield(largeDataset, record => {
  transformAndIndex(record);
});
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** long-running data processing loops (indexing, sorting, diffing large arrays) on the main thread where you want to minimize yielding overhead while remaining input-responsive.
- **Do NOT use when:** the work can be moved to a Web Worker — that is always the preferred solution for CPU-intensive tasks; or when cross-browser compatibility is required without a fallback.
- **Alternative:** `scheduler.yield()` (Chrome 129+) for a higher-level yielding primitive that incorporates priority hints; `queueMicrotask` for lower-overhead yielding when input responsiveness is not the concern.

### Pattern 12 — `Temporal.Duration` Arithmetic and Rounding [official]

**Description.** `Temporal.Duration` represents a span of time with separate fields for years, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, and nanoseconds, avoiding the precision loss and timezone ambiguity of `Date`-subtraction arithmetic. `duration.add()`, `duration.subtract()`, `duration.round()`, and `duration.total()` operate on these fields with configurable rounding modes and a `relativeTo` anchor for calendar-aware month/year math. Requires the TC39 Temporal polyfill until engines ship natively (behind flags in V8/SpiderMonkey as of 2026).

```js
import { Temporal } from '@js-temporal/polyfill';

// Calendar-aware duration arithmetic
const start = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2025-01-31');
const end   = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-03-01');

// Duration between two dates, calendar-aware
const duration = start.until(end, { largestUnit: 'months' });
console.log(duration.toLocaleString()); // P13M1D (13 months, 1 day)

// Round a duration to the nearest week
const approx = duration.round({
  largestUnit: 'weeks',
  smallestUnit: 'days',
  roundingMode: 'halfExpand',
  relativeTo: start
});
console.log(approx.weeks, approx.days); // 56 weeks, 5 days (approx)

// Total in a single unit
const totalDays = duration.total({ unit: 'days', relativeTo: start });
console.log(totalDays); // 394
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** building date pickers, event scheduling, subscription billing logic, or any date arithmetic where month/year-aware rounding is required and `Date` millisecond subtraction produces wrong results.
- **Do NOT use when:** the polyfill's ~60 KB bundle size is unacceptable for the use case — for simple "days between two timestamps" arithmetic, a millisecond difference divided by `86_400_000` suffices.
- **Alternative:** `date-fns` or `Luxon` for mature cross-browser date arithmetic; `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` for display-only relative time strings without calculation.

---

### Pattern 13 — `Response.error()` and `Response.redirect()` Static Constructors in Service Workers [official]

**Description.** `Response.error()` creates a network-error response (opaque type, status 0) that causes the browser to treat the request as failed — useful in Service Worker `fetch` handlers to deliberately block requests. `Response.redirect(url, status)` creates a redirect response (301, 302, etc.) without requiring a round-trip to the network. Both are available in Service Workers and Fetch API contexts. They are the idiomatic way to implement request blocking, URL rewriting, and transparent redirect logic at the service worker layer.

```js
// Service Worker: block ads, rewrite CDN URLs, redirect old paths
self.addEventListener('fetch', (event) => {
  const url = new URL(event.request.url);

  // Block known ad domains
  if (isAdDomain(url.hostname)) {
    event.respondWith(Response.error()); // network error to caller
    return;
  }

  // Transparently rewrite legacy CDN path
  if (url.pathname.startsWith('/static/v1/')) {
    const newUrl = url.href.replace('/static/v1/', '/static/v2/');
    event.respondWith(Response.redirect(newUrl, 301));
    return;
  }

  // Redirect deprecated API endpoint
  if (url.pathname === '/api/legacy') {
    event.respondWith(Response.redirect('/api/v2', 308));
    return;
  }

  // Default: pass through to network
  event.respondWith(fetch(event.request));
});

function isAdDomain(hostname) {
  return ['ads.example.com', 'tracking.example.net'].includes(hostname);
}
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** implementing request blocking (content filtering, security policies), transparent URL migration, or redirect logic that should not add a network round-trip.
- **Do NOT use when:** redirects need to carry cookies or authorization headers — opaque redirects in Service Workers drop headers; use `fetch(newUrl)` and return the actual response instead.
- **Alternative:** `new Response(null, { status: 302, headers: { Location: url } })` for manual response construction; `fetch(request)` pass-through for unmodified requests.

---

### Pattern 14 — Module Workers (`new Worker(url, { type: 'module' })`) [official]

**Description.** Module Workers accept `{ type: 'module' }` as a constructor option, enabling `import` / `export` syntax, static imports, dynamic `import()`, and top-level `await` inside the worker script — eliminating `importScripts()` and the need to bundle worker code into a single IIFE. Shared module caches are maintained per origin so modules loaded by both the main thread and a worker are parsed once. Baseline 2023. Module workers also support `import.meta.url` for relative asset resolution inside the worker.

```js
// main.js — launch a module worker
const worker = new Worker(new URL('./data-worker.js', import.meta.url), {
  type: 'module'
});

worker.postMessage({ task: 'sort', data: largeArray });
worker.onmessage = ({ data }) => {
  console.log('sorted:', data.result.slice(0, 5));
};

// data-worker.js — can use ES module syntax
import { sort } from './algorithms/quicksort.js'; // static import works

self.onmessage = async ({ data: { task, data } }) => {
  if (task === 'sort') {
    const result = sort(data);
    self.postMessage({ result });
  }
};
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** worker scripts need to share library code with the main thread without duplication; or when the worker requires tree-shakeable imports and top-level `await` for initialization.
- **Do NOT use when:** the bundler does not support worker module chunking (some Webpack 4 / Rollup configurations); or when targeting environments where module workers are not supported — check with `typeof Worker !== 'undefined'` and `{ type: 'module' }` support detection.
- **Alternative:** Classic workers with `importScripts()` for maximum compatibility; bundler-inlined workers (`new Worker(new Blob([...])`) for single-file deployments.

---

### Pattern 15 — `Promise.withResolvers()` for External Recurring Event Queue [official]

**Description.** `Promise.withResolvers()` (ES2024) returns `{ promise, resolve, reject }` from a single call, eliminating the `new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })` executor pattern. Its primary novel use case — beyond one-shot signals — is building asynchronous event queues: each time a consumer awaits the current "ticket" promise and a producer resolves it, a new ticket is immediately issued, enabling a `while (true)` async consumer loop that awaits each event in sequence without buffering or race conditions.

```js
// Async event queue: producer resolves each ticket, consumer awaits in order
function createEventQueue() {
  let current = Promise.withResolvers();

  return {
    emit(value) {
      const { resolve } = current;
      current = Promise.withResolvers(); // issue next ticket before resolving
      resolve({ value, next: current.promise });
    },
    [Symbol.asyncIterator]() {
      let ticket = current.promise;
      return {
        async next() {
          const { value, next } = await ticket;
          ticket = next;
          return { value, done: false };
        },
        return() { return { done: true }; }
      };
    }
  };
}

const queue = createEventQueue();

// Consumer: processes events in order, never misses one
(async () => {
  for await (const event of queue) {
    console.log('received:', event);
    if (event === 'stop') break;
  }
})();

// Producer: emits events from anywhere
queue.emit('first');
queue.emit('second');
queue.emit('stop');
```

**Tradeoff.**
- **Use when:** building typed async event queues where order matters and events must not be dropped; replacing `EventEmitter` patterns where `async for...of` iteration is preferable to callback registration.
- **Do NOT use when:** events can be missed by slow consumers (backpressure is not handled here — the producer emits freely); use a `ReadableStream` with a `QueuingStrategy` if buffering and backpressure are required.
- **Alternative:** `EventTarget` + `addEventListener` for callback-based consumption; `ReadableStream` with `ReadableStreamDefaultController` for backpressure-aware event queues.

## Cycle 33 Community Gotchas

**CG33-1. `ReadableStream.from()` Consumes the Source Iterable Exactly Once — Subsequent Reads Fail Silently** [community] — `ReadableStream.from(iter)` pulls chunks from the iterable's `next()` method one at a time; once the stream is fully consumed or cancelled, the underlying iterator's `return()` is called and the iterator is exhausted. WHY it causes problems: developers who call `stream.tee()` expect both branches to independently replay the source iterable — but `tee()` buffers chunks in memory between the two readers rather than replaying the original iterable; code that tries to re-pipe a fully consumed stream (e.g., logging and then sending) gets zero bytes on the second pipe because the iterator is already at `done: true`. Fix: always call `stream.tee()` before any consumption if you need two independent readers; never attempt to re-read a stream after a first `pipeTo`/`getReader` cycle; for replay semantics, wrap the iterable factory (not the stream) in a function and call it twice.

**CG33-2. `transferControlToOffscreen()` Permanently Transfers Canvas Control — `getContext()` on the Original Element Returns `null` Forever** [community] — After `canvas.transferControlToOffscreen()`, the original `<canvas>` DOM element becomes a placeholder: any subsequent call to `canvas.getContext('2d')` or `canvas.getContext('webgl')` returns `null` — not an error, but a silent `null`. WHY it causes problems: teams that conditionally use OffscreenCanvas (feature-detecting and falling back to main-thread canvas) often forget to gate the fallback path on whether `transferControlToOffscreen` was called; the fallback calls `canvas.getContext('2d')` expecting a live context, gets `null`, then tries to call `ctx.fillRect(...)` and throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null`. Fix: track a boolean flag (`let transferred = false`) set to `true` after the transfer call; always check this flag before accessing the canvas context in any code path that might run on either side.

**CG33-3. Navigation API `event.intercept()` Must Be Called Synchronously in the `navigate` Handler — Async Call Throws** [community] — `event.intercept({ handler })` must be invoked during the synchronous execution of the `navigate` event handler. The handler callback itself may be async, but the `intercept()` call must happen before the first `await`. WHY it causes problems: developers who `await` a permission check or authentication verification before calling `event.intercept()` find that the navigation has already committed by the time they call `intercept`, throwing `DOMException: Navigation was already committed` — the URL has changed but the content has not updated, leaving the page in an inconsistent state. Fix: call `event.intercept()` unconditionally (or after a synchronous check of cached state only) at the top of the handler; defer async work to inside the `handler` async function passed as the option.

**CG33-4. `MessagePort` Leaks When Neither End Calls `close()` — Ports Are Not GC-Eligible While the MessageChannel Is Reachable** [community] — `MessageChannel` ports hold strong references to each other's event listeners; a port that has an `onmessage` listener set on it is kept alive by the browser's event dispatch infrastructure even if your JavaScript code drops all other references to it. WHY it causes problems: in patterns where `MessageChannel` is used for one-shot RPC (create channel, send request, get response, done), teams that never call `port.close()` after the reply is received accumulate live ports for every RPC call; in applications making thousands of RPC calls per session (e.g., micro-frontend communication buses), this produces a measurable memory leak visible in Chrome DevTools memory snapshots as growing `MessagePort` count. Fix: always call `port1.close()` and `port2.close()` after the exchange is complete; for one-shot patterns, close the port inside the `onmessage` handler immediately after processing the first message.

**CG33-5. `navigator.permissions.query()` Returns a Snapshot `state` at Query Time — Not a Live Binding — Only `onchange` Reflects Updates** [community] — The `status.state` property on a `PermissionStatus` object reflects the state at the moment of the last `change` event or the initial query — it does not automatically update to reflect real-time permission changes unless you listen to `onchange`. WHY it causes problems: code that stores `const { state } = await navigator.permissions.query(...)` and later checks `state === 'granted'` will always check the originally captured string (a primitive), never the live value; even storing `const status = await ...` and checking `status.state` without an `onchange` listener can return a stale value if the permission was revoked between the query and the check — the `state` property IS live on the object, but it only updates when the browser dispatches a `change` event, which requires the listener to have been registered. Fix: always register `status.addEventListener('change', handler)` immediately after querying if you need live state; re-read `status.state` inside that handler rather than caching the string value.

**CG33-6. `reportError()` in a Worker Does Not Forward the Error to the Main Thread Automatically** [community] — Calling `reportError(err)` inside a Web Worker dispatches an `ErrorEvent` on the worker's global scope — not on `window`. The worker's own `onerror` / `self.addEventListener('error', ...)` handler is triggered, but the main thread's `window.onerror` is only notified if the worker's error event is NOT cancelled (i.e., no handler calls `event.preventDefault()`). WHY it causes problems: teams that add `self.addEventListener('error', handler)` inside a worker to call `reportError` for enrichment inadvertently suppress the automatic propagation to the main thread (because adding any listener to a worker's `error` event cancels the default propagation behavior in some engines); the error tracking SDK on the main thread never fires. Fix: inside a worker error handler, after your enrichment logic, either do not call `event.preventDefault()` (let it propagate) OR explicitly forward the error to the main thread via `self.postMessage({ type: 'error', message: err.message, stack: err.stack })` and dispatch it there.

**CG33-7. Module Worker `import.meta.url` Resolves Relative to the Worker Script — Not the Main Thread's Document URL** [community] — Inside a module worker, `import.meta.url` is the URL of the worker script file, not the main page. WHY it causes problems: developers who construct asset URLs inside the worker using `new URL('./assets/data.json', import.meta.url)` get a path relative to the worker file's location, which is correct — but teams that move worker files to a different directory (e.g., from `/src/workers/` to `/src/workers/heavy/`) without updating all `new URL(...)` calls inside the worker find that asset loads silently return 404s because the relative base has changed; additionally, if the worker is served from a CDN path different from the main app, `import.meta.url` will resolve to the CDN origin, making relative fetches cross-origin and triggering CORS errors. Fix: always use explicit absolute paths or pass asset URLs as `postMessage` data from the main thread rather than constructing them inside the worker; if relative construction is necessary, audit `import.meta.url` usage whenever the worker file is relocated.
