### 12. `node:test` Module Mocking — Isolating Imports in Unit Tests (Node.js 22.3+) [official]

`node:test` ships a built-in module mocker via `t.mock.module(specifier, { namedExports })` that replaces a module's exports for the duration of the current test context without touching the real module on disk. Unlike Jest's `jest.mock()`, Node's module mocker takes effect synchronously and does not require hoisting transforms. In Node.js 22.3+ the API supports intercepting ESM named and default exports, letting you swap in stub implementations for `fetch`, `fs`, database clients, or any other dependency without spawning a real process.

```javascript
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

// ── Module under test: src/notifier.mjs ──────────────────────────────────
// import { sendEmail } from './mailer.mjs';
// export async function notifyUser(user) {
//   await sendEmail(user.email, 'Welcome!');
//   return { sent: true, to: user.email };
// }

// ── Test: mock the mailer module ──────────────────────────────────────────
test('notifyUser sends email and returns receipt', async (t) => {
  const sendEmail = t.mock.fn(async () => {});

  t.mock.module('./mailer.mjs', {
    namedExports: { sendEmail },
  });

  // Dynamic import AFTER mock registration — picks up the stub
  const { notifyUser } = await import('./notifier.mjs?t=' + Date.now());
  const result = await notifyUser({ email: 'user@example.com' });

  assert.equal(result.sent, true);
  assert.equal(sendEmail.mock.callCount(), 1);
  assert.equal(sendEmail.mock.calls[0].arguments[0], 'user@example.com');
});

// ── Mocking a built-in module (e.g., node:fs/promises) ───────────────────
test('loadConfig reads and parses the config file', async (t) => {
  const readFile = t.mock.fn(async () => Buffer.from('{"debug":true}'));
  t.mock.module('node:fs/promises', { namedExports: { readFile } });

  const { loadConfig } = await import('./config.mjs?v=' + Date.now());
  const cfg = await loadConfig('/etc/app.json');
  assert.equal(cfg.debug, true);
  assert.equal(readFile.mock.callCount(), 1);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Because ESM has a module registry per realm, the cache-busting query string trick (`?t=Date.now()`) is necessary to force a fresh module evaluation after the mock is installed — without it the previously-cached module (with the real exports) is returned. This creates a new module namespace per test and can accumulate many garbage module records if run in the same process without isolation. Use `isolation: 'process'` (the default) to avoid registry leakage across test files.

---

### 13. `EventTarget` / `CustomEvent` — DOM-Compatible Event Bus in Node.js (Baseline 2022) [official]

Node.js 19+ ships `EventTarget` and `CustomEvent` as globals matching the browser spec. `EventTarget` is the foundation of `AbortSignal`, `ReadableStream`, and `MessageChannel`; using it for custom event buses produces code portable between browser, Deno, and Node.js runtimes. Unlike Node's `EventEmitter`, `EventTarget` supports the `{ once: true }` option and accepts `{ signal }` for automatic listener removal on abort. `CustomEvent.detail` carries arbitrary structured payload without a separate `args` array.

```javascript
// ── Portable event bus using EventTarget ─────────────────────────────────
class AppBus extends EventTarget {
  emit(type, detail) {
    this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent(type, { detail }));
  }
}

const bus = new AppBus();

// ── One-shot subscriber ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
bus.addEventListener('order:created', ({ detail }) => {
  console.log('Order created:', detail.orderId);
}, { once: true });

// ── Signal-bound subscriber: auto-removed when signal aborts ─────────────
const controller = new AbortController();
bus.addEventListener('order:created', ({ detail }) => {
  console.log('Audit log:', detail.orderId);
}, { signal: controller.signal });

bus.emit('order:created', { orderId: 'ORD-001' });
// Both listeners fire

controller.abort();
bus.emit('order:created', { orderId: 'ORD-002' });
// Only the audit listener is gone — 'once' listener already removed

// ── node:test: verify once and signal removal ─────────────────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('once listener fires exactly once', () => {
  const target = new EventTarget();
  let count = 0;
  target.addEventListener('ping', () => count++, { once: true });
  target.dispatchEvent(new Event('ping'));
  target.dispatchEvent(new Event('ping'));
  assert.equal(count, 1);
});

test('signal listener is removed when signal aborts', () => {
  const ctrl   = new AbortController();
  const target = new EventTarget();
  let count = 0;
  target.addEventListener('ping', () => count++, { signal: ctrl.signal });
  target.dispatchEvent(new Event('ping')); // fires: count = 1
  ctrl.abort();
  target.dispatchEvent(new Event('ping')); // no-op: listener removed
  assert.equal(count, 1);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `EventTarget` does not have `removeAllListeners()`, `listenerCount()`, or error-event semantics found in Node's `EventEmitter` — migrating existing `EventEmitter`-heavy code requires adding manual tracking. Uncaught errors thrown inside `EventTarget` listeners are swallowed and dispatched as `error` events on `globalThis` (or lost entirely in some Node.js versions) — always wrap listener bodies in try/catch for error surfaces.

---

### 14. `Intl.Segmenter` — Unicode-Aware Text Segmentation (Baseline 2024) [official]

`Intl.Segmenter` splits text into grapheme clusters, words, or sentences according to Unicode segmentation rules, respecting locale-specific conventions. Unlike splitting on whitespace or character offsets, it correctly handles multi-codepoint emoji (e.g., skin-tone modifiers, ZWJ sequences), ligatures, and CJK word boundaries. `granularity: 'grapheme'` is the correct way to count "visible characters" in a string; `granularity: 'word'` yields word segments with an `isWordLike` flag distinguishing words from punctuation and whitespace.

```javascript
// ── Grapheme-correct string length ────────────────────────────────────────
const emoji = '👨‍👩‍👧‍👦'; // family emoji — 1 grapheme, 11 code units
console.log(emoji.length);                         // 11 — misleading
const seg = new Intl.Segmenter('en', { granularity: 'grapheme' });
console.log([...seg.segment(emoji)].length);       // 1 — correct

// ── Word segmentation for a search index ─────────────────────────────────
function extractWords(text, locale = 'en') {
  const segmenter = new Intl.Segmenter(locale, { granularity: 'word' });
  return [...segmenter.segment(text)]
    .filter(s => s.isWordLike)
    .map(s => s.segment.toLowerCase());
}
console.log(extractWords('Hello, world! How are you?'));
// ['hello', 'world', 'how', 'are', 'you']

// ── CJK word split (no spaces in Chinese) ─────────────────────────────────
const zhSeg = new Intl.Segmenter('zh-CN', { granularity: 'word' });
const zh    = '今天天气很好。';
console.log([...zhSeg.segment(zh)].map(s => s.segment));
// ['今天', '天气', '很好', '。']

// ── node:test: grapheme count vs code-unit count ──────────────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('Intl.Segmenter counts graphemes correctly for ZWJ emoji', () => {
  const text     = '👩‍💻🌍';  // 2 graphemes, many code units
  const segmenter = new Intl.Segmenter('en', { granularity: 'grapheme' });
  const graphemes = [...segmenter.segment(text)];
  assert.equal(graphemes.length, 2);
  assert.ok(text.length > 2);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `Intl.Segmenter` with `granularity: 'word'` uses a bundled Unicode word-boundary dictionary, which may not match the expectations of full-text search engines that apply stemming, stopword removal, or language-specific tokenisation rules — treat it as a lightweight tokeniser and post-process its output. The segmenter object itself is expensive to construct; reuse a single instance per locale+granularity combination rather than creating it inside loops.

---

### 15. `Array.fromAsync()` — Collect Async Iterables Into Arrays (ES2024, Baseline 2024) [official]

`Array.fromAsync(asyncIterable, mapFn?, thisArg?)` is the async counterpart to `Array.from()`. It consumes an async iterable (or sync iterable, or array-like), optionally applying a mapping function, and returns a `Promise<Array>`. This replaces the boilerplate `const result = []; for await (const item of src) result.push(item)` and the ad-hoc `async function collectAll(iter) { ... }` helper that appears in almost every codebase using `for await`. It also handles sync iterables, making it a natural async upgrade path for `Array.from`.

```javascript
// ── Collect all pages from a paginated API into a flat array ─────────────
async function* fetchAllPages(url) {
  let next = url;
  while (next) {
    const { items, nextUrl } = await fetch(next).then(r => r.json());
    yield* items;
    next = nextUrl;
  }
}

const allProducts = await Array.fromAsync(fetchAllPages('/api/products'));
console.log(allProducts.length); // total count across all pages

// ── With map function: transform while collecting ─────────────────────────
async function* readLines(filePath) {
  const { open } = await import('node:fs/promises');
  const file = await open(filePath);
  try {
    for await (const line of file.readLines()) yield line;
  } finally {
    await file.close();
  }
}

const parsed = await Array.fromAsync(
  readLines('/var/log/app.log'),
  line => JSON.parse(line)
);

// ── Works on sync iterables too (upgrade path from Array.from) ────────────
const doubled = await Array.fromAsync([1, 2, 3], async (x) => x * 2);
console.log(doubled); // [2, 4, 6]

// ── node:test ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('Array.fromAsync collects async generator output', async () => {
  async function* gen() { yield 1; yield 2; yield 3; }
  const result = await Array.fromAsync(gen());
  assert.deepEqual(result, [1, 2, 3]);
});

test('Array.fromAsync applies map function to each item', async () => {
  const result = await Array.fromAsync([10, 20], async x => x / 10);
  assert.deepEqual(result, [1, 2]);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `Array.fromAsync` collects the entire iterable into memory before resolving, so it is unsuitable for infinite or very large async generators — use `for await...of` with a `break` condition instead. The map function is awaited sequentially, not concurrently; for parallel mapping collect to a plain array first and then apply `Promise.all(arr.map(asyncFn))`. Available in Node.js 22+ natively; use `core-js/actual/array/from-async` for older targets.

---

## Cycle 41 Community Gotchas

**Gotcha 1 — `Array.fromAsync` Map Function Is Sequential, Not Concurrent** [community] — `Array.fromAsync(iterable, asyncMapper)` awaits each mapped promise before requesting the next item from the iterable. Developers expecting parallel execution (similar to `Promise.all([...arr].map(asyncMapper))`) are surprised that 100 async map operations take the sum of their individual durations rather than the maximum. WHY it causes problems: the API looks identical to `Array.from(arr, syncMapper)` and documentation focuses on the "collects async iterable" use case; the sequential-await behavior of the map function is a footnote. Fix: if the source is finite and concurrent execution is desired, collect to an array first and then apply `Promise.all(arr.map(asyncMapper))`.

**Gotcha 2 — `structuredClone` Silently Strips Class Prototype Methods** [community] — `structuredClone({ ... })` always returns a plain `Object` even when the input is an instance of a custom class. Properties are deep-cloned but the prototype chain is not preserved — the result fails `instanceof MyClass` checks, and any methods defined on `MyClass.prototype` are inaccessible on the clone. WHY it causes problems: developers use `structuredClone` as a universal deep-copy utility and ship code that breaks subtly when the cloned object is passed to a function expecting a typed instance. Fix: for class instances, implement a `clone()` method using `Object.assign(new MyClass(), this)` or a serialise/deserialise pair; reserve `structuredClone` for plain data objects.

**Gotcha 3 — `AbortSignal.any()` Is Not Available Below Node.js 20.3 / Chrome 116** [community] — `AbortSignal.any([sig1, sig2])` is a relatively recent addition; code that uses it in shared utilities silently throws `TypeError: AbortSignal.any is not a function` in environments older than Node.js 20.3. WHY it causes problems: Node.js 18 (LTS until April 2025) does not have `AbortSignal.any`, so cross-platform libraries that depend on it ship broken code to many production servers during the LTS overlap window. Fix: feature-detect before use (`typeof AbortSignal.any === 'function'`) or apply a minimal polyfill: `AbortSignal.any ??= (sigs) => { const c = new AbortController(); sigs.forEach(s => s.addEventListener('abort', () => c.abort(s.reason))); return c.signal; }`.

**Gotcha 4 — `node:test` Module Mock Requires Dynamic Import After `mock.module()` Is Called** [community] — A top-level `import { something } from './module.mjs'` at the top of a test file is evaluated before any test runs, so the module is already cached in the ESM registry before `t.mock.module()` can replace it. Calling `mock.module` and then using the already-imported binding returns the real implementation, not the mock. WHY it causes problems: developers familiar with Jest's hoisted `jest.mock()` calls expect the mock to intercept all uses of the module name globally — but Node's module mocker only affects imports that occur after the mock is registered. Fix: always use a dynamic `await import('./module.mjs?v=...')` inside the test body, after calling `t.mock.module()`.

**Gotcha 5 — `Intl.Segmenter` Construction Is Expensive — Do Not Create Inside Loops** [community] — Each `new Intl.Segmenter(locale, options)` call loads a Unicode segmentation table for the requested locale and options combination. Creating a new `Intl.Segmenter` on every call of a text-processing function in a hot loop can be 50–200x slower than reusing a single cached instance. WHY it causes problems: developers prototype with `new Intl.Segmenter()` at the call site (matching the natural pattern for other `Intl` constructors) and do not notice the performance regression in unit tests that only process small inputs. Fix: cache `Intl.Segmenter` instances keyed by `${locale}:${granularity}` in a module-level `Map`, initialised lazily on first use.

**Gotcha 6 — `Math.sumPrecise` Does Not Fix Literal Imprecision** [community] — `Math.sumPrecise([0.1, 0.2])` still returns `0.30000000000000004`. Developers who adopt `Math.sumPrecise` expecting it to solve all floating-point arithmetic issues are confused when the classic `0.1 + 0.2` problem persists. WHY it causes problems: the imprecision in `0.1 + 0.2` occurs because both decimal literals are already imprecise when parsed by the JS engine — `Math.sumPrecise` solves accumulation errors across long sums, not individual term precision. Fix: understand that `Math.sumPrecise` targets large-array summation stability; for exact decimal arithmetic use `Decimal.js` or store monetary values as integers (cents) so individual operations remain exact.

## Cycle 42 — 2026-05-14

### 1. `Promise.try()` — Uniform Async Error Surface (Baseline 2025) [official]

`Promise.try(fn, ...args)` calls `fn` synchronously with the supplied arguments and wraps its outcome in a Promise, regardless of whether `fn` is synchronous or asynchronous. A synchronous return value produces an immediately fulfilled Promise; a synchronous throw produces an immediately rejected one; an async return propagates naturally. This eliminates the classic `Promise.resolve().then(fn)` workaround, which defers execution to a microtask even for sync functions, and the even more fragile `new Promise(r => r(fn()))` pattern that fails to catch synchronous throws cleanly. `Promise.try` makes it safe to write middleware and plugin systems that accept callbacks of unknown sync/async nature.

```javascript
// ── Uniform error surface for a plugin system ─────────────────────────────
async function runPlugin(plugin, context) {
  // plugin.execute may be sync or async — both are handled identically
  return Promise.try(plugin.execute.bind(plugin), context);
}

const syncPlugin  = { execute: (ctx) => `sync result for ${ctx.id}` };
const asyncPlugin = { execute: async (ctx) => `async result for ${ctx.id}` };
const badPlugin   = { execute: () => { throw new Error('plugin crashed'); } };

// All three call-sites look identical; errors go through .catch uniformly
await runPlugin(syncPlugin,  { id: 'A' }).then(console.log); // 'sync result for A'
await runPlugin(asyncPlugin, { id: 'B' }).then(console.log); // 'async result for B'
await runPlugin(badPlugin,   { id: 'C' }).catch(console.error); // Error: plugin crashed

// ── node:test ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('Promise.try catches sync throws as rejections', async () => {
  const p = Promise.try(() => { throw new Error('boom'); });
  await assert.rejects(p, { message: 'boom' });
});

test('Promise.try forwards arguments to callback', async () => {
  const result = await Promise.try((a, b) => a + b, 3, 7);
  assert.equal(result, 10);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `Promise.try` always schedules resolution as a microtask even when the callback is synchronous, introducing one event-loop tick of latency. If you need a truly synchronous result and control the callback's type, call the function directly. Available natively in Node.js 24+; use `core-js/actual/promise/try` or a one-liner shim (`Promise.try ??= (fn, ...args) => new Promise(r => r(fn(...args)))`) for older targets.

---

### 2. `Promise.withResolvers()` — Deferred Pattern Without Nesting (Baseline 2024) [official]

`Promise.withResolvers()` returns `{ promise, resolve, reject }` as a plain object, making the resolution functions available in the same outer scope as the promise without nesting them in an executor callback. This is the standard formalisation of the "deferred" pattern that developers have hand-rolled with `let resolve, reject; const p = new Promise((res, rej) => { resolve = res; reject = rej; })` since Promises were introduced. It is especially valuable when resolve/reject must be called from multiple event listeners or passed to external callbacks without a wrapper closure. The method is subclass-aware and respects custom `Promise` constructors.

```javascript
// ── Event-to-Promise bridge: readable stream to async iterable ────────────
import { createReadStream } from 'node:fs';

async function* streamLines(path) {
  const stream = createReadStream(path, { encoding: 'utf8' });
  let { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers();

  stream.on('error', reject);
  stream.on('end',   resolve);
  stream.on('readable', resolve);

  let buffer = '';
  while (true) {
    await promise;
    if (!stream.readable && buffer === '') break;
    let chunk;
    while ((chunk = stream.read()) !== null) {
      buffer += chunk;
      const lines = buffer.split('\n');
      buffer = lines.pop(); // keep incomplete last line
      for (const line of lines) yield line;
    }
    ({ promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers()); // re-arm
  }
  if (buffer) yield buffer;
}

// ── External resolver: resolve/reject surfaced to caller ─────────────────
function createTimeoutPromise(ms) {
  const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(`Timeout after ${ms}ms`)), ms);
  return { promise, cancel: () => { clearTimeout(timer); resolve(); } };
}

// ── node:test ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('Promise.withResolvers resolve and reject work', async () => {
  const { promise, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers();
  resolve(42);
  assert.equal(await promise, 42);
});

test('Promise.withResolvers reject propagates', async () => {
  const { promise, reject } = Promise.withResolvers();
  reject(new Error('deferred fail'));
  await assert.rejects(promise, { message: 'deferred fail' });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Exposing `resolve`/`reject` outside the executor makes it possible to accidentally call them after the promise is already settled (subsequent calls are no-ops but indicate a logic bug). Prefer the `new Promise(executor)` pattern for short, self-contained async operations where the settlement logic is local to the constructor body; reserve `withResolvers` for cases where the settlement is genuinely external to the promise's construction site.

---

### 3. Iterator Helpers — Lazy Chainable Operations on Any Iterator (Baseline Widely Available) [official]

The Iterator Helpers specification adds `map`, `filter`, `flatMap`, `take`, `drop`, `reduce`, `toArray`, `forEach`, `find`, `some`, `every` as methods on `Iterator.prototype`, plus the statics `Iterator.from()`, `Iterator.concat()`, and `Iterator.zip()`. Unlike their `Array.prototype` counterparts, these methods are lazy: each element is pulled through the chain on demand, producing no intermediate arrays. `Iterator.from(iterable)` wraps any iterable (including `Set`, `Map`, generator, or custom iterator) into a full `Iterator` with all helpers attached, without converting to an array first.

```javascript
// ── Lazy pipeline: process a large CSV without loading it all ─────────────
import { createReadStream } from 'node:fs';
import { createInterface } from 'node:readline';

async function* csvRows(path) {
  const rl = createInterface({ input: createReadStream(path) });
  let header = null;
  for await (const line of rl) {
    if (!header) { header = line.split(','); continue; }
    const values = line.split(',');
    yield Object.fromEntries(header.map((h, i) => [h, values[i]]));
  }
}

// Process only the first 100 rows where revenue > 10000, lazily
const topRows = await Iterator.from(csvRows('sales.csv'))
  .filter(row => Number(row.revenue) > 10_000)
  .take(100)
  .map(row => ({ id: row.id, revenue: Number(row.revenue) }))
  .toArray();

// ── Iterator.concat: chain multiple sources without spreading ─────────────
const all = Iterator.concat(
  Iterator.from(new Set([1, 2, 3])),
  Iterator.from(new Map([['a', 4], ['b', 5]]).values()),
  [6, 7, 8]
);
console.log(all.toArray()); // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]

// ── node:test ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('Iterator.from + filter + take is lazy (no full scan)', () => {
  let seen = 0;
  function* naturals() { let n = 0; while (true) { seen++; yield n++; } }
  const result = Iterator.from(naturals()).filter(n => n % 2 === 0).take(3).toArray();
  assert.deepEqual(result, [0, 2, 4]);
  assert.ok(seen < 10, 'should not scan more than necessary');
});

test('Iterator.concat chains multiple iterables', () => {
  const result = Iterator.concat([1, 2], [3, 4], [5]).toArray();
  assert.deepEqual(result, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Iterator helpers are lazy and cannot be rewound — once consumed, the iterator is exhausted. Calling `.toArray()` materialises everything, defeating the memory efficiency for infinite generators; always `take(n)` before `toArray()` on unbounded sources. `Iterator.zip` (available in Chrome 131+, Node.js 22.12+) is not yet in all LTS Node.js builds — feature-detect with `typeof Iterator.zip === 'function'` before use.

---

### 4. `Object.groupBy()` and `Map.groupBy()` — Declarative Collection Grouping (Baseline 2024) [official]

`Object.groupBy(iterable, keyFn)` partitions an iterable into groups, returning a null-prototype plain object keyed by the string/symbol values returned from `keyFn`. `Map.groupBy(iterable, keyFn)` does the same but accepts any value as a key (objects, numbers, symbols) and returns a `Map`. Both supersede the manual `reduce`-to-object pattern that was the community standard before ES2024. The grouping function receives `(element, index)`, and elements are placed into groups in iteration order. Groups are arrays of original element references — not copies.

```javascript
// ── Object.groupBy: partition orders by status ────────────────────────────
const orders = [
  { id: 1, status: 'pending',   total: 100 },
  { id: 2, status: 'shipped',   total: 200 },
  { id: 3, status: 'pending',   total: 150 },
  { id: 4, status: 'delivered', total: 75  },
  { id: 5, status: 'shipped',   total: 300 },
];

const byStatus = Object.groupBy(orders, o => o.status);
// { pending: [{...},{...}], shipped: [{...},{...}], delivered: [{...}] }
console.log(byStatus.pending.length);  // 2
console.log(byStatus.delivered[0].id); // 4

// ── Map.groupBy: group by a non-string key (Date bucket) ──────────────────
function weekBucket(date) {
  const d = new Date(date);
  d.setHours(0, 0, 0, 0);
  d.setDate(d.getDate() - d.getDay()); // round to Sunday
  return d;
}

const events = [
  { name: 'Alpha', date: '2026-05-11' },
  { name: 'Beta',  date: '2026-05-13' },
  { name: 'Gamma', date: '2026-05-18' },
];

const byWeek = Map.groupBy(events, e => weekBucket(e.date));
// Map keyed by Date objects — only Map.groupBy supports non-primitive keys

// ── node:test ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('Object.groupBy correctly partitions items', () => {
  const items  = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];
  const groups = Object.groupBy(items, n => n % 2 === 0 ? 'even' : 'odd');
  assert.deepEqual(groups.even, [2, 4, 6]);
  assert.deepEqual(groups.odd,  [1, 3, 5]);
});

test('Object.groupBy result has null prototype (no inherited keys)', () => {
  const result = Object.groupBy(['a'], s => s);
  assert.equal(Object.getPrototypeOf(result), null);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `Object.groupBy` coerces all key values to strings — objects passed as keys become `'[object Object]'`, silently merging all such entries into one group. Use `Map.groupBy` whenever the key type is non-primitive. The returned arrays reference the original elements directly; mutations to elements affect both the grouped result and the original iterable, so clone elements (`structuredClone`) if immutable grouping snapshots are needed.

### 5. ES2025 `Set` Composition Methods — Set Algebra Without Manual Loops [official]

ES2025 added seven methods to `Set.prototype`: `union(other)`, `intersection(other)`, `difference(other)`, `symmetricDifference(other)`, `isSubsetOf(other)`, `isSupersetOf(other)`, and `isDisjointFrom(other)`. All methods accept any "set-like" object that has `size`, `has()`, and `keys()`, meaning they interoperate with `Map` (keyed by entries) and custom collections. All return new `Set` instances — they are non-mutating. These methods are now Baseline Widely Available across all modern browsers and Node.js 22+.

```javascript
// ── Permission system: required vs granted capabilities ───────────────────
const required  = new Set(['read', 'write', 'execute']);
const granted   = new Set(['read', 'write', 'admin']);

const missing   = required.difference(granted);          // Set { 'execute' }
const extra     = granted.difference(required);          // Set { 'admin' }
const common    = required.intersection(granted);        // Set { 'read', 'write' }
const all       = required.union(granted);               // Set { 'read', 'write', 'execute', 'admin' }
const exclusive = required.symmetricDifference(granted); // Set { 'execute', 'admin' }

console.log(required.isSubsetOf(granted));     // false — 'execute' is missing
console.log(new Set(['read']).isSubsetOf(granted)); // true
console.log(missing.isDisjointFrom(common));   // true — no overlap

// ── Feature flag gating: compute effective flags ──────────────────────────
function effectiveFlags(base, overrides, disabled) {
  return base.union(overrides).difference(disabled);
}

const result = effectiveFlags(
  new Set(['featureA', 'featureB']),
  new Set(['featureC']),
  new Set(['featureB'])
);
console.log([...result]); // ['featureA', 'featureC']

// ── node:test ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('Set.intersection returns shared elements', () => {
  const a = new Set([1, 2, 3, 4]);
  const b = new Set([3, 4, 5, 6]);
  assert.deepEqual([...a.intersection(b)], [3, 4]);
});

test('Set.difference does not mutate receiver', () => {
  const a = new Set([1, 2, 3]);
  const b = new Set([2, 3]);
  const d = a.difference(b);
  assert.equal(a.size, 3); // original unchanged
  assert.deepEqual([...d], [1]);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** All composition methods return a new `Set` with no mutation of the receiver — assigning to a throwaway variable silently discards the result; ESLint's `no-unused-expressions` rule will not catch a bare method call but `no-unused-vars` will catch an assigned-but-unused result. `isSubsetOf` / `isSupersetOf` short-circuit on size mismatch before iterating elements, making them efficient for large sets. Performance degrades to `O(n)` for `intersection` and `difference` since no sorted-set optimisation is applied — for very large sets use a sorted data structure.

### 6. `RegExp.escape()` — Safe Dynamic Regex Construction (Baseline 2025) [official]

`RegExp.escape(string)` escapes all regex-syntax-significant characters in the input string so it can safely be embedded as a literal pattern in a `RegExp` constructor argument. The first character of the result is always hex-escaped (e.g., `h` → `\x68`) to prevent it from being misread as a backreference or quantifier prefix when spliced into a larger pattern. Before this method, developers used community utilities like `escape-string-regexp` or hand-rolled replacers, which frequently missed edge cases (e.g., the `/` delimiter in `/.../` literal syntax, or `\0` as a null character). `RegExp.escape` covers all cases defined in the ECMAScript `SyntaxCharacter` grammar.

```javascript
// ── Safe user-driven search highlighting ─────────────────────────────────
function highlightAll(text, userQuery) {
  const pattern = new RegExp(RegExp.escape(userQuery), 'gi');
  return text.replace(pattern, match => `<mark>${match}</mark>`);
}

// userQuery contains regex metacharacters — still safe
console.log(highlightAll('Price is $5.00 (USD)', '$5.00'));
// 'Price is <mark>$5.00</mark> (USD)'

// ── Multi-keyword match: each keyword escaped individually ─────────────────
function buildKeywordPattern(keywords, flags = 'gi') {
  const escaped = keywords.map(RegExp.escape).join('|');
  return new RegExp(escaped, flags);
}

const pattern = buildKeywordPattern(['node.js', 'v8', 'tc39?', 'c++']);
console.log('node.js uses v8'.match(pattern)); // ['node.js', 'v8']
// 'tc39?' and 'c++' metacharacters safely escaped

// ── node:test ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('RegExp.escape prevents metacharacter injection', () => {
  const userInput = '$.+*?[]()|{}\\^/';
  const re = new RegExp(RegExp.escape(userInput));
  assert.ok(re.test(userInput),     'escaped literal must match itself');
  assert.ok(!re.test('anything'),   'must not match unrelated strings');
});

test('RegExp.escape escapes the first character even if plain letter', () => {
  const escaped = RegExp.escape('hello');
  assert.ok(escaped.startsWith('\\x'), 'first char should be hex-escaped');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `RegExp.escape` escapes the first character unconditionally (even plain letters), producing patterns like `\x68ello` for `hello`. This is safe for use inside `new RegExp(...)` but looks alarming if logged or stored — never post-process or trim the output. The method is a Baseline 2025 newcomer (May 2025); use `escape-string-regexp@5` for compatibility with older environments. `RegExp.escape` does not sanitise input for use in other contexts such as CSS selectors or HTML attributes.

### 7. `Float16Array` — Half-Precision Typed Arrays for ML and GPU Workloads (Baseline 2025) [official]

`Float16Array` is a typed array subclass storing IEEE 754 half-precision (16-bit) floating-point numbers, analogous to `Float32Array` but at half the memory footprint. It pairs with `DataView.prototype.getFloat16()`/`setFloat16()` for reading single FP16 values at arbitrary byte offsets. The primary use cases are WebGPU buffers, WebGL vertex data, and deep-learning model weights where FP16 is the storage format. `Math.f16round(x)` is the companion helper that rounds a standard JS number to the nearest FP16 value, useful for validating that computations remain within FP16 range before storing.

```javascript
// ── Round-trip: JS number → FP16 storage → JS number ─────────────────────
const weights = new Float16Array(4);
weights[0] = 0.5;
weights[1] = 1.0;
weights[2] = 0.123456789; // rounded to nearest FP16
weights[3] = 70000;       // > 65504: stored as Infinity

console.log(weights[0]); // 0.5 (exactly representable in FP16)
console.log(weights[2]); // ~0.123046875 (nearest FP16 value)
console.log(weights[3]); // Infinity

// ── DataView.setFloat16: explicit byte-order control for GPU buffers ───────
const buf  = new ArrayBuffer(8);
const view = new DataView(buf);
view.setFloat16(0, 3.14, /*littleEndian=*/true);
view.setFloat16(2, 2.71, true);
console.log(view.getFloat16(0, true)); // ~3.140625

// ── Math.f16round: validate before storage ───────────────────────────────
function safeStoreF16(arr, index, value) {
  const f16 = Math.f16round(value);
  if (!isFinite(f16)) throw new RangeError(`${value} overflows FP16 range`);
  arr[index] = f16;
}

// ── node:test ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('Float16Array stores BYTES_PER_ELEMENT of 2', () => {
  assert.equal(Float16Array.BYTES_PER_ELEMENT, 2);
});

test('Math.f16round rounds to nearest FP16', () => {
  const rounded = Math.f16round(0.1);
  assert.ok(Math.abs(rounded - 0.1) < 0.001);
  assert.ok(rounded !== 0.1, 'FP16 cannot exactly represent 0.1');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `Float16Array` values are stored in FP16 precision but read back as standard JS Float64 numbers, so arithmetic done outside the typed array is still full-precision — the precision loss is only at storage and retrieval boundaries. This means `arr[0] + arr[1]` is computed as Float64, not Float16; for GPU-accurate simulation use `Math.f16round` explicitly on each intermediate result. Available in Node.js 22+; polyfill with `float16` npm package for older targets.

---

### 8. `using` Declarations — Deterministic Resource Disposal (ES2025, Limited Availability) [official]

The `using` declaration (Explicit Resource Management, TC39 Stage 4 / ES2025) automatically calls `[Symbol.dispose]()` on a resource when its block scope exits — whether by normal return, early return, or thrown exception. `await using` does the same for `[Symbol.asyncDispose]()`. `DisposableStack` and `AsyncDisposableStack` aggregate multiple disposables for manual orchestration. All disposal errors are wrapped in `SuppressedError`, guaranteeing every disposable's cleanup runs even if earlier ones throw. TypeScript 5.2+ compiles `using` to `try/finally` for older JS targets.

```javascript
// ── Database connection lifecycle ─────────────────────────────────────────
import { createConnection } from 'node:net';

class DbConnection {
  constructor(host, port) { this.socket = createConnection(port, host); }
  async query(sql) { /* ... */ }
  [Symbol.dispose]() {
    this.socket.destroy();
    console.log('connection closed');
  }
}

async function fetchUser(id) {
  using conn = new DbConnection('localhost', 5432); // closed on scope exit
  return conn.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}`);
}

// ── DisposableStack: aggregate multiple resources ─────────────────────────
function withTempFiles(createTempFile) {
  const stack = new DisposableStack();
  const tmp1  = stack.use(createTempFile('a.tmp'));
  const tmp2  = stack.use(createTempFile('b.tmp'));
  // Both files deleted on stack disposal — in reverse order (tmp2, tmp1)
  return { tmp1, tmp2, [Symbol.dispose]: () => stack.dispose() };
}

// ── SuppressedError: all disposers run even if one throws ─────────────────
class Flaky {
  [Symbol.dispose]() { throw new Error('cleanup failed'); }
}

try {
  using a = new Flaky();
  using b = new Flaky();
  throw new Error('business logic error');
} catch (e) {
  // e is SuppressedError: error=cleanup failed, suppressed=business logic error
  console.log(e instanceof SuppressedError); // true
}

// ── node:test: verify disposal order ──────────────────────────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('using disposes in reverse declaration order', () => {
  const log = [];
  class Disposable {
    constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
    [Symbol.dispose]() { log.push(this.name); }
  }
  {
    using a = new Disposable('A');
    using b = new Disposable('B');
    using c = new Disposable('C');
  }
  assert.deepEqual(log, ['C', 'B', 'A']);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `using` is limited to block scopes — it cannot appear at module top level (a syntax error) or in `for...in` initializers. Resources captured in closures are disposed when the declaring scope exits, not when the closure is called — returning a closure that references a `using`-declared resource produces a use-after-disposal bug that TypeScript cannot catch. Browser support is still limited (not Baseline as of 2026); use TypeScript compilation or a Babel transform for production targets outside Node.js 22+.

---

### 9. `Error.isError()` — Reliable Cross-Realm Error Detection (TC39 Stage 4) [official]

`Error.isError(value)` returns `true` if `value` is an intrinsic `Error` instance, using an internal brand check that works across realm boundaries (iframes, `vm.runInNewContext()`, Worker threads). `instanceof Error` fails for cross-realm errors because each realm has its own `Error` constructor; `Object.prototype.toString.call(e) === '[object Error]'` can be spoofed by setting `Symbol.toStringTag`. `Error.isError` closes both gaps with a reliable, unspoofable check, matching the approach used by `Array.isArray` for arrays. It is included in the ECMAScript 2026 draft and is shipping in Chrome 130+/Node.js 24+.

```javascript
// ── Cross-realm error detection in a serialiser ───────────────────────────
function serializeValue(value) {
  if (Error.isError(value)) {
    return {
      type:    'error',
      name:    value.name,
      message: value.message,
      stack:   value.stack,
      cause:   value.cause != null ? serializeValue(value.cause) : undefined,
    };
  }
  if (Array.isArray(value)) return value.map(serializeValue);
  if (value && typeof value === 'object') {
    return Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(value).map(([k, v]) => [k, serializeValue(v)]));
  }
  return value;
}

// ── Cross-realm: vm.runInNewContext creates a separate Error constructor ──
import vm from 'node:vm';
const vmError = vm.runInNewContext('new Error("cross-realm")');
console.log(vmError instanceof Error); // false — different realm!
console.log(Error.isError(vmError));   // true  — brand check works

// ── Spoofed object: Error.isError is unfakeable ────────────────────────────
const fake = { [Symbol.toStringTag]: 'Error', message: 'fake' };
console.log(Object.prototype.toString.call(fake)); // '[object Error]' — fooled
console.log(Error.isError(fake));                  // false — brand check resists

// ── node:test ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('Error.isError identifies native errors', () => {
  assert.ok(Error.isError(new Error('e')));
  assert.ok(Error.isError(new TypeError('te')));
  assert.ok(!Error.isError({ message: 'fake', name: 'Error' }));
  assert.ok(!Error.isError(null));
  assert.ok(!Error.isError('string error'));
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `Error.isError` only returns `true` for objects created by native `Error` constructors — plain objects with an `Error`-shaped interface (sometimes used in test mocks or serialised payloads) return `false`. If your codebase passes mock error objects through error-handling middleware, you may need a fallback: `Error.isError(e) || (typeof e === 'object' && e !== null && 'message' in e)`. Feature-detect before use: `typeof Error.isError === 'function'`.

---

### 10. `node:test` Snapshot Testing — Stable Regression Baselines Without External Libraries [official]

`node:test` snapshot testing (stable since Node.js 23.4.0) stores serialised values in `.snapshot` files alongside test files. Calling `t.assert.snapshot(value)` compares `value` to the stored baseline; run with `--test-update-snapshots` to regenerate baselines. `snapshot.setResolveSnapshotPath(fn)` customises where snapshot files are stored, and `snapshot.setDefaultSnapshotSerializers(fns)` allows plugging in custom serialisers (e.g., stable JSON, XML, or custom DSL). This covers the primary use case of Jest's `toMatchSnapshot` / `toMatchInlineSnapshot` without requiring a third-party test framework.

```javascript
// ── test/ui-components.test.mjs ───────────────────────────────────────────
import { test, snapshot } from 'node:test';

// Optional: store snapshots alongside test files with .snap extension
snapshot.setResolveSnapshotPath(testFilePath =>
  testFilePath.replace(/\.test\.mjs$/, '.test.snap')
);

function renderBadge(label, value, color) {
  return `<span class="badge badge--${color}">${label}: ${value}</span>`;
}

test('badge renders correctly', (t) => {
  t.assert.snapshot(renderBadge('Status', 'Active', 'green'));
  t.assert.snapshot(renderBadge('Count',  42,       'blue'));
});

// ── Serialise complex objects: stable key order via custom serialiser ──────
snapshot.setDefaultSnapshotSerializers([
  (value) => {
    if (typeof value === 'object' && value !== null) {
      return JSON.stringify(value, Object.keys(value).sort(), 2);
    }
    return String(value);
  }
]);

test('API response shape is stable', (t) => {
  const response = { status: 200, body: { users: [{ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }] } };
  t.assert.snapshot(response); // keys serialised in sorted order
});

// ── Workflow ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// Generate baselines: node --test --test-update-snapshots test/ui-components.test.mjs
// Verify in CI:       node --test test/ui-components.test.mjs
```

**Tradeoff:** Snapshot files must be committed to version control and reviewed in code review — large or unstable snapshots (e.g., containing timestamps or random IDs) produce spurious diff noise. Always scrub dynamic values before snapshotting (`{ ...obj, createdAt: '<REDACTED>' }`). Snapshot tests can pass incorrectly if the baseline was generated from a bug — always review the initial `.snap` file contents carefully. The custom serialiser is global per test file, not per test — set it once at the top of the file.

---

### 11. `node:test` Test Plans — Assert a Fixed Number of Assertions Will Run [official]

`t.plan(count)` declares that exactly `count` assertions (or subtests) must execute within the test. If the test body runs fewer than `count` assertions (e.g., a callback never fires, or early return skips a branch) the test fails at teardown with a "plan not met" diagnostic. If more assertions run than planned, the test fails immediately. Test plans solve a silent failure mode where async callbacks containing assertions never fire and the test falsely passes because no assertion threw. Plans are set via `test(name, { plan: n }, fn)` or `t.plan(n)` inside the body.

```javascript
// ── Plan ensures the callback fires the expected number of times ──────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { EventEmitter } from 'node:events';

test('EventEmitter fires exactly 3 data events', (t, done) => {
  t.plan(3); // test fails if fewer or more than 3 assertions execute

  const emitter  = new EventEmitter();
  const received = [];

  emitter.on('data', (chunk) => {
    received.push(chunk);
    assert.ok(typeof chunk === 'string', 'each chunk is a string'); // counts as 1
  });

  emitter.emit('data', 'hello');
  emitter.emit('data', 'world');
  emitter.emit('data', '!');
  // If the listener was never registered, plan(3) catches the silent failure
  done();
});

// ── Plan with subtests: ensure all branches execute ────────────────────────
test('processes each item category', { plan: 3 }, async (t) => {
  const items = ['widget', 'gadget', 'doohickey'];
  for (const item of items) {
    await t.test(`processes ${item}`, () => {
      assert.ok(item.length > 0);
    });
  }
});

// ── Declare plan in options rather than body ───────────────────────────────
test('quick assertion count guard', { plan: 2 }, (t) => {
  assert.equal(1 + 1, 2);
  assert.ok(true);
  // A third assert.equal here would fail the test immediately
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `t.plan(n)` counts `assert.*` calls and `t.test()` subtests, but does not count `assert.throws`/`assert.rejects` as two assertions — each is still one plan unit. Plans add maintenance burden: changing the assertion count in a test requires updating the plan number; teams should treat plan values as part of the test contract and update them deliberately. Avoid plans in tests with conditional branching where assertion count varies — use separate tests for each branch instead.

---

### 12. `node:test` Built-in Code Coverage — Zero-Dependency Branch and Line Reporting [official]

`node --test --experimental-test-coverage` collects V8 line, branch, and function coverage and prints an ASCII summary table at the end of the test run. Coverage thresholds can be enforced programmatically via `lineCoverage`, `branchCoverage`, and `functionCoverage` options in `run()`. Coverage regions can be excluded with inline comments: `/* node:coverage disable */` / `/* node:coverage enable */` wraps an excluded block, and `/* node:coverage ignore next */` skips a single line. The `--test-coverage-include` and `--test-coverage-exclude` flags target specific file patterns, and the `lcov` reporter generates files compatible with `genhtml` and CI dashboards.

```javascript
// ── Inline coverage exclusion for untestable production branches ──────────
export function processPayload(data) {
  if (!data) throw new TypeError('data required');

  /* node:coverage ignore next 3 */
  if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production-only-path') {
    return specialProductionHandler(data); // excluded from coverage stats
  }

  return data.toString().trim();
}

// ── Programmatic run with enforced thresholds ─────────────────────────────
// scripts/run-tests.mjs
import { run } from 'node:test';

const stream = run({
  files:                ['src/**/*.test.mjs'],
  coverage:             true,
  lineCoverage:         90,   // fail if line coverage < 90%
  branchCoverage:       80,
  functionCoverage:     95,
  coverageExcludeGlobs: ['src/generated/**', 'src/vendor/**'],
});

stream.on('test:coverage', (data) => {
  const pct = data.totals.coveredLinePercent.toFixed(1);
  console.log('Lines covered:', pct + '%');
});

await new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  stream.on('end',   resolve);
  stream.on('error', reject);
});

// ── node:test: parameterised tests to cover all branches ─────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('null input throws', () => {
  assert.throws(() => processPayload(null), TypeError);
});
test('valid input trims string', () => {
  assert.equal(processPayload('  hello  '), 'hello');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `--experimental-test-coverage` is still experimental (the flag name may change before graduation) and reports V8 bytecode coverage rather than source-map-remapped coverage — TypeScript or JSX source files show coverage on the compiled output, not the original source, unless source maps are explicitly supported. Coverage only applies to files that were actually `import`ed or `require`d during the test run — dead-code modules that were never loaded are not reported as 0% covered, creating a false sense of completeness.

---

### 13. `WeakRef` and `FinalizationRegistry` — Cache-Friendly Weak Object References [official]

`WeakRef` holds a weak reference to an object that does not prevent garbage collection. `deref()` returns the target or `undefined` if it has been collected. `FinalizationRegistry` registers a callback to run after an object is collected, receiving a held value (not the collected object itself). The canonical use case is a "dispose-on-eviction" cache: keep strong references only while the cache holder is alive, and let the GC free entries automatically. Both are Baseline Widely Available (Chrome 84, Firefox 79, Safari 14.1, Node.js 14.6+).

```javascript
// ── Weak value cache: automatic eviction without explicit bookkeeping ──────
class WeakCache {
  #cache    = new Map();
  #registry = new FinalizationRegistry((key) => {
    // Called after the value is GC'd — remove the stale map entry
    this.#cache.delete(key);
  });

  get(key) {
    return this.#cache.get(key)?.deref();
  }

  set(key, value) {
    this.#registry.register(value, key, value); // third arg = unregister token
    this.#cache.set(key, new WeakRef(value));
  }

  has(key) {
    return this.get(key) !== undefined;
  }

  delete(key) {
    const ref = this.#cache.get(key);
    if (ref) this.#registry.unregister(ref.deref()); // cancel cleanup
    this.#cache.delete(key);
  }
}

// ── Usage: large objects evicted by GC automatically ─────────────────────
const cache = new WeakCache();
let bigObject = { data: new Uint8Array(1024 * 1024) }; // 1 MB
cache.set('large-buffer', bigObject);
console.log(cache.has('large-buffer')); // true (strong ref alive)

bigObject = null; // drop strong reference — GC may now collect it
// After GC: cache.has('large-buffer') → false, registry callback fires

// ── node:test: test structural behaviour (not GC timing) ─────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('WeakCache returns value while strong ref exists', () => {
  const wc  = new WeakCache();
  const obj = { value: 42 };
  wc.set('k', obj);
  assert.equal(wc.get('k'), obj); // same reference, strong ref alive
  assert.ok(wc.has('k'));
});

test('WeakCache.delete removes entry immediately', () => {
  const wc  = new WeakCache();
  const obj = { x: 1 };
  wc.set('k', obj);
  wc.delete('k');
  assert.ok(!wc.has('k'));
});
```

**Tradeoff:** GC timing is engine-defined and non-deterministic — `deref()` may return the object or `undefined` at any time after the strong reference is dropped, and FinalizationRegistry callbacks may be batched, delayed, or (in theory) never run on short-lived processes. Never use `WeakRef`/`FinalizationRegistry` for logic that must execute reliably; they are only suitable for optional cleanup and cache eviction. Do not write tests that assert GC-dependent behaviour — test only that the cache holds values while a strong reference exists.

---

### 14. `Temporal.PlainDate` Arithmetic — Calendar-Safe Date Calculations [official]

`Temporal.PlainDate` represents a calendar date without time or timezone, analogous to SQL's `DATE`. Arithmetic via `.add(duration)` and `.subtract(duration)` is calendar-aware: adding one month to January 31 yields February 28/29, not a day overflow. `.until(other)` and `.since(other)` return a `Temporal.Duration` between two dates, respecting the calendar system. `PlainDate.compare(a, b)` returns a `-1/0/1` comparator compatible with `Array.prototype.sort`. This API is available via the `@js-temporal/polyfill` package now, with native support landing in browsers as Temporal exits Stage 3 and approaches Baseline.

```javascript
// ── Install polyfill: npm install @js-temporal/polyfill ──────────────────
import { Temporal } from '@js-temporal/polyfill';

// ── Calendar-correct month arithmetic ─────────────────────────────────────
const jan31      = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-01-31');
const nextMonth  = jan31.add({ months: 1 });
console.log(nextMonth.toString()); // '2026-02-28' — clamped to last day of Feb

const today    = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-05-14');
const deadline = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-06-30');
const timeLeft = today.until(deadline, { largestUnit: 'days' });
console.log(`${timeLeft.days} days remaining`); // '47 days remaining'

// ── Business day counter: skip weekends ───────────────────────────────────
function addBusinessDays(date, n) {
  let current = date;
  let added   = 0;
  while (added < n) {
    current = current.add({ days: 1 });
    if (current.dayOfWeek <= 5) added++; // 1=Mon…5=Fri per ISO 8601
  }
  return current;
}

const sla = addBusinessDays(Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-05-14'), 5);
console.log(sla.toString()); // '2026-05-21' (skips Sat/Sun)

// ── Sorting dates with PlainDate.compare ──────────────────────────────────
const dates = ['2026-03-15', '2026-01-01', '2026-12-31'].map(Temporal.PlainDate.from);
dates.sort(Temporal.PlainDate.compare);
console.log(dates.map(d => d.toString())); // ['2026-01-01', '2026-03-15', '2026-12-31']

// ── node:test ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('Temporal.PlainDate clamps month overflow', () => {
  const d = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-01-31').add({ months: 1 });
  assert.equal(d.month, 2);
  assert.equal(d.day,   28); // 2026 is not a leap year
});

test('Temporal.PlainDate.until returns correct duration', () => {
  const a    = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-05-01');
  const b    = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-05-14');
  const diff = a.until(b, { largestUnit: 'days' });
  assert.equal(diff.days, 13);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `Temporal.PlainDate` deliberately omits time and timezone information — if you need to convert to/from a Unix timestamp or JS `Date`, you must go through `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` or `Temporal.Instant`, choosing a timezone explicitly. The polyfill adds ~50 KB gzipped to a bundle; for production browser targets, use dynamic import and progressive enhancement until native Temporal is Baseline. `PlainDate` arithmetic defaults to the ISO 8601 calendar — non-ISO calendar systems require an explicit `calendar` option and may clamp differently.

### 15. `node:test` `mock.timers` with `setImmediate` and Mocked `Date` — Complete Timer Queue Control [official]

`node:test`'s `mock.timers` module (Node.js 22+) can mock `setImmediate` in addition to `setTimeout`/`setInterval`, and mocking `Date` alongside timers ensures `Date.now()` and `new Date()` reflect the advanced clock. `t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['setTimeout', 'setImmediate', 'Date'] })` activates all three; `t.mock.timers.tick(ms)` advances the clock by `ms` milliseconds, firing any timers that have elapsed. This combination eliminates the need for `sinon.useFakeTimers()` in `node:test` suites and makes timestamp-dependent logic fully deterministic in tests.

```javascript
// ── Deterministic timer queue including setImmediate ─────────────────────
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('setImmediate fires in correct order with mock timers', (t) => {
  t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['setTimeout', 'setImmediate', 'Date'] });

  const log = [];
  setTimeout(()   => log.push('timeout-10ms'), 10);
  setImmediate(() => log.push('immediate'));
  setTimeout(()   => log.push('timeout-0ms'),   0);

  assert.deepEqual(log, []); // nothing fired yet

  t.mock.timers.tick(0);  // fires timeout-0ms and setImmediate
  t.mock.timers.tick(10); // fires timeout-10ms
  assert.deepEqual(log, ['timeout-0ms', 'immediate', 'timeout-10ms']);
});

// ── TTL cache validation: time-based expiry with mocked Date ──────────────
class TtlCache {
  #store = new Map();
  set(key, value, ttlMs) {
    this.#store.set(key, { value, expiresAt: Date.now() + ttlMs });
  }
  get(key) {
    const entry = this.#store.get(key);
    if (!entry) return undefined;
    return Date.now() < entry.expiresAt ? entry.value : undefined;
  }
}

test('TtlCache respects expiry with mocked Date', (t) => {
  t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['Date'] });

  const cache = new TtlCache();
  cache.set('x', 'hello', 500); // expires 500ms from mock epoch

  assert.equal(cache.get('x'), 'hello');   // valid at t=0

  t.mock.timers.tick(499);
  assert.equal(cache.get('x'), 'hello');   // still valid at t=499

  t.mock.timers.tick(1);                   // advance to t=500
  assert.equal(cache.get('x'), undefined); // expired
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Mocking `setImmediate` does not mock `process.nextTick` or `queueMicrotask` — microtask-queue callbacks still run immediately and cannot be frozen by `mock.timers`. If code under test uses `setInterval`, calling `runAll()` on a still-active interval creates an infinite loop; always call `clearInterval` before `runAll()`, or use `tick(duration)` with a finite ceiling. Mocking `Date` affects all date construction in the process for the duration of the test, including third-party modules — be aware of unintended side effects when mocking globally.

## Cycle 42 Community Gotchas

**Gotcha 1 — `Promise.try` Does Not Synchronously Return Even for Synchronous Callbacks** [community] — `Promise.try(() => 42)` always returns a Promise, never a raw value. Code written as `const result = Promise.try(syncFn); doSomethingWith(result)` passes a Promise object to `doSomethingWith`, not the return value. WHY it causes problems: developers use `Promise.try` as a "safe call" wrapper expecting to get the value back directly when the function is synchronous — the same way `syncFn()` would return it. The microtask boundary is invisible and the bug often only appears in edge cases where the caller checks the type of `result`. Fix: always `await` the result of `Promise.try`, even when you know the callback is synchronous.

**Gotcha 2 — `Object.groupBy` Returns a Null-Prototype Object, Breaking Inherited Method Calls** [community] — The object returned by `Object.groupBy` has `null` as its prototype (`Object.getPrototypeOf(result) === null`). Code that subsequently calls `result.hasOwnProperty('key')` or `result.toString()` throws `TypeError: result.hasOwnProperty is not a function` because these inherited methods are absent. WHY it causes problems: developers use `Object.groupBy` output as a plain object and pass it to utilities that assume a normal `Object` prototype — serialisers, loggers, and ORMs that call `.toString()` or `.constructor` all break silently. Fix: wrap the result when prototype methods are needed: `Object.assign(Object.create(Object.prototype), result)`, or use only `Object.keys(result)` and bracket access.

**Gotcha 3 — Iterator Helpers Consume the Iterator Permanently; There Is No Reset** [community] — Once an `Iterator` is fully or partially consumed by a helper chain (`.filter(...).take(n).toArray()`), the underlying iterator's internal state is advanced and cannot be rewound. Calling `.toArray()` on the same helper-chain variable again returns an empty array, not the original elements. WHY it causes problems: developers used to `Array` methods (which read from the unchanged array each time) expect to be able to call `.filter(...).take(10).toArray()` twice on the same iterator and get the same result. Fix: create a new iterator from the source each time (`Iterator.from(array)` re-wraps the original array), or materialise the partial result to an array before applying further operations.

**Gotcha 4 — `using` Declarations Dispose at Scope Exit, Not When the Last Reference Is Dropped** [community] — A `using conn = openConnection()` declared at the top of a function disposes `conn` when the function returns — but returning a closure that uses `conn` extends the apparent lifetime of `conn` without extending its disposal lifetime. The closure holds a reference to the now-disposed object, producing use-after-disposal bugs at call time. WHY it causes problems: developers familiar with Go's `defer` or C#'s `using` expect disposal to happen when the last reference is dropped, not when the declaring scope exits — the difference only manifests when closures escape the scope, which may happen in passing. Fix: move `using` declarations to the narrowest possible scope; never capture `using`-declared values in closures or return them from the function.

**Gotcha 5 — `Error.isError()` Returns `false` for Plain-Object Mock Errors** [community] — Mock error objects such as `{ message: 'fail', name: 'Error', stack: '...' }` pass `instanceof Error` checks in the same realm but return `false` from `Error.isError()`. Test code that creates mock errors as plain objects and then passes them through production error-handling paths (which use `Error.isError`) will silently cause those paths to ignore the mocks. WHY it causes problems: migrating from `instanceof Error` to `Error.isError` breaks tests that use plain-object error mocks without updating the mock factories to use real `Error` instances. Fix: update mock factories to `Object.assign(new Error(message), extraProps)` so mocks pass both `instanceof Error` and `Error.isError`.

**Gotcha 6 — `node:test` Snapshot File Must Be Regenerated Intentionally After Any Output Change** [community] — When `t.assert.snapshot(value)` is called with a value whose serialised form differs from the stored baseline, the test immediately fails with a diff — it does not auto-update. Developers who refactor component output intentionally must run `node --test --test-update-snapshots` and commit the updated `.snap` file before CI passes. WHY it causes problems: developers make intentional improvements, CI fails, and the team perceives this as a flaky test — they delete the snapshot and re-run, losing the safety that the baseline provides. Fix: treat snapshot updates as a deliberate workflow step: run `--test-update-snapshots`, inspect the diff in `git diff`, and commit the snapshot as part of the feature PR.

**Gotcha 7 — `Float16Array` Silently Overflows to `Infinity` Without Throwing** [community] — Assigning a value greater than 65504 (the maximum finite FP16 value) to a `Float16Array` element silently stores `Infinity` without any error or warning. Similarly, values below −65504 become `-Infinity` silently. WHY it causes problems: ML pipelines that load weights from a Float32 model checkpoint and store them in Float16 without range-checking silently corrupt the model when any weight exceeds FP16 range, producing NaN gradients and diverging training runs with no obvious diagnostic. Fix: always validate with `Math.f16round(value)` — if the result is non-finite, the value is out of FP16 range. Add a guard: `if (!isFinite(Math.f16round(w))) throw new RangeError(...)`.

**Gotcha 8 — `Set` Composition Methods Return Elements in Receiver-Insertion Order, Not Value Order** [community] — `setA.intersection(setB)` preserves the order of elements as they appear in `setA`, not `setB`. When two sets have the same elements in different insertion orders, `setA.union(setB)` appends `setB` elements after `setA`'s, so `b.union(a)` produces a different order than `a.union(b)`. Code that compares the array form of two union results for equality will fail when the inputs were built in different orders. WHY it causes problems: developers assume set operations are commutative for output order — they are commutative for membership, but not for iteration order. Fix: if a deterministic stable output order matters, always sort the result: `[...setA.union(setB)].toSorted()`.

## Cycle 43 — 2026-05-14

### 1. `Promise.withResolvers()` — Externalised Resolve/Reject for Deferred Patterns [official]

`Promise.withResolvers()` returns `{ promise, resolve, reject }` as a plain object, eliminating the ceremony of capturing resolve/reject from inside an executor closure. The primary use case is wiring event emitters and stream events to a Promise without nesting the entire subscription inside the executor. Unlike the manual `let resolve; const p = new Promise(r => resolve = r)` pattern, the intent is explicit and the resolve/reject functions are in the same scope as the promise from the first line. Baseline 2024: Chrome 119, Firefox 121, Node.js 22.

```javascript
// ── Stream → async iterable using Promise.withResolvers ───────────────────
import { Readable } from 'node:stream';
import { test }     from 'node:test';
import assert       from 'node:assert/strict';

async function* readableToChunks(stream) {
  let { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers();

  stream.on('error',    (err)  => reject(err));
  stream.on('end',      ()     => resolve(null));     // null = done sentinel
  stream.on('readable', ()     => resolve(stream));   // data available

  while (true) {
    const src = await promise;
    if (src === null) return;                         // stream ended cleanly

    let chunk;
    while ((chunk = stream.read()) !== null) yield chunk;

    // Re-arm for the next readable / end event
    ({ promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers());
  }
}

test('readableToChunks yields all data', async () => {
  const stream = Readable.from(['hello', ' ', 'world']);
  const chunks = [];
  for await (const chunk of readableToChunks(stream)) {
    chunks.push(chunk.toString());
  }
  assert.deepEqual(chunks.join(''), 'hello world');
});

// ── Timeout-race safety: always pair with a deadline ─────────────────────
async function waitForEvent(emitter, event, timeoutMs = 3000) {
  const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(`Timeout: ${event}`)), timeoutMs);
  emitter.once(event, (data) => { clearTimeout(timer); resolve(data); });
  return promise;
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The deferred promise pattern makes it trivial to create promises that never settle if the source event never fires — always race against a timeout (`Promise.race([promise, deadline])`) in test and production code. `Promise.withResolvers()` is generic and supports subclassing via `Promise.withResolvers.call(SubclassConstructor)`, but this is rarely needed. Unlike `new Promise()`, the returned object is a plain object, not itself a thenable — ensure you always `await promise`, not `await { promise, resolve, reject }`.

---

### 2. `Array.fromAsync()` — Materialising Async Iterables and Mixed Promise Arrays [official]

`Array.fromAsync(items, mapFn?)` is the async analogue of `Array.from()`. It accepts async iterables (generators, readable streams, paginated APIs), sync iterables of promises, and array-like objects with promise-valued indexed properties. Unlike `Promise.all([...iter].map(fn))`, `Array.fromAsync` awaits items sequentially — this trades concurrency for lazy back-pressure, making it appropriate for large or infinite iterables where loading all items into memory upfront is impractical. Baseline 2024: available across modern browsers and Node.js 22.

```javascript
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert   from 'node:assert/strict';

// ── Paginated API consumer ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
async function* fetchAllPages(endpoint) {
  let cursor = null;
  do {
    const url  = cursor ? `${endpoint}?after=${cursor}` : endpoint;
    const resp = await fetch(url);
    const body = await resp.json();
    yield* body.items;
    cursor = body.nextCursor ?? null;
  } while (cursor !== null);
}

// Materialise all pages as a single flat array (sequential awaits per item)
// const allItems = await Array.fromAsync(fetchAllPages('/api/events'));

// ── MapFn applied to each resolved value ─────────────────────────────────
async function doubleAfterDelay(n) {
  await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 5)); // simulate async work
  return n * 2;
}

test('Array.fromAsync applies async mapFn sequentially', async () => {
  const result = await Array.fromAsync([1, 2, 3], doubleAfterDelay);
  assert.deepEqual(result, [2, 4, 6]);
});

// ── Mixed array: sync values and Promises ────────────────────────────────
test('Array.fromAsync unwraps promises in a sync iterable', async () => {
  const mixed  = [Promise.resolve('a'), 'b', Promise.resolve('c')];
  const result = await Array.fromAsync(mixed);
  assert.deepEqual(result, ['a', 'b', 'c']);
});

// ── Contrast: use Promise.all for concurrent resolution ──────────────────
// Promise.all([...iter].map(fn)) — all requests run in parallel
// Array.fromAsync(iter, fn) — each request waits for the previous to settle
```

**Tradeoff:** `Array.fromAsync` processes items sequentially, so 100 items with 100 ms each take ~10 seconds total, whereas `Promise.all(arr.map(fn))` takes ~100 ms for all items. Use `Array.fromAsync` for lazy iterables and back-pressure scenarios; use `Promise.all` for known finite arrays of independent operations. If the async iterable throws, `Array.fromAsync` rejects and the partially-collected array is discarded — there is no partial-results mode analogous to `Promise.allSettled`.
