### Pattern 9 — `import.meta.url` and `import.meta.resolve()` for Module-Relative Paths [official]

`import.meta.url` gives every ES module its own absolute URL (or `file://` path in Node.js), solving the `__dirname`/`__filename` absence in ES module scope. `import.meta.resolve(specifier)` resolves a specifier against the current module's URL using the same algorithm the runtime uses for imports, respecting `package.json` `"exports"` maps and import maps. Both are synchronous and available without any imports.

```javascript
// Node.js: replace __dirname / __filename
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
import { dirname, join }  from 'node:path';
import { readFileSync }   from 'node:fs';

const __filename = fileURLToPath(import.meta.url);
const __dirname  = dirname(__filename);

// Load a sibling data file relative to this module
const schema = JSON.parse(
  readFileSync(join(__dirname, 'schema.json'), 'utf8')
);

// import.meta.resolve: resolve package entry points
const coreUrl = import.meta.resolve('some-lib/core');
// respects package.json "exports" map conditions

// Browser: pass query params to a module
// <script type="module" src="./app.mjs?theme=dark&locale=en-GB"></script>
const params = new URL(import.meta.url).searchParams;
const theme  = params.get('theme')  ?? 'light';
const locale = params.get('locale') ?? 'en-US';

// Detect if this module is the entrypoint (Node.js)
import { argv } from 'node:process';
const isMain = fileURLToPath(import.meta.url) === argv[1];
if (isMain) { runCLI(); }
```

**Tradeoff.** `import.meta.url` is the URL of the source file before bundling — after Rollup/webpack/esbuild processes the code, `import.meta.url` may point to the output bundle's URL, not the original source file. Asset-loading patterns that use `new URL('./assets/logo.svg', import.meta.url)` require bundler-specific handling (Vite/webpack treat this form specially to emit the asset correctly). Always test asset resolution in both development and production builds; the path is correct in unbundled dev but may shift in bundled output.

---

### Pattern 10 — `import defer` for Lazy Synchronous Module Evaluation [official]

`import defer * as ns from 'module'` (TC39 Stage 3) loads a module and all its transitive dependencies into the module cache but defers their evaluation until the first property access on `ns`. Unlike dynamic `import()`, which is asynchronous, deferred import evaluation is synchronous — no `await` is needed and the calling code retains synchronous semantics. Modules with top-level `await` cannot be deferred; the runtime throws at load time. This pattern mirrors Node.js CommonJS `require()` laziness in an ES module world.

```javascript
// Eagerly loads + executes heavy-analytics module at startup -> slow boot
import * as analytics from './analytics.js';

// Deferred: module is fetched but NOT executed until first access
import defer * as analytics from './analytics.js';

function trackEvent(name, data) {
  // analytics module evaluates HERE on first property access, not at import
  analytics.track(name, data); // synchronous — no await needed
}

// Conditional loading pattern: avoids executing debug tools in production
import defer * as debugTools from './debug-tools.js';

if (process.env.DEBUG) {
  debugTools.init(); // executes module only in debug builds
}

// Works with re-exports: accessing any export triggers evaluation
import defer * as utils from './utils.js';
const { format } = utils; // triggers evaluation here
```

**Tradeoff.** `import defer` is incompatible with modules that have side effects at evaluation time (polyfills, CSS-in-JS injection, global augmentation). Deferring such modules means the side effect fires at an unpredictable point — the first property access — rather than at the module graph evaluation phase. Teams that rely on deterministic side-effect ordering (e.g., polyfill must run before any application code) must keep those modules as eager imports. Also, because the module is fetched but not evaluated, `import defer` does not help with network latency; it only saves evaluation CPU time.

---

### Pattern 11 — `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` for DST-Correct Scheduling [official]

`Temporal.ZonedDateTime` is the richest Temporal type: it holds a wall-clock date+time, a named IANA time zone, and a calendar. It is the correct type for scheduling events that must respect Daylight Saving Time transitions and for converting between time zones. Unlike `new Date()`, which only understands UTC and the host local zone, `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` carries the zone name — meaning addition of a 1-day duration correctly jumps over DST boundaries rather than adding exactly 86400 seconds.

```javascript
import { Temporal } from '@js-temporal/polyfill';

// Create a ZonedDateTime in New York
const meeting = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from(
  '2026-03-08T10:00:00[America/New_York]' // day before DST spring-forward
);

// Add 1 day — correctly lands at 10:00 AM after the spring-forward
const nextDay = meeting.add({ days: 1 });
console.log(nextDay.toString());
// '2026-03-09T10:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]' (note -04:00, not -05:00)

// Wrong with Date:
const d = new Date('2026-03-08T10:00:00-05:00');
const wrongNext = new Date(d.getTime() + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000);
// lands at 11:00 AM — off by one hour because it added exactly 86400s

// Convert between zones
const london = meeting.withTimeZone('Europe/London');
console.log(london.hour); // 15 (UTC+0, 5 hours ahead of EST)

// Round-trip to/from legacy Date
const asDate = new Date(meeting.epochMilliseconds);
const backToZDT = Temporal.Instant
  .fromEpochMilliseconds(asDate.getTime())
  .toZonedDateTimeISO('America/New_York');
```

**Tradeoff.** `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` objects are immutable — every mutation returns a new instance. This is correct and safe, but code ported from legacy `Date` (which uses mutating `.setFullYear()` etc.) produces many short-lived allocation sequences. In tight animation or game loops that compute timestamps at 60fps, batch the Temporal arithmetic outside the render loop and cache the result rather than recomputing every frame.

---

### Pattern 12 — `Atomics.waitAsync()` for Non-Blocking Shared Memory Coordination [official]

`Atomics.waitAsync(ta, index, value, timeout?)` is the main-thread-safe counterpart to the blocking `Atomics.wait()`. It checks whether `ta[index] === value`; if so it returns a pending `Promise` that resolves to `"ok"` when another thread calls `Atomics.notify(ta, index)`, or to `"timed-out"` after the timeout. The main thread is never blocked — the Promise is queued as a microtask callback. It reached Baseline 2025 status.

```javascript
const sab    = new SharedArrayBuffer(16);
const flags  = new Int32Array(sab);

// Main thread: wait for worker to signal readiness (non-blocking)
async function waitForWorkerReady() {
  const READY_INDEX = 0;
  const READY_VALUE = 0; // initial value before worker sets it to 1

  const result = Atomics.waitAsync(flags, READY_INDEX, READY_VALUE, 5000);

  if (!result.async) {
    // Value already changed before we even called waitAsync
    console.log('already ready');
    return;
  }

  const outcome = await result.value;
  if (outcome === 'timed-out') throw new Error('Worker startup timed out');
  console.log('worker is ready');
}

// Worker thread: signal the main thread
// worker.js
const flags = new Int32Array(sharedBuffer);
// ... initialize resources ...
Atomics.store(flags, 0, 1);  // write new value
Atomics.notify(flags, 0, 1); // wake one waiter

// Producer/consumer pattern using waitAsync
async function consumeWhenAvailable(buffer, index) {
  while (true) {
    const current = Atomics.load(buffer, index);
    if (current !== 0) {
      const data = Atomics.exchange(buffer, index, 0);
      process(data);
    } else {
      const r = Atomics.waitAsync(buffer, index, 0, 1000);
      if (r.async) await r.value;
    }
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Atomics.waitAsync` returns a fresh Promise object on every call even when the wait resolves synchronously (`result.async === false`), adding GC pressure in extremely tight polling loops. For scenarios where microtask scheduling is acceptable but allocation must be minimised, consider a hybrid: poll with `Atomics.load` first and only fall back to `waitAsync` after N misses. Also note that the Promise does not guarantee the memory state is still the expected value when it resolves — a second read via `Atomics.load` is always required after `await result.value`.

---

### Pattern 13 — `DisposableStack` for Conditional and Dynamic Resource Accumulation [official]

`DisposableStack` (part of TC39 Explicit Resource Management, Stage 4) is a programmatic complement to the `using` keyword: it accumulates disposables at runtime and disposes them all (LIFO) when `.dispose()` is called. It supports three registration methods: `.use(resource)` for objects with `[Symbol.dispose]`, `.adopt(value, fn)` for values without a dispose method (calls `fn(value)` at disposal), and `.defer(fn)` for arbitrary cleanup callbacks. `stack.move()` transfers all registrations to a new stack, enabling ownership handoff.

```javascript
function buildRequestContext(req) {
  const stack = new DisposableStack();

  // Register cleanup for a resource without Symbol.dispose
  const conn = stack.adopt(openDbConnection(), conn => conn.close());

  // Conditionally register additional cleanup
  if (req.headers['x-trace']) {
    const span = tracer.startSpan('request');
    stack.adopt(span, s => s.finish());
  }

  // Deferred teardown regardless of resource type
  stack.defer(() => metrics.record('request.cleanup'));

  // Transfer ownership to caller; stack is now empty (will not double-dispose)
  return {
    conn,
    cleanup: stack.move(), // caller must call cleanup.dispose()
  };
}

// Caller uses the transferred stack
async function handleRequest(req) {
  const { conn, cleanup } = buildRequestContext(req);
  using _ = cleanup; // disposes when handleRequest() returns or throws

  const data = await conn.query('SELECT 1');
  return data;
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Unlike `using`, `DisposableStack` does not automatically call `.dispose()` — you must either explicitly call it or wrap the stack in a `using _ = stack` declaration. Teams that forget to propagate the stack into a `using` declaration will silently leak resources with no runtime warning. Linters can flag `DisposableStack` instances that are never used with `using` or never have `.dispose()` called directly.

---

### Pattern 14 — `Temporal.PlainDate` for Calendar Arithmetic Without Time Zone Ambiguity [official]

`Temporal.PlainDate` represents a calendar date (year, month, day) with no time or timezone component. It is the correct choice for birthdays, contract dates, billing cycles, and any domain value that is "a date on a calendar" rather than "a moment in time". Unlike `new Date()` (which is always a timestamp), `PlainDate` arithmetic never silently changes based on the host timezone. `add()` and `subtract()` accept a `Temporal.Duration` with date-only fields; `since()` and `until()` return Durations. `with()` returns a new `PlainDate` with one field replaced.

```javascript
import { Temporal } from '@js-temporal/polyfill';

// Create and inspect
const birthday = Temporal.PlainDate.from('1990-07-04');
console.log(birthday.year, birthday.month, birthday.day); // 1990 7 4
console.log(birthday.dayOfWeek); // 3 (Wednesday, ISO weekday)

// Arithmetic
const today    = Temporal.Now.plainDateISO();
const daysOld  = birthday.until(today, { largestUnit: 'days' }).days;

// Next birthday calculation
let nextBirthday = birthday.with({ year: today.year });
if (Temporal.PlainDate.compare(nextBirthday, today) <= 0) {
  nextBirthday = nextBirthday.add({ years: 1 });
}
const daysUntil = today.until(nextBirthday).days;
console.log(`Birthday in ${daysUntil} days`);

// End of month (handles variable month lengths)
const lastDayOfMonth = today.with({ day: today.daysInMonth });

// Sorting: use Temporal.PlainDate.compare
const dates = ['2026-12-01', '2026-01-15', '2026-06-30']
  .map(s => Temporal.PlainDate.from(s))
  .sort(Temporal.PlainDate.compare);
```

**Tradeoff.** Converting `Temporal.PlainDate` to a legacy `Date` for use with APIs that require timestamps requires choosing a time of day and time zone — an ambiguous choice that `PlainDate` intentionally avoids. The conversion `plainDate.toZonedDateTime({ timeZone: 'UTC', plainTime: '00:00' }).toInstant().epochMilliseconds` is verbose but explicit. Abstracting this into a project-level helper (`toTimestamp(date, tz)`) prevents teams from accidentally converting to local midnight (which shifts the date in UTC-positive zones).

---

### Pattern 15 — `Promise.withResolvers()` + Async Queue for Backpressure-Aware Pipelines [official]

`Promise.withResolvers()` (ES2024, Baseline 2024) returns `{ promise, resolve, reject }` — externalising the executor that would otherwise be trapped inside `new Promise(...)`. This makes it easy to build demand-driven async queues where producers only advance when consumers have requested the next value, implementing pull-based backpressure without a ReadableStream.

```javascript
// Demand-driven async queue with bounded buffer
class AsyncQueue {
  #items   = [];
  #waiters = [];
  #closed  = false;

  push(item) {
    if (this.#closed) throw new Error('Queue is closed');
    if (this.#waiters.length > 0) {
      // A consumer is already waiting — resolve immediately
      this.#waiters.shift().resolve({ value: item, done: false });
    } else {
      this.#items.push(item);
    }
  }

  close() {
    this.#closed = true;
    for (const w of this.#waiters) w.resolve({ value: undefined, done: true });
    this.#waiters.length = 0;
  }

  next() {
    if (this.#items.length > 0) {
      return Promise.resolve({ value: this.#items.shift(), done: false });
    }
    if (this.#closed) {
      return Promise.resolve({ value: undefined, done: true });
    }
    // No item yet — park consumer until producer pushes
    const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers();
    this.#waiters.push({ resolve, reject });
    return promise;
  }

  [Symbol.asyncIterator]() { return this; }
}

// Usage
const queue = new AsyncQueue();
setTimeout(() => { queue.push(1); queue.push(2); queue.close(); }, 100);

for await (const item of queue) {
  console.log(item); // 1, 2
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Promise.withResolvers()` externalises control, which is powerful but also easy to misuse: keeping a reference to `resolve` in a data structure that outlives its natural scope (e.g., storing it in a module-level `Map` without a TTL) creates memory leaks that are invisible to GC because the Promise itself holds a closure reference. Always pair external resolvers with a timeout or cancellation token that calls `reject(timeoutError)` if the producer never delivers, preventing promises from lingering indefinitely.

---

## Cycle 46 Community Gotchas

**Gotcha 25 — `Promise.try()` Executes Synchronously; Code After It in the Microtask Queue Sees a Different Execution Order Than `Promise.resolve().then()`** [community] — Developers who migrate from `Promise.resolve().then(fn)` to `Promise.try(fn)` observe that callbacks that relied on micro-task deferral (e.g., state mutations that should only take effect after the current synchronous frame completes) now fire immediately. WHY it causes problems: React-style batched state update flushing and MobX-style computed recomputation hooks both depend on the microtask timing boundary to batch multiple synchronous mutations before re-rendering; replacing `.then(fn)` with `Promise.try(fn)` inside framework internals causes updates to fire mid-batch, breaking invariants. Fix: only use `Promise.try` for pure utility wrappers where the synchronous vs. deferred distinction does not matter; keep `Promise.resolve().then(fn)` where microtask deferral is intentional.

**Gotcha 26 — `Object.groupBy` Coerces Non-String Keys to `"[object Object]"`; All Object-Keyed Groups Collapse to One** [community] — `Object.groupBy(items, item => item.category)` where `category` is an object reference silently coerces all keys to the same string, producing a single group named `"[object Object]"` containing every item. WHY it causes problems: developers who use a status object as a grouping key (`item.status === statusEnum.ACTIVE`) expect object identity semantics but receive string coercion semantics; the result looks correct during development when all categories stringify differently, then silently breaks when two categories happen to share `toString()` output. Fix: use `Map.groupBy` whenever the grouping key is an object reference; reserve `Object.groupBy` for string/Symbol keys.

**Gotcha 27 — `using` Resources Inside `switch` and `for...in` Initialisers Are Forbidden; `SyntaxError` at Parse Time** [community] — Attempting `for (using x = acquireResource() in obj)` or declaring `using` at the top level of a `switch` case body (without a wrapping block `{}`) is a `SyntaxError`. WHY it causes problems: developers who habitually scope resource declarations at the head of `switch` arms (a pattern from TypeScript's `const` declarations) find the code refuses to parse; TypeScript's error message points to the `using` keyword without explaining the limitation. Fix: always wrap `switch` case bodies in explicit block statements `{ using x = ...; ... }` to create a lexical scope for `using` declarations, or hoist the resource to the enclosing function scope.

**Gotcha 28 — `structuredClone` Throws `DataCloneError` for Class Instances With Methods; Prototype Chain Is Not Preserved** [community] — `structuredClone(new MyClass())` throws `DataCloneError: MyClass could not be cloned` in environments that do not support cloning custom class instances, and even when it succeeds (e.g., a class with only data properties and no non-serializable values), the result is a plain object — not a `MyClass` instance — because `structuredClone` preserves data but not the prototype. WHY it causes problems: code that checks `cloned instanceof MyClass` after a `structuredClone` call always returns `false`, causing duck-typing-based validation to silently pass objects through incorrect branches. Fix: implement a `clone()` factory method on the class (`static clone(instance) { return new MyClass(structuredClone(instance.data)); }`) rather than passing class instances directly to `structuredClone`.

**Gotcha 29 — `import.meta.url` in Bundled Output Refers to the Bundle File, Not the Original Source; Asset URLs Computed at Build Time vs. Runtime** [community] — `new URL('./assets/icon.svg', import.meta.url)` works correctly in Vite's development server (where each module is served individually) but in production bundles the URL may point to the bundle chunk rather than the original file path, causing 404 errors unless the bundler is configured to rewrite the asset reference. WHY it causes problems: the development build succeeds with the correct asset URL while production silently returns a 404 because the bundle URL has no `assets/icon.svg` sibling at the computed path. Fix: always verify asset URL patterns produce correct paths in production builds; in Vite, the `new URL('./asset', import.meta.url)` pattern is explicitly supported and rewrites the URL at bundle time — use it exactly as documented and never dynamically compute the `./asset` segment at runtime.

**Gotcha 30 — `Temporal.ZonedDateTime.add({ days: 1 })` Preserves Wall-Clock Time Across DST; Adding `{ hours: 24 }` Does Not** [community] — `zdt.add({ days: 1 })` correctly lands at the same wall-clock time on the next calendar day even across a DST transition, while `zdt.add({ hours: 24 })` always adds exactly 86400 seconds and will land at a different wall-clock time on DST transition days. WHY it causes problems: developers who treat days and 24-hour intervals as interchangeable port DST-safe scheduling code from legacy `Date` (where `+24*3600*1000` was the only option) and then observe that recurring daily alarms fire one hour early or late on DST days. Fix: always use calendar units (`{ days: 1 }`) for scheduling business-day-aligned events; use time units (`{ hours: 24 }`) only for fixed-duration intervals where the wall-clock shift is intended and acceptable.

**Gotcha 31 — `Atomics.waitAsync` Promise Resolves to `"ok"` Even If the Index Value Has Changed Back by the Time the Continuation Runs; Double-Check After Await Is Mandatory** [community] — After `await result.value` resolves to `"ok"`, the shared index value may have been modified again by another thread between the `Atomics.notify` call and the resumption of the awaiting microtask. WHY it causes problems: consumer code that assumes the presence of a value immediately after the `"ok"` resolution reads stale or reset data, producing data races that are difficult to reproduce because the window between notify and microtask resumption is tiny. Fix: always re-read the index with `Atomics.load(ta, index)` after `await result.value`, and if the value is not what was expected, loop back to call `waitAsync` again — treat `"ok"` as "something changed" not "the value is X".

**Gotcha 32 — `Map.groupBy` Returns a Map With Object-Key Lookups That Fail for Reconstructed Key Objects; Keys Must Be the Exact Same Reference Used in the Callback** [community] — `grouped.get({ label: 'low' })` always returns `undefined` even if a key object with an identical shape was used during grouping, because `Map` uses reference equality (SameValueZero), not structural equality. WHY it causes problems: teams that serialise grouped results to JSON (which converts Map keys via `toJSON` or spread) and then try to reconstruct lookups by creating new key objects find every `.get()` call returns `undefined`, leading to silent undefined-propagation bugs rather than obvious errors. Fix: keep a reference to the original key objects in a companion record or use `Object.groupBy` with string keys and reconstruct group membership via string lookup, which is serialisation-safe.

## Cycle 47 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 1 — Iterator Helpers: Lazy Chainable Pipeline via `.map()` / `.filter()` / `.take()` / `.drop()` [official]

ECMAScript 2025 promoted the Iterator Helpers proposal to Stage 4, making `Iterator.prototype.map`, `.filter`, `.take`, `.drop`, `.flatMap`, `.reduce`, `.forEach`, `.find`, `.some`, `.every`, and `.toArray` part of the language. Unlike their `Array` counterparts, iterator helpers are **lazy**: each element is pulled one at a time through the entire chain rather than creating an intermediate array at each step. This allows pipelines over infinite generators, large streams, or expensive computations to avoid allocating memory proportional to the full source. The helpers also short-circuit correctly: a `.filter(...).take(5)` on an infinite generator stops consuming from the source once five matching elements have been emitted. All returned helper objects implement both the iterator protocol (`next()`) and the iterable protocol (`[Symbol.iterator]()`), so they can be passed directly to `for...of`, spread into arrays, or fed to another helper. Baseline 2025 — available across all major browsers since March 2025.

```javascript
// Infinite Fibonacci generator — never terminates on its own
function* fibonacci() {
  let [a, b] = [1, 1];
  while (true) {
    yield a;
    [a, b] = [b, a + b];
  }
}

// Lazy pipeline: filter evens, take first 5, double them, collect
const result = fibonacci()
  .filter(n => n % 2 === 0)   // lazy — no intermediate array
  .take(5)                     // stops the source after 5 matches
  .map(n => n * 2)             // still lazy
  .toArray();                  // terminal — materialises the array

console.log(result); // [4, 16, 68, 288, 1220]

// Iterator.from() wraps a legacy iterator-protocol object so it
// inherits all helper methods from Iterator.prototype
const legacyIter = {
  i: 0,
  next() { return { value: this.i++, done: this.i > 5 }; },
};
const wrapped = Iterator.from(legacyIter);
console.log(wrapped.map(x => x ** 2).toArray()); // [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]
```

**Tradeoff.** Because the pipeline is lazy, helpers do **not** return a reified snapshot — they share the same underlying iterator. Branching a pipeline (storing the helper object in two variables and iterating both) is not forking: the second variable sees only the unconsumed tail after the first variable has advanced the head. If you need independent traversals of the same data, either materialise with `.toArray()` first or re-invoke the source generator for each consumer.

---

### Pattern 2 — `Iterator.concat()` for Lazy Sequential Composition of Multiple Iterables [official]

`Iterator.concat(...iterables)` (Baseline 2026, available March 2026) is the lazy counterpart of `Array.prototype.concat`: it yields all elements of the first iterable, then the second, and so on, without loading any of them into memory simultaneously. Unlike `[...a, ...b]` — which first spreads both arrays into a new array — `Iterator.concat` is pull-based: it does not call `[Symbol.iterator]()` on iterable `n+1` until iterable `n` is fully exhausted. This makes it safe to use with resource-consuming iterables (open file handles, generators with side effects) because they are initialised in order rather than all at once. The method accepts iterables, not raw iterators; a raw iterator object that only implements `next()` must first be wrapped with `Iterator.from()`. The returned object is a proper `Iterator` instance and supports all downstream helpers.

```javascript
import { readLines } from 'node:fs/promises'; // hypothetical stream-based reader

// Two separate async-free iterables; opened on demand, not all at once
const header = ['id,name,score'];
const rows   = ['1,Alice,95', '2,Bob,88', '3,Carol,72'];
const footer = ['---end---'];

// Concatenated lazily — footer is not "started" until rows is exhausted
const allLines = Iterator.concat(header, rows, footer);

for (const line of allLines) {
  process.stdout.write(line + '\n');
}
// Output:
// id,name,score
// 1,Alice,95
// 2,Bob,88
// 3,Carol,72
// ---end---

// Compose with downstream helpers without materialising
const nonComments = Iterator.concat(header, rows, footer)
  .filter(line => !line.startsWith('#'))
  .take(10);

console.log(nonComments.toArray());
```

**Tradeoff.** `Iterator.concat` is limited by JavaScript's function argument count (`arguments.length`); concatenating hundreds of thousands of iterables via `Iterator.concat(...massiveArray)` will hit engine limits. For dynamic collections of iterables, use `Iterator.from(massiveArray).flatMap(iter => iter)` instead, which applies the same lazy sequencing through the `flatMap` helper.

---

### Pattern 3 — `Array.fromAsync()` for Collecting Async Iterables Without `for await` Boilerplate [official]

`Array.fromAsync(asyncIterable, mapFn?)` (Baseline 2024, available January 2024) converts an async iterable — such as a `ReadableStream`, an `AsyncGenerator`, or a Node.js `stream.Readable` — into a `Promise<Array>` with optional element transformation. It is the async analogue of `Array.from()` and eliminates the common `const arr = []; for await (const x of iter) arr.push(x);` boilerplate pattern. Unlike `Promise.all(array.map(...))`, which launches all promises concurrently, `Array.fromAsync` advances the async iterable **sequentially**: it awaits each `next()` promise before requesting the next item, which respects backpressure and avoids overwhelming producers. When a `mapFn` is provided, its return value is always awaited even if the source is a sync iterable, meaning `Array.fromAsync([p1, p2], x => x)` resolves each promise whereas `Array.fromAsync([p1, p2])` from a sync array would also await the elements (sync iterable values are awaited automatically).

```javascript
// Async generator that pages through an API
async function* fetchAllPages(url) {
  let cursor = null;
  do {
    const resp  = await fetch(url + (cursor ? `?cursor=${cursor}` : ''));
    const body  = await resp.json();
    yield* body.items;        // yield each item individually
    cursor = body.nextCursor;
  } while (cursor);
}

// Collect everything without explicit for-await loop
const allItems = await Array.fromAsync(
  fetchAllPages('https://api.example.com/data'),
  item => ({ ...item, fetchedAt: Date.now() })   // mapFn — awaited per item
);
console.log(allItems.length);

// Works with ReadableStream line-reader (Node 18+)
const stream   = (await fetch('https://example.com/large.csv')).body;
const decoder  = new TextDecoderStream();
const reader   = stream.pipeThrough(decoder);
const lines    = await Array.fromAsync(reader);  // materialise all decoded chunks
```

**Tradeoff.** Sequential iteration is intentional but is slower than concurrent `Promise.all` for independent promises. If the source is simply an array of independent `Promise` values and ordering of resolution does not matter, `Promise.all(promises)` remains ~5× faster in practice. Use `Array.fromAsync` when the producer enforces ordering (generators, streams) or when you need backpressure; use `Promise.all` for fan-out scenarios where all work can start immediately.

---

### Pattern 4 — `RegExp.escape()` for Safe Dynamic Pattern Construction [official]

`RegExp.escape(string)` (Baseline 2025, available May 2025) returns a new string with all characters that have special meaning in regular expression syntax escaped, making the result safe to embed as a literal sub-pattern inside a `RegExp` constructor call. Before this method, developers used hand-rolled replacements like `str.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')` — which were incomplete: they missed edge cases like `-` when unquoted inside character classes, the first alphanumeric character triggering a back-reference interpretation (`\1`), line terminators, and lone surrogates. `RegExp.escape` handles all of these correctly by applying the ECMA-262-specified escaping algorithm. The output is safe to use with any combination of flags, including `v` mode.

```javascript
// Without RegExp.escape — "." in domain acts as wildcard
function highlightDomain(text, domain) {
  return text.replace(
    new RegExp(`(https?://${domain})`, 'gi'),   // BUG: "." matches any char
    '<mark>$1</mark>'
  );
}

// With RegExp.escape — domain treated as literal string
function highlightDomainSafe(text, domain) {
  const escaped = RegExp.escape(domain);        // "example.com" -> "\\x65xample\\.com"
  return text.replace(
    new RegExp(`(https?://${escaped})`, 'gi'),  // safe
    '<mark>$1</mark>'
  );
}

// Real-world: search-and-highlight with user input
function buildHighlightRegex(query, flags = 'gi') {
  return new RegExp(RegExp.escape(query), flags);
}

const re = buildHighlightRegex('$100.00 (USD)');
console.log('Price: $100.00 (USD) total'.replace(re, '<b>$&</b>'));
// "Price: <b>$100.00 (USD)</b> total"
```

**Tradeoff.** `RegExp.escape` escapes more characters than strictly necessary — it also escapes `,`, `-`, `=`, `<`, `>`, `#`, `!`, punctuators, and the first alphanumeric character of the string using `\xNN` notation. The resulting pattern is safe but not human-readable. If readability of the pattern string matters (e.g., it is persisted for user display), consider a minimal custom escaper for the specific context; if safety is the sole concern, always prefer `RegExp.escape`.

---

### Pattern 5 — RegExp Inline Modifiers `(?flags:pattern)` for Localised Flag Overrides [official]

RegExp modifiers (Baseline 2025, available September 2025) introduce the `(?flags:pattern)` and `(?flags1-flags2:pattern)` syntax, allowing the `i` (case-insensitive), `m` (multiline), and `s` (dotall) flags to be enabled or disabled for a **bounded** sub-expression rather than applying globally. This eliminates the common workaround of splitting a single pattern into multiple `RegExp` objects with different flags and combining them with `|`, and avoids writing duplicate patterns with different capitalisation. The modifier group is non-capturing; only the three supported flags may appear in the modifier list. Attempting to use `g`, `y`, `d`, `u`, or `v` as inline modifiers produces a `SyntaxError` because those flags have engine-wide effects incompatible with local scoping.

```javascript
// Match a keyword case-insensitively but require exact-case value
// "let", "const", or "var" followed by an identifier of exact case
const declaration = /(?i:let|const|var)\s+([A-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_]*)/;

console.log(declaration.test('LET MyVar'));    // true — keyword matched case-insensitively
console.log(declaration.test('let myvar'));    // false — identifier must start with uppercase

// Disable global `i` flag locally for a critical sub-expression
const logLine = /(?i:ERROR|WARN|INFO)\s+(?-i:[A-Z]{3}-\d{4})/i;
// The outer `i` flag applies everywhere EXCEPT the (?-i:...) group
// Code "ERR-1234" must be upper-case; "error" or "Error" in the level is fine

console.log(logLine.test('error ERR-1234')); // true
console.log(logLine.test('error err-1234')); // false — code must be upper-case

// Mixed dotall: match across lines in header block, not in body
const httpMessage = /(?s:^HTTP.*?\r\n\r\n)(?-s:.+)/;
// Header section (up to blank line) uses dotall; body uses default single-line
```

**Tradeoff.** Inline modifiers make patterns more expressive but significantly harder to read for developers unfamiliar with the syntax. In shared codebases, a well-commented pair of separate `RegExp` objects is often more maintainable than a single complex pattern with multiple modifier groups. Reserve inline modifiers for cases where the semantic unity of the pattern is important — such as a parser that would otherwise require splitting the pattern at the grammar level.

---

### Pattern 6 — `Uint8Array.toBase64()` / `fromBase64()` / `toHex()` / `fromHex()` for Native Binary Encoding [official]

ES2025 added `Uint8Array.prototype.toBase64()`, `Uint8Array.fromBase64()`, `Uint8Array.prototype.toHex()`, and `Uint8Array.fromHex()` (Baseline 2025, available September 2025), replacing the decades-old `btoa` / `atob` workaround that required converting binary data to a Latin-1 string before encoding. The new methods operate directly on typed arrays: `toBase64()` accepts an `alphabet` option (`"base64"` or `"base64url"`) and an `omitPadding` boolean, while `fromBase64()` accepts the same options plus `lastChunkHandling` (`"loose"`, `"strict"`, or `"stop-before-partial"`) for controlling how incomplete trailing groups are handled. The companion `toHex()` and `fromHex()` methods provide zero-dependency hex encoding without libraries or `Array.from(buf).map(b => b.toString(16).padStart(2,'0')).join('')` boilerplate.

```javascript
// Encoding a binary response as URL-safe base64 (no padding)
const response = await fetch('/api/thumbnail');
const buffer   = new Uint8Array(await response.arrayBuffer());

const urlSafe  = buffer.toBase64({ alphabet: 'base64url', omitPadding: true });
// Safe to embed in a query string or URL fragment
const url      = `/preview?img=${urlSafe}`;

// Decoding back — must match the same options
const decoded  = Uint8Array.fromBase64(urlSafe, {
  alphabet: 'base64url',
  lastChunkHandling: 'strict',  // reject input with incomplete final group
});
console.log(decoded.byteLength === buffer.byteLength); // true

// Hex encoding for debugging / checksums
const hash = new Uint8Array(
  await crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256', buffer)
);
const hex = hash.toHex();  // "a3f2...64c1" — 64 hex chars for SHA-256
console.log(`SHA-256: ${hex}`);

// Decoding hex token from server
const serverToken = Uint8Array.fromHex('deadbeef0102');
console.log(serverToken); // Uint8Array(6) [ 222, 173, 190, 239, 1, 2 ]
```

**Tradeoff.** `btoa(String.fromCharCode(...bytes))` remains the only option for environments that have not yet shipped the new methods (Safari < 18, Node < 22, some embedded runtimes). The `es-arraybuffer-base64` shim (maintained by es-shims) provides a spec-compliant polyfill, but adds ~4 KB to the bundle. For environments where bundle size is critical and only standard base64 is needed (no URL-safe variant, no partial-chunk control), `btoa` + the `TextDecoder` roundtrip remains viable.

---

### Pattern 7 — `Math.sumPrecise()` for Accurate Floating-Point Accumulation [official]

`Math.sumPrecise(iterable)` (Baseline 2026, available April 2026) computes the sum of a numeric iterable using a precision-preserving algorithm — equivalent to computing the exact mathematical sum of all input values and then rounding the final result to the nearest IEEE 754 double. Unlike a naive `reduce((acc, x) => acc + x, 0)`, which accumulates rounding errors at every addition (catastrophic cancellation), `Math.sumPrecise` avoids intermediate rounding entirely. The method returns `+0` for an empty iterable, returns `NaN` if any element is `NaN`, and throws `TypeError` if any element is not a number. It does **not** fix the fundamental imprecision of floating-point literals themselves (`0.1 + 0.2` is still `0.30000000000000004` because both literals are already rounded when parsed), but it eliminates the compounding rounding errors that accumulate across a long series of additions.

```javascript
// Catastrophic cancellation with naive reduce
const values = [1e20, 0.1, -1e20];
const naive  = values.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
console.log(naive);                   // 0 — 0.1 is lost entirely

// Math.sumPrecise correctly preserves 0.1
console.log(Math.sumPrecise(values)); // 0.1

// Financial totalling — avoid currency micro-errors in large line-item sums
function totalCents(lineItems) {
  // Work in integer cents to avoid decimal issues, then use sumPrecise
  // for the final aggregate to guarantee no accumulation error
  const cents = lineItems.map(item => Math.round(item.price * 100));
  return Math.sumPrecise(cents) / 100;
}

// Sensor fusion — average of 1000 float readings without drift
function preciseAverage(readings) {
  return Math.sumPrecise(readings) / readings.length;
}

const floats = Array.from({ length: 1_000 }, (_, i) => i * 0.001);
console.log(preciseAverage(floats)); // 0.4995 — precise, no drift
```

**Tradeoff.** `Math.sumPrecise` has a higher constant factor than a simple loop accumulation because the algorithm internally maintains extra precision state (a multi-precision accumulator). For very hot paths over small arrays (< 20 elements), the overhead may be measurable in micro-benchmarks. Use `Math.sumPrecise` when correctness is required — financial calculations, scientific measurements, statistical aggregations — and a plain `reduce` when speed matters more than last-digit precision.

---

### Pattern 8 — Import Attributes (`with { type: "json" }`) for Type-Safe Module Loading [official]

Import attributes (Baseline 2025, available April 2025) allow static and dynamic `import` statements to carry metadata that the host environment uses to select a parsing strategy for the module. The syntax uses the `with` keyword (the earlier `assert` keyword was dropped from the standard and is non-standard). The most important current attribute is `type: "json"`, which instructs the runtime to parse the fetched resource as JSON and expose it as a default export — and to **fail** if the server does not serve the file with a JSON MIME type, preventing CSRF-style attacks where an attacker serves a JavaScript file at a URL expected to return safe data. The `type: "css"` attribute returns a constructable `CSSStyleSheet` adoptable via `document.adoptedStyleSheets`. JSON modules expose only a `default` export; named imports produce a `SyntaxError`.

```javascript
// Static import — JSON module (type-safe, rejects non-JSON MIME)
import config from './config.json' with { type: 'json' };
console.log(config.apiVersion); // direct property access, no JSON.parse()

// Dynamic import — useful for code-split config loading
async function loadLocale(lang) {
  const module = await import(`./locales/${lang}.json`, {
    with: { type: 'json' }
  });
  return module.default; // { greeting: "Hello", farewell: "Goodbye" }
}

// CSS module — inject design token stylesheet into shadow root
import tokens from './design-tokens.css' with { type: 'css' };

customElements.define('my-card', class extends HTMLElement {
  connectedCallback() {
    const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
    shadow.adoptedStyleSheets = [tokens];
    shadow.innerHTML = `<div class="card">...</div>`;
  }
});

// Re-export with attribute preserved
export { config as appConfig } from './config.json' with { type: 'json' };
```

**Tradeoff.** JSON modules are cached by URL for the page lifetime, making them unsuitable for data that changes at runtime (use `fetch` + `Response.json()` for live data). The `with` keyword is rejected by older bundlers and transpilers that only recognise `assert`; Webpack 5.73+, Rollup 3.5+, and Vite 4.2+ support `with`, but older configs need updating. Importantly, using the wrong keyword (`assert` instead of `with`) does not always produce a loud error in all environments — some runtimes silently ignore the attribute, removing the MIME-type guard without warning.

---

### Pattern 9 — `Map.prototype.getOrInsert()` / `getOrInsertComputed()` for Idiomatic Upsert [official]

`Map.prototype.getOrInsert(key, defaultValue)` and `Map.prototype.getOrInsertComputed(key, callbackFn)` (TC39 Stage 4, shipping in browsers in 2026) provide atomic get-or-insert semantics that eliminate the double-lookup pattern of `if (!map.has(key)) map.set(key, default); return map.get(key);`. The `getOrInsert` variant takes a static default value and inserts it only when the key is absent, returning the existing or newly inserted value. The `getOrInsertComputed` variant accepts a function that is called **only when the key is absent**, enabling lazy initialisation of expensive default values (e.g., constructing a new `Set` or fetching a resource) without computing the default unnecessarily when the key already exists. `WeakMap` gains the same two methods, enabling the same pattern for object-keyed weak caches.

```javascript
// Before: error-prone double-lookup pattern
function groupBefore(items, keyFn) {
  const groups = new Map();
  for (const item of items) {
    const key = keyFn(item);
    if (!groups.has(key)) groups.set(key, []);  // lookup 1
    groups.get(key).push(item);                  // lookup 2
  }
  return groups;
}

// After: single-lookup, no redundancy
function groupAfter(items, keyFn) {
  const groups = new Map();
  for (const item of items) {
    groups.getOrInsertComputed(keyFn(item), () => []).push(item);
  }
  return groups;
}

// Counter pattern — increment or initialise to 1
function countOccurrences(words) {
  const counts = new Map();
  for (const word of words) {
    counts.set(word, counts.getOrInsert(word, 0) + 1);
  }
  return counts;
}

// WeakMap memoisation with lazy initialisation
const cache = new WeakMap();
function getMemoized(obj) {
  return cache.getOrInsertComputed(obj, () => expensiveCompute(obj));
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `getOrInsert` always evaluates its second argument before the call, so `map.getOrInsert(key, new Set())` constructs a new `Set` on every call even when the key already exists — this is the same eagerness problem as a default function parameter. Always use `getOrInsertComputed` when the default value is non-trivial to construct; reserve `getOrInsert` for primitive literals, `null`, `undefined`, or `0` where construction cost is zero.

### Pattern 10 — `Float16Array` for Memory-Efficient Neural Network and WebGPU Weights [official]

`Float16Array` (Baseline 2025, available April 2025) is the first new TypedArray addition in years, storing 16-bit half-precision floating-point values (IEEE 754 binary16) at 2 bytes per element — half the size of `Float32Array`. It is accompanied by `Math.f16round(value)` for rounding a double to the nearest float16 value, and `DataView.prototype.getFloat16` / `setFloat16` for byte-level access. The primary use cases are WebGPU shader buffer uploads (where most neural network weights are stored as `fp16`), WebGL texture uploads with `HALF_FLOAT` format, and memory-constrained ML inference in the browser (stable diffusion, transformer models) where loading millions of weights as `Float32Array` would exhaust device memory. On platforms with native `fp16` hardware support (most modern GPUs and Apple Silicon CPUs), arithmetic on `Float16Array` is faster than `Float32Array`; on platforms without native support, the engine must emulate each operation with double-precision rounding, making it slower.

```javascript
// Load a quantised neural network weight file (fp16 format)
async function loadWeights(url) {
  const response = await fetch(url);
  const buffer   = await response.arrayBuffer();
  // Interpret raw bytes directly as fp16 — no conversion needed
  return new Float16Array(buffer);
}

// Round-trip: convert Float32 model to Float16 for WebGPU upload
function quantiseToFp16(float32Weights) {
  const fp16 = new Float16Array(float32Weights.length);
  for (let i = 0; i < float32Weights.length; i++) {
    // Math.f16round rounds the double to the nearest fp16 value
    fp16[i] = Math.f16round(float32Weights[i]);
  }
  return fp16;
}

// DataView for mixed-precision binary format parsing
function parseMixedPrecisionBuffer(buffer) {
  const view = new DataView(buffer);
  return {
    timestamp: view.getFloat64(0, true),   // 8 bytes — double precision
    weight:    view.getFloat16(8, true),   // 2 bytes — half precision
    bias:      view.getFloat16(10, true),  // 2 bytes — half precision
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Float16Array` provides memory savings and potential throughput gains for GPU workloads, but the reduced precision (3.3 significant decimal digits vs 7.2 for `Float32Array`) can introduce visible artefacts in non-ML use cases such as audio DSP or colour grading. Never use `Float16Array` for general-purpose arithmetic where accumulation of rounding error matters — use it exclusively for data transfer to GPU pipelines or storage of pre-trained weights where fp16 precision is already an architectural constraint.

### Pattern 11 — `WeakRef` + `FinalizationRegistry` for Optional Caching Without Memory Leaks [official]

`WeakRef` (Baseline since April 2021) holds a weak reference to an object that does not prevent garbage collection; `FinalizationRegistry` registers a cleanup callback that fires (non-deterministically) after the referent is collected. Together they enable a cache that automatically evicts entries when the environment runs low on memory, without the developer needing to implement an LRU eviction policy. The pattern: store computed objects in a `Map<key, WeakRef<value>>`; on lookup, call `.deref()` — if it returns `undefined`, the value was collected and must be recomputed; register each value with a `FinalizationRegistry` that deletes the dead `WeakRef` entry from the `Map` to prevent unbounded key accumulation. Crucially, garbage collection timing is entirely up to the engine and may never occur in short-lived scripts, so `WeakRef` caches are an optimistic optimisation — they must degrade gracefully to recomputation.

```javascript
const registry = new FinalizationRegistry((key) => {
  // Clean up the stale WeakRef entry when the value is collected
  cache.delete(key);
});

const cache = new Map(); // Map<string, WeakRef<object>>

function getCached(key, computeFn) {
  const ref = cache.get(key);
  if (ref !== undefined) {
    const value = ref.deref();
    if (value !== undefined) {
      return value; // Cache hit — object still alive
    }
    // Cache miss — ref is dead; entry will be cleaned by registry
  }

  // Recompute and cache
  const value = computeFn(key);
  cache.set(key, new WeakRef(value));
  registry.register(value, key);  // register cleanup using key as token
  return value;
}

// Usage: cache parsed DOM trees from large HTML strings
function getParsedDocument(html) {
  return getCached(html, (src) => new DOMParser().parseFromString(src, 'text/html'));
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The TC39 specification explicitly warns that relying on `WeakRef` for any timing-sensitive behaviour "is likely to be disappointed": GC may be deferred indefinitely, and behaviour differs across V8, SpiderMonkey, and JavaScriptCore. Never use `WeakRef` for lifecycle-critical logic, resource management that requires prompt cleanup, or observable application state. Use it only as a performance hint — a memory-sensitive cache that falls back gracefully to recomputation when entries have been collected.

### Pattern 12 — `Promise.any()` for First-Success Semantics Across Multiple Sources [official]

`Promise.any(iterable)` (Baseline — widely available since September 2021) returns a promise that fulfils with the value of the **first** promise in the iterable to fulfil, ignoring all rejections unless every promise rejects, in which case it rejects with an `AggregateError` containing all rejection reasons. This is the semantic dual of `Promise.all`: where `Promise.all` requires all to succeed, `Promise.any` requires only one. It is the correct primitive for multi-source fallback patterns — racing a primary CDN against a fallback CDN, trying multiple geocoding providers, or racing a cached response against a live fetch. Unlike `Promise.race`, which also resolves/rejects on the first **rejection**, `Promise.any` continues waiting for a fulfillment even after some promises reject, making it resilient to partial failures.

```javascript
// Multi-CDN asset loading — use whichever responds first without error
async function fetchFromAnyCDN(path) {
  const cdns = [
    'https://cdn1.example.com',
    'https://cdn2.example.com',
    'https://cdn3.example.com',
  ];

  try {
    return await Promise.any(
      cdns.map(base =>
        fetch(`${base}/${path}`).then(r => {
          if (!r.ok) throw new Error(`${r.status} from ${base}`);
          return r;
        })
      )
    );
  } catch (err) {
    // AggregateError — all CDNs failed; err.errors is an array of reasons
    console.error('All CDNs failed:', err.errors);
    throw err;
  }
}

// Primary + fallback with timeout
async function resolveWithFallback(primary, fallback, timeoutMs = 2000) {
  const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('timeout')), timeoutMs)
  );
  // Race primary against timeout; if primary times out, fallback runs
  return Promise.any([primary, timeout.then(() => fallback)]);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Promise.any` does **not** cancel the losing promises — all other fetches continue running to completion even after the first one fulfils. In network-constrained environments this wastes bandwidth; pair it with `AbortController` signals if the losing requests should be terminated. Also note that `Promise.any([])` (empty iterable) **always rejects** with an `AggregateError` whose `.errors` array is empty — unlike `Promise.all([])` which fulfils with `[]`. Always check for the empty-iterable case before calling `Promise.any`.

### Pattern 13 — `Iterator.prototype.reduce()` / `.toArray()` as Safe Terminal Operations [official]

While the lazy helpers (`.map`, `.filter`, `.take`) are non-terminal, `.reduce(fn, initialValue?)` and `.toArray()` are **terminal**: they consume the entire remaining iterator and return a concrete value. Understanding their interaction with the iterator's state and with preceding lazy stages is critical for correct usage. `reduce` without an `initialValue` on an empty iterator throws `TypeError` (unlike `Array.prototype.reduce`, which throws on empty with no initial value for the same reason — but the error is easy to forget when composing pipelines). `.toArray()` is semantically equivalent to `[...iterator]` but avoids the spread operator's implicit `Symbol.iterator` step, making it slightly more explicit and intentional for iterator-protocol objects that also happen to be iterable.

```javascript
// Terminal reduce — always pass initialValue when source may be empty
function sumIterator(iter) {
  return iter.reduce((acc, x) => acc + x, 0); // safe even if iter is empty
}

// Anti-pattern: reduce without initialValue on potentially-empty pipeline
function unsafeSum(data) {
  return data.values()
    .filter(x => x > 100)
    .reduce((a, b) => a + b);  // throws if filter produces no values
}

// Building a frequency map as a terminal reduce
const words = ['the', 'cat', 'sat', 'on', 'the', 'mat'];
const freq = words.values()
  .reduce((map, word) => {
    map.set(word, (map.get(word) ?? 0) + 1);
    return map;
  }, new Map());

// toArray() to materialise before passing to APIs that expect arrays
function processTopK(dataStream, k, scoreFn) {
  return dataStream
    .map(item => ({ item, score: scoreFn(item) }))
    .filter(({ score }) => score > 0)
    .take(k)
    .toArray();   // materialise for JSON.stringify, sort, Array method chaining
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Terminal operations consume the iterator irreversibly — there is no `rewind()` or `reset()`. If you call `.toArray()` on an iterator and then try to iterate it again (e.g., by calling `.map()` on the same variable), the second iteration will immediately complete with no values because the underlying generator has already returned `done: true`. Always treat iterator consumption as a one-way door and re-invoke the source factory if multiple passes are required.

### Pattern 14 — `RegExp` Named Capture Groups and `.indices` (`d` Flag) for Structured Text Parsing [official]

Named capture groups (`(?<name>...)`) give regex sub-matches semantic labels instead of positional indices, and the `d` flag (Baseline — widely available since January 2022) adds a `.indices` property to the match result containing `[start, end]` spans for every capture group. Together they enable structured parsers that produce self-documenting match objects and that can report exact source positions for error highlighting or AST node construction without fragile index arithmetic. The named groups appear in `match.groups.name`, and their indices appear in `match.indices.groups.name` as `[start, end]` tuples. Named backreferences in the pattern use `\k<name>`.

```javascript
// Parse a log line: "2026-05-14T08:23:11Z ERROR [auth] Token expired"
const LOG_RE = /^(?<date>\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T[\d:]+Z)\s+(?<level>ERROR|WARN|INFO)\s+\[(?<module>[^\]]+)\]\s+(?<message>.+)$/d;

function parseLogLine(line) {
  const match = line.match(LOG_RE);
  if (!match) return null;

  const { date, level, module, message } = match.groups;
  const spans = match.indices.groups;      // { date: [0,20], level: [21,26], ... }

  return {
    date:    new Date(date),
    level,
    module,
    message,
    spans,  // useful for source-map / error highlighting
  };
}

const entry = parseLogLine('2026-05-14T08:23:11Z ERROR [auth] Token expired');
console.log(entry.level);                          // "ERROR"
console.log(entry.spans.message);                  // [33, 46]
console.log('2026-05-14T08:23:11Z ERROR [auth] Token expired'
  .slice(...entry.spans.message));                 // "Token expired"

// Named backreference — match repeated opening and closing XML tag
const tag = /<(?<tagName>[a-z]+)>.*?<\/\k<tagName>>/s;
console.log(tag.test('<p>hello</p>'));  // true
console.log(tag.test('<p>hello</div>')); // false
```

**Tradeoff.** The `d` flag forces the engine to track and materialise indices for every named and unnamed capture group, which adds measurable overhead (typically 10–30% slower match time) for patterns with many capture groups in tight loops. Avoid `d` on hot-path regex that does not need position information; add it only when constructing source maps, error spans, or AST nodes where exact positions are required.

### Pattern 15 — `Array.prototype.toSorted()` / `toReversed()` / `toSpliced()` / `with()` for Immutable Array Mutation [official]

ES2023 added four non-destructive counterparts to the classic mutating array methods (Baseline — widely available since July 2023): `toSorted(compareFn?)`, `toReversed()`, `toSpliced(start, deleteCount, ...items)`, and `with(index, value)`. Each returns a **new array** without modifying the original, closing the long-standing asymmetry where `map`, `filter`, and `slice` were non-mutating but `sort`, `reverse`, `splice`, and index-assignment were mutating. These methods integrate cleanly with React/Vue/Solid state patterns where returning a new reference from a state updater is the expected contract, and they eliminate the defensive `[...arr].sort(fn)` copy-before-mutate pattern that was otherwise required whenever the source array must remain untouched.

```javascript
// React state update — no defensive copy needed
function TodoList() {
  const [todos, setTodos] = React.useState([
    { id: 1, text: 'Buy groceries', done: false },
    { id: 2, text: 'Write tests',   done: true  },
    { id: 3, text: 'Ship feature',  done: false },
  ]);

  // toSorted — sort by done status without mutating state
  const sorted = todos.toSorted((a, b) => Number(a.done) - Number(b.done));

  // with — update a single element by index, return new array
  const toggle = (index) =>
    setTodos(prev => prev.with(index, { ...prev[index], done: !prev[index].done }));

  // toSpliced — remove element at index without splice() mutation
  const remove = (index) =>
    setTodos(prev => prev.toSpliced(index, 1));

  // toReversed — display in reverse order without mutating sort order
  const reversed = todos.toReversed();
  // ...
}

// Pipeline-safe chaining — all steps return new arrays
const result = rawData
  .toSorted((a, b) => b.score - a.score) // sorted copy
  .toSpliced(10)                           // keep only top 10 (remove from index 10)
  .with(0, { ...rawData[0], rank: 1 });    // tag first place
```

**Tradeoff.** Each method allocates a new array — for large arrays (> 10,000 elements) called in tight loops, this can put significant pressure on the garbage collector. In hot rendering paths, profile whether the allocation cost outweighs the clarity benefit; if mutation is safe (e.g., a locally owned intermediate array), the classic mutating methods remain faster. The `with(index, value)` method also does not throw on out-of-bounds positive indices — it silently returns a copy with an `undefined` slot — which can mask off-by-one errors. Always validate the index when using `with` in critical code paths.

## Cycle 47 Community Gotchas

**Gotcha 33 — Iterator Helpers Are Consumed by Any Downstream Iteration, Including Accidental Spread; The Same Variable Cannot Be Iterated Twice** [community] — Developers who store an iterator helper (e.g., `const filtered = data.values().filter(...)`) and then spread it into a function call (`fn(...filtered)`) later find the variable is fully consumed; a subsequent `for...of filtered` loop yields nothing. WHY it causes problems: unlike arrays (which reset their `Symbol.iterator` on each `for...of`), iterator helpers are one-shot — spreading is iteration, not cloning — so any code that assumes a stored helper can be re-used across multiple loops or API calls silently receives no data on the second pass, producing empty results without any error or warning. Fix: always call `.toArray()` immediately after the final lazy stage if you need to iterate the result more than once, and treat iterator-helper objects as single-use values with the same semantics as a database cursor.

**Gotcha 34 — `Array.fromAsync` Does Not Call `return()` on Synchronous Iterators When an Error Is Thrown Mid-Iteration; Generator `finally` Blocks Are Skipped** [community] — When `Array.fromAsync` processes a synchronous iterable and an error occurs (either from the iterable itself or from the `mapFn`), it does not call `return()` on the iterator to trigger cleanup, meaning generator `finally` blocks and `using` declarations inside generators are silently bypassed. WHY it causes problems: teams that use `Array.fromAsync` to consume a generator holding open resources (file handles, database cursors) observe that those resources leak when the async collection fails partway through, because the generator's `finally` block — which would normally run on early `return()` — never executes. Fix: wrap the generator body in an explicit `try/finally` that performs cleanup unconditionally, or use `for await...of` with manual `try/catch`, which correctly calls `return()` on the iterator on loop exit.

**Gotcha 35 — `RegExp.escape()` Escapes the First Alphanumeric Character Using `\xNN` Notation; Escaped Strings Are Not Human-Readable and Storing Them as User-Facing Data Confuses Developers** [community] — `RegExp.escape('hello')` returns `'\\x68ello'` not `'hello'`, because the algorithm escapes the first character to prevent it from being interpreted as a back-reference lead (`\h` is safe but `\1` would not be). WHY it causes problems: teams that log or persist the escaped pattern string for debugging find the output cryptic; more critically, code that stores the escaped form in a database expecting to display it as a human-readable "search pattern" to end users renders `\x68ello` rather than `hello`, breaking the UI. Fix: never use `RegExp.escape` output as a user-visible string; use it exclusively as an opaque intermediate value that is immediately embedded inside a `new RegExp(...)` call.

**Gotcha 36 — Import Attributes `type: "json"` JSON Modules Cache for the Entire Page Lifetime; Re-Fetching Dynamic JSON Config via `import()` Does Not Reflect Server-Side Updates** [community] — `await import('./config.json', { with: { type: 'json' } })` called multiple times in a SPA returns the identical cached module object on every call; it does not re-fetch the file even if the server has deployed a new version. WHY it causes problems: feature-flag systems and A/B test configurations that ship JSON files are commonly loaded via dynamic `import()` to avoid bundling; teams who expect each call to reflect the latest server state find that after the first load, the configuration is frozen for the tab's lifetime, causing inconsistent behaviour between page loads. Fix: use `fetch('./config.json').then(r => r.json())` for data that must reflect live server state; reserve JSON module imports for truly static data (translation strings, schema definitions) that does not change within a user session.

**Gotcha 37 — `Map.prototype.getOrInsertComputed` Callback Fires Only Once Per Missing Key; Mutations Inside the Callback That Add the Same Key Again Are Ignored, Not Re-Triggered** [community] — If the `callbackFn` passed to `getOrInsertComputed` itself calls `map.set(key, ...)` for the same key (perhaps indirectly through a shared utility), the map proceeds with the value produced by the callback's return value, not the value set by `map.set` inside the callback, and the `set` call inside the callback is effectively overwritten. WHY it causes problems: recursive data structures that need to register a sentinel placeholder before recursively filling the value (a pattern from cycle-detection in graph serialisation) find the sentinel is overwritten by the return value of `getOrInsertComputed`, breaking cycle detection. Fix: use the explicit `if (!map.has(key)) { map.set(key, sentinel); ... }` pattern for recursive sentinel-placement scenarios; reserve `getOrInsertComputed` for pure, side-effect-free default factory functions.

**Gotcha 38 — `Float16Array` Index Assignment Silently Rounds Values Outside the fp16 Range to `Infinity` or `-Infinity`; No Exception Is Thrown for Overflow** [community] — Assigning a `Float32` value larger than the maximum fp16 representable value (~65,504) to a `Float16Array` slot silently stores `Infinity`, not the original number or a clamped maximum. WHY it causes problems: developers who build weight quantisation pipelines that check for `NaN` to detect precision loss miss the overflow condition entirely because `Infinity` passes `Number.isFinite(arr[i]) === false` but is not `NaN`; the model then produces infinite activations that only manifest as numerical instability several layers later, making the root cause invisible without explicit overflow validation. Fix: always validate float16 quantisation results with `Math.abs(Math.f16round(value)) !== Infinity` before storing; flag or clamp overflowing weights before writing to `Float16Array`.

**Gotcha 39 — `Promise.any()` with an Empty Iterable Always Rejects with `AggregateError`; Unlike `Promise.all([])` Which Resolves to `[]`** [community] — Developers familiar with `Promise.all`'s identity element (empty input = resolve with empty array) apply the same assumption to `Promise.any` and are surprised that `Promise.any([])` rejects. WHY it causes problems: dynamic collections of promises (built from a filtered list of available providers) may become empty after filtering, and code that passes the dynamic array directly to `Promise.any` without checking `length > 0` first throws an unhandled `AggregateError` in production whenever all providers are disabled, a corner case that is difficult to trigger in development. Fix: always guard with `if (promises.length === 0) throw new Error('No providers available')` or wrap with `promises.length > 0 ? Promise.any(promises) : Promise.reject(new Error('empty'))` before calling `Promise.any` on a dynamically constructed array.

**Gotcha 40 — `toSorted()` / `toReversed()` Do Not Propagate `holes` from Sparse Arrays; They Always Produce Dense Arrays, Changing Iteration Behaviour** [community] — `[1,,3].toSorted()` returns `[1, 3, undefined]` — a dense array of length 3 with an explicit `undefined` at index 1 — whereas `[...arr].sort()` on the same sparse array may preserve the hole, resulting in different `Array.prototype.map` / `forEach` skip behaviour. WHY it causes problems: legacy code that relied on `forEach` skipping holes (because `forEach` does not invoke the callback for empty slots) breaks silently when migrated to `toSorted` pipelines, causing callbacks to fire for the new `undefined` slots that would have been skipped before, producing unexpected `undefined` processing branches in downstream handlers. Fix: if your code relies on sparse-array hole-skipping semantics, do not use `toSorted`/`toReversed` on sparse arrays; use `[...arr].sort()` which preserves sparseness, or audit the pipeline to eliminate reliance on holes entirely.
