## Cycle 59 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 135** — Promise.withResolvers() for Deferred Control Inversion
```javascript
// Classic deferred pattern — verbose and fragile
let resolve, reject;
const promise = new Promise((res, rej) => {
  resolve = res;
  reject  = rej;
});
// Problem: resolve/reject are in outer scope before being assigned

// ES2024: Promise.withResolvers() — clean and explicit
const { promise: ready, resolve: markReady, reject: fail } =
  Promise.withResolvers();

// Use case: resolve from an event handler detached from creation site
button.addEventListener('click', () => markReady(button.value), { once: true });
input.addEventListener('input',  () => fail(new Error('cancelled')), { once: true });

const result = await ready; // resolves when button clicked, rejects when input changes

// Use case: expose a promise from a class without exposing the executor
class ResourceLoader {
  #loadPromise;
  #resolve;
  constructor() {
    ({ promise: this.#loadPromise, resolve: this.#resolve } =
      Promise.withResolvers());
  }
  markLoaded(data) { this.#resolve(data); }
  get loaded()     { return this.#loadPromise; }
}
```
Tradeoff: `Promise.withResolvers()` improves readability for deferred patterns but does not change the underlying risk of unresolved promises leaking into garbage-collected closures. Always pair with a timeout or AbortSignal to avoid promises that silently hang indefinitely when the external event never fires.

**Pattern 136** — Flat Promise Chains vs. Async/Await for Parallel Fan-out
```javascript
// Scenario: fetch user, then concurrently fetch posts and followers

// Promise chain — explicit, pipeable
function getUserFeed(userId) {
  return fetchUser(userId)
    .then(user =>
      Promise.all([
        fetchPosts(user.id),
        fetchFollowers(user.id),
      ]).then(([posts, followers]) => ({ user, posts, followers }))
    )
    .catch(err => {
      throw new Error(`getUserFeed failed for ${userId}`, { cause: err });
    });
}

// Async/await — easier to read, same semantics
async function getUserFeedAsync(userId) {
  try {
    const user = await fetchUser(userId);
    const [posts, followers] = await Promise.all([
      fetchPosts(user.id),
      fetchFollowers(user.id),
    ]);
    return { user, posts, followers };
  } catch (err) {
    throw new Error(`getUserFeed failed for ${userId}`, { cause: err });
  }
}

// Anti-pattern: sequential awaits lose concurrency
async function getUserFeedSlow(userId) {
  const user      = await fetchUser(userId);    // sequential
  const posts     = await fetchPosts(user.id);  // waits for user
  const followers = await fetchFollowers(user.id); // waits for posts
  return { user, posts, followers };            // 3× slower
}
```
Tradeoff: `Promise.all` fails fast on the first rejection, which is desirable for mandatory resources. For optional sidecars (analytics, recommendations), use `Promise.allSettled` and filter by `status === 'fulfilled'` — partial failures should not break the critical path.

**Pattern 137** — Generator Functions for Lazy Infinite Sequences
```javascript
// Infinite sequence — only computes on demand
function* naturals(start = 0) {
  let n = start;
  while (true) yield n++;
}

// Composable lazy pipeline with generator helpers
function* map(iter, fn) {
  for (const x of iter) yield fn(x);
}

function* filter(iter, pred) {
  for (const x of iter) if (pred(x)) yield x;
}

function* take(iter, n) {
  let count = 0;
  for (const x of iter) {
    if (count++ >= n) return;
    yield x;
  }
}

// Compose: first 5 even squares starting at 1
const result = [
  ...take(
    filter(
      map(naturals(1), x => x * x),
      x => x % 2 === 0
    ),
    5
  )
];
console.log(result); // [4, 16, 36, 64, 100]

// Practical: paginated API cursor
async function* fetchAllPages(endpoint) {
  let cursor = null;
  do {
    const url      = cursor ? `${endpoint}?cursor=${cursor}` : endpoint;
    const response = await fetch(url).then(r => r.json());
    yield* response.items;
    cursor = response.nextCursor;
  } while (cursor);
}

for await (const item of fetchAllPages('/api/items')) {
  process(item); // processes items page by page, no memory spike
}
```
Tradeoff: Generator-based pipelines avoid building intermediate arrays but make debugging harder — the lazy execution means errors surface at consumption time, not at pipeline construction time. Use `Array.from(take(gen, n))` to eagerly materialise during debugging so stack traces point to the correct generator frame.

**Pattern 138** — Structured Destructuring with Rename + Default in Function Parameters
```javascript
// Simple destructured param — brittle if callers omit keys
function createUser({ name, role, age }) { /* ... */ }

// Robust: rename, default, and a default empty object guard
function createUser({
  name,
  role       = 'viewer',
  age        = null,
  metadata   = {},
  createdAt  = new Date().toISOString(),
} = {}) {
  return { name, role, age, metadata, createdAt };
}

createUser({ name: 'Alice' });    // role='viewer', age=null, ...
createUser();                     // entire param defaults to {} — no TypeError

// Nested destructuring for deep API responses
function parseApiUser({
  id,
  profile: {
    displayName: name,
    avatar:      { url: avatarUrl = '/default.png' } = {},
  } = {},
  permissions: { canEdit = false, canDelete = false } = {},
}) {
  return { id, name, avatarUrl, canEdit, canDelete };
}

const user = parseApiUser({
  id: 1,
  profile: { displayName: 'Bob' }, // avatar missing — falls back to default
  // permissions missing — falls back to defaults
});
// { id: 1, name: 'Bob', avatarUrl: '/default.png', canEdit: false, canDelete: false }
```
Tradeoff: Deep nested destructuring with defaults is powerful but becomes hard to read beyond 3 levels. At that depth, flatten with explicit `?.` access: `const avatarUrl = user?.profile?.avatar?.url ?? '/default.png'`. Reserve deep destructuring for well-typed parameter objects where a TypeScript interface documents the shape.

**Pattern 139** — AbortController for Cancellable Async Operations
```javascript
// Cancellable fetch with timeout
function fetchWithTimeout(url, ms = 5000) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timerId    = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(
    new DOMException(`Timed out after ${ms}ms`, 'TimeoutError')
  ), ms);

  return fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal })
    .then(res => { clearTimeout(timerId); return res.json(); })
    .catch(err => {
      clearTimeout(timerId);
      if (err.name === 'AbortError') throw new Error(`Request timed out: ${url}`);
      throw err;
    });
}

// React-style cleanup: cancel on component unmount
function useUserData(userId) {
  const [data, setData] = React.useState(null);

  React.useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();

    fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`, { signal: controller.signal })
      .then(r => r.json())
      .then(setData)
      .catch(err => {
        if (err.name !== 'AbortError') console.error(err);
      });

    return () => controller.abort(); // cleanup on unmount or userId change
  }, [userId]);

  return data;
}

// Propagating signal through call stack
async function processItems(items, signal) {
  for (const item of items) {
    signal.throwIfAborted();           // ES2023 — throws AbortError if aborted
    await processItem(item, signal);   // pass signal downstream
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `AbortController` only cancels the network request — it does not cancel JavaScript execution or rollback side effects already applied. For multi-step workflows (fetch → transform → persist), check `signal.aborted` or call `signal.throwIfAborted()` at each step boundary. Ignoring the signal after network cancellation leads to zombie processes writing stale data.

**Pattern 140** — Symbol.iterator for Custom Iterable Collections
```javascript
class Range {
  constructor(start, end, step = 1) {
    this.start = start;
    this.end   = end;
    this.step  = step;
  }

  [Symbol.iterator]() {
    let current = this.start;
    const { end, step } = this;
    return {
      next() {
        if (current < end) {
          const value = current;
          current += step;
          return { value, done: false };
        }
        return { value: undefined, done: true };
      },
      [Symbol.iterator]() { return this; } // makes the iterator itself iterable
    };
  }
}

const range = new Range(0, 10, 2);
console.log([...range]);             // [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
console.log(Array.from(range));      // [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
for (const n of range) { /* works */ }
const [first, second] = range;      // destructuring works

// Generator-based shorthand — simpler and re-entrant
class Range2 {
  constructor(start, end, step = 1) {
    Object.assign(this, { start, end, step });
  }
  *[Symbol.iterator]() {
    for (let i = this.start; i < this.end; i += this.step) yield i;
  }
}

// Difference: generator-based is re-iterable (each call creates a new generator)
const r = new Range2(1, 4);
console.log([...r]); // [1, 2, 3]
console.log([...r]); // [1, 2, 3]  — re-iterable
```
Tradeoff: Implementing `[Symbol.iterator]` makes custom data structures interoperate seamlessly with all JS iteration contexts (`for...of`, spread, destructuring, `Array.from`). The generator-based form is always re-iterable; the manual iterator form is not re-iterable by default unless the returned iterator stores a copy of initial state. Use the generator form unless you need fine-grained control over the iteration state machine.

**Pattern 141** — Computed Property Names and Dynamic Object Construction
```javascript
// Building objects with dynamic keys — avoids intermediate assignments
function buildQueryParams(filters) {
  return Object.fromEntries(
    Object.entries(filters)
      .filter(([, v]) => v !== null && v !== undefined && v !== '')
      .map(([k, v]) => [k, String(v)])
  );
}

// Computed keys from constants — avoids typos, enables refactoring
const FIELDS = { NAME: 'name', AGE: 'age', ROLE: 'role' };

const user = {
  [FIELDS.NAME]: 'Alice',
  [FIELDS.AGE]:  30,
  [FIELDS.ROLE]: 'admin',
};

// Dynamic dispatch table — replaces large switch/if-else chains
const handlers = {
  ['user/login']:   handleLogin,
  ['user/logout']:  handleLogout,
  ['post/create']:  handlePostCreate,
  ['post/delete']:  handlePostDelete,
};

function dispatch(action) {
  const handler = handlers[action.type];
  if (!handler) throw new Error(`Unknown action: ${action.type}`);
  return handler(action.payload);
}

// Merging with computed override key — immutable update pattern
function updateField(obj, field, value) {
  return { ...obj, [field]: value };  // does not mutate obj
}
```
Tradeoff: Computed property names with `Object.fromEntries` + `Object.entries` pipelines are expressive but have non-trivial GC pressure from intermediate array allocations. For hot paths (thousands of objects per frame), build objects imperatively with direct key assignment. Profile first — readability wins unless the microbenchmark proves otherwise.

**Pattern 142** — Nullish Coalescing Assignment (??=) and Logical Assignment Operators
```javascript
// ??= : assign only if left-hand side is null or undefined (not 0, '', false)
let config = null;
config ??= { theme: 'dark', lang: 'en' };  // assigns
config ??= { theme: 'light' };             // skips — config already non-nullish

// Compare to ||= which assigns on ANY falsy value (including 0, '')
let count = 0;
count ||= 10;   // assigns — 0 is falsy!
count ??= 10;   // skips   — 0 is not null/undefined

// &&= : assign only if left-hand side is truthy
let user = { name: 'Alice', verified: false };
user.name &&= user.name.trim().toLowerCase(); // only trims if name is truthy

// Practical: initialise cache lazily
const cache = {};
function get(key, compute) {
  cache[key] ??= compute();  // compute() called only on cache miss
  return cache[key];
}

// Practical: default nested config without overwriting existing keys
function mergeDefaults(target, defaults) {
  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(defaults)) {
    target[key] ??= value;  // skip if key already set (even to false/0/'')
  }
  return target;
}

mergeDefaults(userPrefs, { theme: 'light', fontSize: 14, notifications: true });
```
Tradeoff: `??=` is strictly safer than `||=` for numeric or boolean fields where `0` and `false` are valid values. In practice, teams must agree on which operator to use in shared config utilities — mixing `??=` and `||=` in the same codebase for the same use case creates subtle bugs when falsy-but-valid values arrive. Prefer `??=` as the default; use `||=` only when falsy values genuinely mean "not set".

**Pattern 143** — WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry for Optional Cache Invalidation
```javascript
// WeakRef: hold a reference that does not prevent GC
class ImageCache {
  #cache = new Map();           // key → WeakRef<ImageBitmap>
  #registry;

  constructor() {
    // FinalizationRegistry: notified when a cached bitmap is GC'd
    this.#registry = new FinalizationRegistry(key => {
      // Called asynchronously after GC — not guaranteed timing
      this.#cache.delete(key);
      console.debug(`Cache evicted: ${key}`);
    });
  }

  set(key, bitmap) {
    this.#cache.set(key, new WeakRef(bitmap));
    this.#registry.register(bitmap, key);  // register for cleanup notification
  }

  get(key) {
    const ref = this.#cache.get(key);
    if (!ref) return null;
    const bitmap = ref.deref();   // null if GC'd since WeakRef was created
    if (!bitmap) {
      this.#cache.delete(key);    // eager cleanup without waiting for registry
      return null;
    }
    return bitmap;
  }
}

const cache = new ImageCache();
let bmp = await createImageBitmap(blob);
cache.set('hero', bmp);
bmp = null;              // strong reference dropped — GC may now collect it

const cached = cache.get('hero'); // null if GC'd, ImageBitmap if still alive
```
Tradeoff: `WeakRef` and `FinalizationRegistry` are intentionally non-deterministic — the GC decides when and whether cleanup callbacks run. Never rely on them for correctness (releasing locks, closing files, accounting). They are appropriate only for optional performance caches where eviction is acceptable. The `FinalizationRegistry` callback may not fire in short-lived processes; always implement an explicit eviction strategy as the primary path.

**Pattern 144** — Tagged Template Literals for Safe SQL/HTML/URL Interpolation
```javascript
// SQL safe interpolation — values parameterised, never interpolated raw
function sql(strings, ...values) {
  const text   = strings.reduce((acc, str, i) =>
    acc + str + (i < values.length ? `$${i + 1}` : ''), '');
  return { text, values };
}

const userId = 42;
const query  = sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${userId} AND active = ${true}`;
// { text: 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1 AND active = $2', values: [42, true] }
await db.query(query.text, query.values);  // safe parameterised query

// HTML escaping tag — prevents XSS
function html(strings, ...values) {
  const escape = s => String(s)
    .replace(/&/g,  '&amp;')
    .replace(/</g,  '&lt;')
    .replace(/>/g,  '&gt;')
    .replace(/"/g,  '&quot;')
    .replace(/'/g,  '&#39;');
  return strings.reduce((acc, str, i) =>
    acc + str + (i < values.length ? escape(values[i]) : ''), '');
}

const userInput = '<script>alert("xss")</script>';
const markup    = html`<p>Hello, ${userInput}!</p>`;
// <p>Hello, &lt;script&gt;alert(&quot;xss&quot;)&lt;/script&gt;!</p>

// URL construction tag — encodes each interpolated segment
function url(strings, ...values) {
  return strings.reduce((acc, str, i) =>
    acc + str + (i < values.length ? encodeURIComponent(values[i]) : ''), '');
}

const search = url`/api/search?q=${userInput}&page=${2}`;
// /api/search?q=%3Cscript%3Ealert(%22xss%22)%3C%2Fscript%3E&page=2
```
Tradeoff: Tagged templates enforce escaping at the interpolation boundary rather than relying on developers to remember to call `escape()` at every call site. The tradeoff is that the tag function must be used consistently — a single untagged template literal with user data bypasses all protection. Enforce tag usage via ESLint `no-restricted-syntax` rules that warn on untagged template literals containing identifiers that typically hold user input.

**Pattern 145** — Iterator Helpers (ES2025) — `.map()`, `.filter()`, `.take()`, `.drop()`
```javascript
// ES2025 Iterator Helpers — lazy pipeline without intermediate arrays
function* integers(start = 0) {
  while (true) yield start++;
}

// Iterator.prototype.map / filter / take / drop
const firstFiveEvenSquares = integers(1)
  .map(x => x * x)
  .filter(x => x % 2 === 0)
  .take(5)
  .toArray();
console.log(firstFiveEvenSquares); // [4, 16, 36, 64, 100]

// .drop() — skip the first N elements
const page2 = integers(1).drop(10).take(10).toArray(); // [11..20]

// .flatMap() — flatten one level of nested iterables
function* words(text) {
  yield* text.split(/\s+/);
}
const lines = ['hello world', 'foo bar baz'];
const allWords = lines.values()
  .flatMap(words)
  .toArray();
// ['hello', 'world', 'foo', 'bar', 'baz']

// .reduce() and .forEach() — terminal operations
const sum = integers(1).take(100).reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0); // 5050

// Polyfill check — feature-detect before use
const hasIteratorHelpers = typeof [][Symbol.iterator]().map === 'function';
if (!hasIteratorHelpers) {
  // Fall back to generator-based pipeline or core-js polyfill
}
```
Tradeoff: Iterator helpers produce a single lazy pipeline with no intermediate arrays, which is ideal for large or infinite sequences. The tradeoff is limited browser support in 2024 (Chrome 122+, Firefox 131+, Safari 18+). Polyfill via `core-js@3.37+` or use a generator-based fallback. The `.toArray()` terminal method is explicit, which prevents accidental re-iteration, but it does materialise the entire sequence into memory — pair with `.take(n)` for infinite sources.

**Pattern 146** — Object.groupBy() / Map.groupBy() for Collection Partitioning
```javascript
// ES2024 Object.groupBy — group array elements by a computed key
const items = [
  { id: 1, status: 'active',   type: 'user' },
  { id: 2, status: 'inactive', type: 'user' },
  { id: 3, status: 'active',   type: 'admin' },
  { id: 4, status: 'inactive', type: 'admin' },
];

const byStatus = Object.groupBy(items, item => item.status);
// {
//   active:   [ {id:1,...}, {id:3,...} ],
//   inactive: [ {id:2,...}, {id:4,...} ],
// }

// Map.groupBy — use when keys are non-string (objects, Symbols, numbers)
const byType = Map.groupBy(items, item => item.type);
byType.get('admin'); // [ {id:3,...}, {id:4,...} ]

// Replace manual reduce-based grouping
// Before (verbose)
const grouped = items.reduce((acc, item) => {
  (acc[item.status] ??= []).push(item);
  return acc;
}, {});

// After (concise)
const grouped2 = Object.groupBy(items, item => item.status);

// Practical: group log entries by severity
const logs = await fetchLogs();
const { error = [], warn = [], info = [] } =
  Object.groupBy(logs, log => log.level);
console.log(`Errors: ${error.length}, Warnings: ${warn.length}`);
```
Tradeoff: `Object.groupBy` creates a null-prototype object (`Object.create(null)`), which means prototype methods like `hasOwnProperty` are not available on the result — iterate with `Object.entries()` or `Object.keys()`. Use `Map.groupBy` when the keys must be non-string types (object references, Symbols) or when you need `Map`-specific methods like `forEach` and ordered insertion semantics.

**Pattern 147** — Explicit Resource Management with `using` and Symbol.dispose
```javascript
// ES2025 Explicit Resource Management — deterministic cleanup
class DatabaseConnection {
  #conn;

  constructor(dsn) {
    this.#conn = openConnection(dsn);
    console.log('Connection opened');
  }

  query(sql) { return this.#conn.execute(sql); }

  // Called automatically at end of 'using' block scope
  [Symbol.dispose]() {
    this.#conn.close();
    console.log('Connection closed');
  }
}

// Synchronous resource — using keyword
function processReport() {
  using conn = new DatabaseConnection(process.env.DB_DSN);
  const data = conn.query('SELECT * FROM report');
  return transform(data);
  // conn[Symbol.dispose]() is called here — even if transform() throws
}

// Async resource — Symbol.asyncDispose + await using
class FileHandle {
  async [Symbol.asyncDispose]() {
    await this.#handle.close(); // async cleanup
  }
}

async function processFile(path) {
  await using fh = await FileHandle.open(path);
  return await fh.readAll();
  // fh[Symbol.asyncDispose]() called on scope exit
}

// DisposableStack for managing multiple resources
function withResources() {
  using stack = new DisposableStack();
  const db   = stack.use(new DatabaseConnection(DB_DSN));
  const cache = stack.use(new CacheClient());
  // Both disposed in LIFO order when scope exits
}
```
Tradeoff: `using` provides deterministic cleanup with cleaner syntax than try/finally, but requires TypeScript 5.2+ or the `@babel/plugin-proposal-explicit-resource-management` plugin. The `[Symbol.dispose]` contract is synchronous — heavyweight async teardown belongs in `[Symbol.asyncDispose]` with `await using`. For environments that cannot transpile the new syntax, the equivalent try/finally pattern remains fully functional and should be the fallback.

**Pattern 148** — Array.prototype.at() and Relative Indexing
```javascript
// Array.at() — negative indices count from the end
const arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50];

// Before: brittle length arithmetic
arr[arr.length - 1];  // 50
arr[arr.length - 2];  // 40

// After: clean negative indexing
arr.at(-1);  // 50
arr.at(-2);  // 40
arr.at(0);   // 10 — works like bracket notation for non-negative indices

// Out of bounds returns undefined — does NOT throw
arr.at(100);  // undefined
arr.at(-100); // undefined

// Works on strings too
'hello'.at(-1); // 'o'
'hello'.at(0);  // 'h'

// Practical: ring buffer pop
function processQueue(queue) {
  while (queue.length > 0) {
    const latest  = queue.at(-1);   // peek last
    const first   = queue.at(0);    // peek first
    processItem(first);
    queue.shift();
  }
}

// TypedArray and String support
const typed = new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
typed.at(-1); // 5

// Chaining — readable last-element access in pipelines
const mostRecent = events
  .filter(e => e.type === 'login')
  .at(-1);  // last login event or undefined
```
Tradeoff: `Array.at(-1)` is strictly cleaner than `arr[arr.length - 1]` but returns `undefined` for both out-of-bounds AND genuine `undefined` values in the array. If you need to distinguish "index exists but is undefined" from "index out of range", use `arr.length - 1` comparison explicitly. Baseline support as of mid-2022 across all major browsers — safe to use without polyfill in any modern baseline.

**Pattern 149** — Microtask vs. Macrotask Scheduling with queueMicrotask() and setTimeout()
```javascript
// Execution order: synchronous → microtasks → macrotasks
console.log('1 — sync');

setTimeout(() => console.log('4 — macrotask'), 0);

Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log('3 — microtask (promise)'));

queueMicrotask(() => console.log('2 — microtask (explicit)'));

// Output: 1 — sync, 2 — microtask (explicit), 3 — microtask (promise), 4 — macrotask
// Note: queueMicrotask and .then() both schedule microtasks; ordering depends on registration order

// Practical: batch DOM reads before next paint without forcing reflow
function batchDOMUpdates(updates) {
  queueMicrotask(() => {
    for (const fn of updates) fn();
  });
}

// Practical: defer callback to end of current synchronous operation
class EventEmitter {
  #listeners = new Map();

  emit(event, data) {
    const handlers = this.#listeners.get(event) ?? [];
    // Use microtask so emit() returns before handlers run
    // Handlers see fully constructed state
    for (const handler of handlers) {
      queueMicrotask(() => handler(data));
    }
  }
}

// Anti-pattern: using Promise.resolve().then() just to schedule a microtask
// queueMicrotask(() => cb()) is clearer and avoids Promise overhead
```
Tradeoff: `queueMicrotask` schedules work before any I/O or rendering callbacks, making it suitable for ensuring state consistency within a single event loop tick. However, over-using microtasks to defer work creates a microtask queue flood — a long chain of `queueMicrotask` calls starves the macrotask queue (I/O, rendering, timers). For work that should yield to the event loop, use `setTimeout(fn, 0)` or `scheduler.yield()` (where available).

### Community Gotchas

**G97** — Floating Promises in Event Handlers and Class Methods
Developers write `async` event handlers or class methods and call them without awaiting, creating floating promises whose rejections are silently swallowed.
Why this matters: `button.addEventListener('click', async () => { await riskyFetch(); })` — if `riskyFetch()` throws, the error goes to `unhandledRejection`, not to any visible catch block. In class methods, `this.init()` called in a constructor returns a Promise that is never awaited; errors disappear silently. The constructor completes before `init()` resolves, leaving the instance in a partially initialised state that later methods assume is complete.
Fix: Attach a `.catch()` handler to every fire-and-forget async call: `button.addEventListener('click', () => riskyFetch().catch(handleError))`. Use a static async factory method (`static async create()`) instead of calling async methods from constructors. Enable the `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` or `eslint-plugin-promise/catch-or-return` lint rules to catch this at the lint stage.

**G98** — Destructuring null/undefined API Responses Without a Guard
Developers destructure API response objects directly without guarding against `null` or `undefined`, causing `TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'X' of undefined`.
Why this matters: `const { data: { user } } = await fetchProfile(id)` throws when the API returns `null`, a 404 response body, or when `fetchProfile` resolves with `undefined` on network error. This is the leading cause of "white screen" crashes in React apps — the component renders, the fetch resolves to `undefined`, destructuring throws, the error boundary (if any) catches it, but the user sees a blank page with no diagnostic.
Fix: Always provide a fallback before destructuring deep structures: `const { data: { user } = {} } = await fetchProfile(id) ?? {}`. Better: validate at the boundary with a schema parser (`zod`, `valibot`) that throws a descriptive error on shape mismatch. TypeScript's `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` and strict null checks surface these at compile time — enable them in `tsconfig.json`.

**G99** — Generator Single-Use: Iterating a Generator Twice Yields Nothing
Generators return `this` from `[Symbol.iterator]()`, making them self-iterating — but a generator instance is consumed after the first iteration, and a second `for...of` loop over the same instance produces no values without any error or warning.
Why this matters: `const gen = fibonacci(); [...gen]; [...gen]` — the second spread is silently empty. Developers who store a generator in a variable and pass it to multiple consumers (e.g., pass to `Array.from` and then to another function) hit this in production with no obvious error. React server components that consume generators as prop values are especially prone to this when the generator is created outside the render function.
Fix: Wrap generators in factory functions (return a new generator on each call) rather than sharing generator instances. Use classes with `*[Symbol.iterator]()` for data structures that need to be re-iterable. When a generator is intentionally single-use, document it explicitly and immediately consume it at construction: `const items = [...generateItems()]`.

**G100** — `parseInt` on Floating-Point Results Silently Truncates, `Math.trunc` Is Explicit
Developers use `parseInt(floatValue)` to strip decimal places, not realising that `parseInt` first converts the argument to a string and re-parses it — which can silently drop precision for very large floats due to scientific notation stringification.
Why this matters: `parseInt(1e21)` returns `1` because `String(1e21)` is `"1e+21"` and `parseInt("1e+21")` parses only the `1` before the non-numeric `e`. `parseInt(0.000001)` returns `0` correctly, but `parseInt(0.0000001)` returns `1` because `String(0.0000001)` is `"1e-7"`. Any financial, scientific, or analytics calculation that rounds floats with `parseInt` risks silent data corruption for out-of-range values.
Fix: Use `Math.trunc(n)` to truncate toward zero, `Math.floor(n)` to round toward negative infinity, or `Math.round(n)` for standard rounding. Reserve `parseInt` exclusively for parsing strings of unknown format. Add an ESLint rule (`no-restricted-syntax`) that flags `parseInt` calls where the argument is a numeric expression rather than a string literal or variable typed as `string`.

**G101** — Default Parameter `= {}` Evaluates a New Object on Every Call
Developers use `function fn(opts = {})` as a safe default for optional options objects without realising a new empty object is allocated on every call where `opts` is omitted. In high-frequency paths (event listeners, render functions, tight loops), this generates significant GC pressure.
Why this matters: `function render(options = {})` called 60 times per frame creates 60 short-lived empty objects per second. V8's hidden-class optimisation cannot inline the allocation away if the function is polymorphic. In Node.js HTTP servers, a middleware with `function handle(req, res, options = {})` called on every request generates thousands of throwaway objects per second under load, degrading GC pause times and throughput.
Fix: Define a shared frozen sentinel outside the function: `const EMPTY = Object.freeze({}); function fn(opts = EMPTY)`. For options that are read-only defaults, `Object.freeze` prevents accidental mutation of the shared default. For options that are mutated internally (e.g., `Object.assign(defaults, opts)`), clone defensively: `const merged = Object.assign({}, EMPTY, opts)` — still only one allocation per call instead of two.

## Cycle 60 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 150** — `Array.fromAsync()` for Collecting Async Iterables
```javascript
// Collect an async generator into an array in one expression
async function* fetchPages(baseUrl, pages) {
  for (let i = 1; i <= pages; i++) {
    const res = await fetch(`${baseUrl}?page=${i}`);
    yield await res.json();
  }
}

// Array.fromAsync collects all yielded values sequentially
const pages = await Array.fromAsync(fetchPages('/api/posts', 5));
console.log(pages.length); // 5 — each page object in order

// mapFn: transform each value as it is collected
const titles = await Array.fromAsync(
  fetchPages('/api/posts', 5),
  page => page.title // mapFn output is also awaited if it returns a Promise
);

// Sync iterables: every yielded value is awaited automatically
const resolved = await Array.fromAsync(
  [Promise.resolve(1), Promise.resolve(2), Promise.resolve(3)]
);
// [1, 2, 3] — Promise values unwrapped for free

// No cleanup on error for sync iterables — prefer for...of when you need finally
```
Tradeoff: `Array.fromAsync` processes values sequentially (one await per element), making it safe for rate-limited APIs and back-pressured streams, but significantly slower than `Promise.all([...source])` for independent work — a 10-item async sequence takes ~10× the single-item latency instead of ~1×. When values are independent and latency matters, collect the promises first and resolve with `Promise.all`.

**Pattern 151** — `Promise.try()` for Uniform Sync/Async Error Handling
```javascript
// Problem: calling a function that might be sync or async
// Naive wrapper doesn't catch synchronous throws in the promise chain
function runCallback(cb) {
  return Promise.resolve(cb()); // throws BEFORE the Promise wraps it
}

// Promise.try() calls the function inside the promise machinery
// so synchronous throws become rejections
function runCallback(cb) {
  return Promise.try(cb);
}

// Practical: plugin/middleware systems where callbacks may be sync or async
class Pipeline {
  #steps = [];
  use(fn) { this.#steps.push(fn); return this; }

  async run(ctx) {
    for (const step of this.#steps) {
      // If step() throws synchronously, the error is caught uniformly
      await Promise.try(step, ctx);
    }
  }
}

// Passing arguments directly avoids an extra closure allocation
const result = await Promise.try(fetchUser, userId);

// Canonical upgrade from the old pattern
// Before: new Promise(resolve => resolve(maybeSync()))
// After:  Promise.try(maybeSync)
```
Tradeoff: `Promise.try(fn)` calls `fn` synchronously on the current tick (unlike `Promise.resolve().then(fn)` which defers one microtask), making it semantically equivalent to an inline `try { resolve(fn()) } catch (e) { reject(e) }`. This preserves call-stack-friendly timing but means the callback runs immediately — avoid using it to defer CPU-heavy work; use `setTimeout` or a scheduler for that.

**Pattern 152** — ES2025 Set Composition Methods
```javascript
const frontend = new Set(['alice', 'bob', 'carol']);
const backend  = new Set(['bob', 'carol', 'dave']);

// union: all members of either team
const allEngineers = frontend.union(backend);
// Set {'alice', 'bob', 'carol', 'dave'}

// intersection: members on both teams
const fullStack = frontend.intersection(backend);
// Set {'bob', 'carol'}

// difference: frontend-only members
const frontendOnly = frontend.difference(backend);
// Set {'alice'}

// symmetricDifference: members on exactly one team
const specialised = frontend.symmetricDifference(backend);
// Set {'alice', 'dave'}

// Predicate methods
console.log(fullStack.isSubsetOf(frontend));       // true
console.log(frontend.isSupersetOf(fullStack));     // true
console.log(frontendOnly.isDisjointFrom(backend)); // true

// Methods accept any set-like object (has size, has(), keys())
const permissions = new Map([['read', true], ['write', false]]);
const required = new Set(['read', 'write']);
const granted = required.intersection(permissions); // Set {'read'}
```
Tradeoff: The seven new Set methods (`union`, `intersection`, `difference`, `symmetricDifference`, `isSubsetOf`, `isSupersetOf`, `isDisjointFrom`) accept any set-like object (not just `Set` instances), making them composable with `Map` and custom collections that expose `size`, `has()`, and `keys()`. However, they always return a new `Set` — they never mutate the receiver — so chaining many operations on large sets creates intermediate allocations. For tight loops over large datasets, accumulate into a pre-allocated `Set` manually instead.

**Pattern 153** — `Error.isError()` for Cross-Realm and Branded Error Detection
```javascript
// instanceof fails across iframes and vm contexts
const vmError = vm.runInNewContext('new Error("oops")');
console.log(vmError instanceof Error); // false — different realm
console.log(Error.isError(vmError));   // true  — branded check

// Safe normalisation in catch blocks
async function safeFetch(url) {
  try {
    return await fetch(url);
  } catch (e) {
    // Third-party libraries sometimes throw strings or plain objects
    const err = Error.isError(e) ? e : new Error(String(e));
    throw err; // guaranteed Error for upstream .catch handlers
  }
}

// Distinguishes real errors from objects that inherit Error.prototype
const fake = Object.create(Error.prototype);
console.log(fake instanceof Error); // true  — misleading
console.log(Error.isError(fake));   // false — not branded

// Works with DOMException (also branded as an Error in the spec)
console.log(Error.isError(new DOMException('abort', 'AbortError'))); // true

// Type narrowing utility
function isError(value) {
  return Error.isError(value);
}
```
Tradeoff: `Error.isError()` uses an internal slot check (branded introspection), making it immune to prototype manipulation and cross-realm failures that plague `instanceof`. The tradeoff is that it only returns `true` for objects allocated by the native `Error` constructor family — a custom class that extends `Error` passes, but a plain object shaped like an Error does not, which can surprise developers who treat duck-typing as sufficient.

**Pattern 154** — `RegExp.escape()` for Safe Dynamic Patterns
```javascript
// WITHOUT escape: user input can break or hijack the regex
function highlight(text, term) {
  return text.replace(new RegExp(term, 'gi'), '<mark>$&</mark>');
}
// highlight('Price: $10.00', '$1') matches 'Price: ' ($ anchors, . wildcards)

// WITH RegExp.escape(): user input is treated as a literal string
function highlightSafe(text, term) {
  return text.replace(
    new RegExp(RegExp.escape(term), 'gi'),
    '<mark>$&</mark>'
  );
}
// RegExp.escape('$10.00') → '\\x2410\\.00' — safe literal

// Build complex patterns that include literal user fragments
function buildSearchPattern(literal, flags = 'gi') {
  return new RegExp(`(?:^|\\s)${RegExp.escape(literal)}(?:\\s|$)`, flags);
}

// Escapes all syntactically significant characters
console.log(RegExp.escape('a.b*c?d[e]f'));
// First char escaped with \xNN syntax, rest with backslash prefixes

// Replaces the community escape helper (was previously hand-rolled)
// Before: str.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')
// After:  RegExp.escape(str)  — handles edge cases like leading digits
```
Tradeoff: `RegExp.escape()` correctly handles all regex metacharacters including edge cases that hand-rolled replacements miss (leading digits, lone surrogates, whitespace variants). The escaped result is intentionally verbose — `RegExp.escape('foo')` produces `'\\x66oo'` with the first character hex-escaped — so using it for human-readable pattern display requires the original unescaped string. Available in browsers since May 2025; use `core-js` for environments that predate it.

**Pattern 155** — Temporal API: Timezone-Correct Date Arithmetic
```javascript
// Date arithmetic that respects DST boundaries
const { Temporal } = globalThis; // or import from '@js-temporal/polyfill'

// ZonedDateTime: exact instant + calendar + timezone in one object
const meetingStart = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from(
  '2025-03-09T09:00:00[America/New_York]'
);

// Add 24 calendar hours — may cross a DST boundary
const next24h = meetingStart.add({ hours: 24 });
// Correctly lands at 10:00 AM (DST spring-forward: clocks went ahead 1h)

// Add 1 calendar day — same clock time the next day
const nextDay = meetingStart.add({ days: 1 });
// Always 09:00 AM the next day regardless of DST

// PlainDate for date-only arithmetic (no timezone involved)
const start = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2025-01-31');
const monthLater = start.add({ months: 1 }); // '2025-02-28' — clamped correctly

// Duration between two ZonedDateTimes in human units
const now  = Temporal.Now.zonedDateTimeISO('UTC');
const release = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from('2025-12-31T00:00:00[UTC]');
const diff = now.until(release, { largestUnit: 'days' });
console.log(`${diff.days} days until release`);

// Convert to legacy Date only at API boundaries
const legacyDate = new Date(meetingStart.epochMilliseconds);
```
Tradeoff: `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` separates `add({ hours: N })` (exact duration, may change wall-clock time at DST) from `add({ days: N })` (calendar duration, same wall time next day), eliminating the DST-arithmetic class of bugs endemic to `Date`. The API is immutable — every operation returns a new object — which is memory-safe but requires unlearning the mutable setter pattern from `Date`. The polyfill (`@js-temporal/polyfill`) is ~50 KB gzipped; evaluate native browser support before including it.

**Pattern 156** — Iterator Helpers Pipeline (ES2024)
```javascript
// Without iterator helpers: creates three intermediate arrays
const result = largeArray
  .filter(x => x.active)
  .map(x => x.value * 2)
  .slice(0, 10);

// With iterator helpers: single lazy pass, no intermediate allocations
const result = largeArray.values()
  .filter(x => x.active)
  .map(x => x.value * 2)
  .take(10)
  .toArray();

// Works on any iterable via Iterator.from()
function* rangeGen(start, end) {
  for (let i = start; i < end; i++) yield i;
}

const firstFiveSquares = Iterator.from(rangeGen(0, 1_000_000))
  .map(n => n * n)
  .filter(n => n % 2 === 0)
  .take(5)
  .toArray();
// [0, 4, 16, 36, 64] — only 5 values ever materialised

// Extend Iterator for custom data structures
class TreeIterator extends Iterator {
  constructor(root) { super(); this.stack = [root]; }
  next() {
    if (!this.stack.length) return { done: true, value: undefined };
    const node = this.stack.pop();
    if (node.right) this.stack.push(node.right);
    if (node.left)  this.stack.push(node.left);
    return { done: false, value: node.value };
  }
}
new TreeIterator(root).filter(v => v > 10).toArray();
```
Tradeoff: Iterator helper methods (`filter`, `map`, `take`, `drop`, `flatMap`, `reduce`, `find`, `every`, `some`, `forEach`, `toArray`) compose lazily — values are only pulled when a consuming operation (`toArray`, `reduce`, `for...of`) requests them. This avoids intermediate array allocations for large datasets but means that side effects inside `map`/`filter` are deferred and interleaved with consumption, which can surprise developers expecting eager evaluation. Baseline widely available since 2024; polyfillable via `es-iterator-helpers`.

**Pattern 157** — `using` / `await using` for Explicit Resource Management
```javascript
// Symbol.dispose: synchronous cleanup
class FileHandle {
  constructor(path) {
    this.path = path;
    this.fd = fs.openSync(path, 'r');
    console.log(`Opened ${path}`);
  }
  [Symbol.dispose]() {
    fs.closeSync(this.fd);
    console.log(`Closed ${this.path}`);
  }
}

function readConfig(path) {
  using handle = new FileHandle(path); // disposed when block exits
  return JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(handle.fd, 'utf8'));
  // handle.fd closed automatically — even if JSON.parse throws
}

// Symbol.asyncDispose: asynchronous cleanup
class DbConnection {
  async [Symbol.asyncDispose]() {
    await this.connection.end();
  }
}

async function runQuery(sql) {
  await using db = await DbConnection.open(config);
  return db.query(sql);
  // db.connection.end() awaited automatically on exit
}

// Multiple resources — disposed in reverse order (LIFO)
{
  using lock  = acquireLock();
  using cache = openCache();
  // cache disposed first, then lock — mirrors acquisition order
}
```
Tradeoff: The `using` declaration (`using x = expr`) ties resource lifetime to lexical scope with guaranteed cleanup via `Symbol.dispose`, eliminating try/finally boilerplate and the class of bugs where a `return` or `throw` skips cleanup. If both the body and a disposer throw, the errors are combined into a `SuppressedError` rather than losing the original. Support requires TypeScript 5.2+ / Babel with the `@babel/plugin-proposal-explicit-resource-management` transform; native browser support is limited as of mid-2025.

**Pattern 158** — Proxy-Based Lazy Initialisation and Schema Validation
```javascript
// Lazy singleton initialisation via Proxy get trap
function lazyInit(factory) {
  let instance;
  return new Proxy({}, {
    get(_, prop) {
      instance ??= factory();
      return Reflect.get(instance, prop);
    }
  });
}

const db = lazyInit(() => new Database(config));
// Database is not constructed until first property access
db.query('SELECT 1'); // constructs now

// Deep-path "optional chaining" Proxy — never throws on missing paths
function safeDeep(obj) {
  return new Proxy(obj ?? {}, {
    get(target, prop) {
      const val = Reflect.get(target, prop);
      return val == null ? safeDeep(null) : safeDeep(val);
    }
  });
}

const name = safeDeep(apiResponse).user.profile.displayName;
// undefined instead of TypeError, no ?.?.?. chain needed

// Schema enforcement Proxy — validate on set
function typed(schema) {
  return new Proxy({}, {
    set(target, prop, value) {
      if (schema[prop] && typeof value !== schema[prop]) {
        throw new TypeError(`${prop} must be ${schema[prop]}`);
      }
      return Reflect.set(target, prop, value);
    }
  });
}

const user = typed({ name: 'string', age: 'number' });
user.name = 'Alice'; // ok
user.age  = 'old';   // TypeError: age must be number
```
Tradeoff: Proxy traps intercept every property access, making them powerful for cross-cutting concerns (logging, validation, lazy init) without modifying the target object. The cost is a ~3–5× slowdown per property access compared to plain object access in V8 — avoid Proxy in hot paths that execute millions of times per second. Always forward through `Reflect` to preserve the correct receiver (`this`) in get/set traps.

**Pattern 159** — `FinalizationRegistry` + `WeakRef` for Optional Cache Eviction
```javascript
// A cache that doesn't prevent GC of its values
class WeakValueCache {
  #cache    = new Map();       // key → WeakRef<value>
  #registry = new FinalizationRegistry(key => {
    // GC collected the value — remove the stale WeakRef entry
    const ref = this.#cache.get(key);
    if (ref && !ref.deref()) this.#cache.delete(key);
  });

  set(key, value) {
    this.#registry.register(value, key, value); // token = value itself
    this.#cache.set(key, new WeakRef(value));
  }

  get(key) {
    return this.#cache.get(key)?.deref(); // undefined if GC'd
  }

  has(key) {
    return this.get(key) !== undefined;
  }
}

const imageCache = new WeakValueCache();
imageCache.set('hero', loadImage('/hero.png'));
// If 'hero' image is GC'd under memory pressure,
// subsequent .get('hero') returns undefined and triggers refetch

// FinalizationRegistry for external resource cleanup (last resort)
const fileRegistry = new FinalizationRegistry(fd => {
  fs.closeSync(fd); // safety net — prefer explicit using/dispose
});

class UnsafeFile {
  #fd;
  constructor(path) {
    this.#fd = fs.openSync(path, 'r');
    fileRegistry.register(this, this.#fd, this);
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `WeakRef` lets a cache hold an object without extending its lifetime, enabling GC-driven eviction under memory pressure — ideal for image/blob caches and memoisation of large computed values. The fundamental caveat is that GC timing is non-deterministic: `ref.deref()` may return a live value on one call and `undefined` on the next without any explicit eviction step. Never use `WeakRef` as a substitute for explicit lifecycle management (use `using` / `Symbol.dispose` for that); treat it as a performance hint only.

**Pattern 160** — `Symbol.toPrimitive` and `Symbol.hasInstance` for Custom Type Semantics
```javascript
// Symbol.toPrimitive: control all three coercion contexts
class Money {
  constructor(amount, currency) {
    this.amount   = amount;
    this.currency = currency;
  }

  [Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) {
    if (hint === 'number') return this.amount;
    if (hint === 'string') return `${this.amount} ${this.currency}`;
    // 'default' (used in + and == contexts)
    return this.amount;
  }
}

const price = new Money(9.99, 'USD');
console.log(+price);            // 9.99
console.log(`${price}`);        // "9.99 USD"
console.log(price + 0.01);      // 10.0 (default hint)

// Symbol.hasInstance: customise instanceof semantics
class Uint8 {
  static [Symbol.hasInstance](value) {
    return Number.isInteger(value) && value >= 0 && value <= 255;
  }
}

console.log(127  instanceof Uint8); // true
console.log(256  instanceof Uint8); // false
console.log(1.5  instanceof Uint8); // false
console.log(-1   instanceof Uint8); // false

// Useful for type-safe discriminated unions at runtime
class HttpSuccess {
  static [Symbol.hasInstance](v) { return v?.status >= 200 && v?.status < 300; }
}
if (response instanceof HttpSuccess) { /* narrowed */ }
```
Tradeoff: `Symbol.toPrimitive` gives fine-grained control over all three coercion hints (`'number'`, `'string'`, `'default'`) in a single method, superseding `valueOf` and `toString` for custom numeric and display semantics. Overusing coercion makes code harder to read — implicit `+price` is surprising to readers who do not know the class. `Symbol.hasInstance` decouples type checking from inheritance, enabling structural or predicate-based `instanceof` without modifying prototypes.

**Pattern 161** — `structuredClone()` with Transferable Objects and Known Limitations
```javascript
// Deep clone without JSON round-trip limitations
const original = {
  date:   new Date(),
  map:    new Map([['key', 'val']]),
  set:    new Set([1, 2, 3]),
  buffer: new ArrayBuffer(16),
  regex:  /foo/gi,
  arr:    new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3]),
};

const clone = structuredClone(original);
clone.date.setFullYear(2000); // original.date unchanged

// Transfer ownership (zero-copy move) instead of cloning
const buffer = new ArrayBuffer(1024 * 1024); // 1 MB
const { port1, port2 } = new MessageChannel();

// Transfer: buffer is moved to port2's realm, original reference neutered
port1.postMessage({ buf: buffer }, { transfer: [buffer] });
// buffer.byteLength === 0 after transfer

// Known limitations — these throw DataCloneError:
// structuredClone(() => {})           // functions
// structuredClone(new Proxy({}, {}))  // Proxy objects
// structuredClone(document.body)      // DOM nodes
// structuredClone(new WeakMap())      // WeakMap / WeakSet
// structuredClone(Symbol('s'))        // Symbols

// Circular references ARE supported (unlike JSON.stringify)
const a = {};
const b = { ref: a };
a.ref = b;
const cloned = structuredClone({ a, b }); // works fine
```
Tradeoff: `structuredClone()` correctly deep-copies `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `RegExp`, typed arrays, and `ArrayBuffer` — all the types `JSON.stringify` fails on — and handles circular references without stack overflow. The hard limits are functions, Proxy objects, DOM nodes, WeakMap/WeakSet, and Symbol keys, all of which throw `DataCloneError`. For graphs containing these types, write a custom recursive clone or use a library like `klona`.

**Pattern 162** — Module-Level `WeakMap` for Truly Private Instance Data
```javascript
// Private WeakMap — inaccessible outside this module file
const _secret = new WeakMap();
const _state  = new WeakMap();

export class Session {
  constructor(token, userId) {
    _secret.set(this, { token });         // not enumerable, not in devtools
    _state.set(this, { userId, hits: 0 });
  }

  get userId() { return _state.get(this).userId; }

  record() {
    const s = _state.get(this);
    s.hits++;
  }

  authenticate(incoming) {
    return incoming === _secret.get(this).token; // never exposed
  }
}

// Comparison: private class fields (#) vs WeakMap approach
class WithFields {
  #token;
  constructor(t) { this.#token = t; }
  // #token is engine-private — accessible to devtools, not to external code
  // WeakMap approach: accessible to any code in the same module closure
  // Use # for most cases; WeakMap for cross-instance access within module
}

// Cross-instance access is where WeakMap shines
export function transferState(from, to) {
  const prev = _state.get(from);
  _state.set(to, { ...prev });
  // Cannot do this with private class fields without an accessor
}
```
Tradeoff: Module-level `WeakMap` encapsulation predates private class fields (`#`) and remains useful when one module needs to access private state of instances belonging to multiple classes (e.g., mixins, factory functions), since `#` fields are inaccessible even within the same module from a sibling class. The tradeoff is ergonomic: `_data.get(this).prop` vs `this.#prop` — the latter is terser, type-inferred by TypeScript, and does not require a closure. Prefer `#` for single-class encapsulation and WeakMap for cross-class within-module patterns.

**Pattern 163** — `Object.hasOwn()` as a Safe `hasOwnProperty` Replacement
```javascript
// The classic trap: hasOwnProperty can be shadowed
const malicious = Object.create(null);
malicious.hasOwnProperty = () => true; // shadows the method
malicious.hasOwnProperty('foo'); // always true — lie

// Object.hasOwn() cannot be shadowed — it's a static method
Object.hasOwn(malicious, 'foo'); // false — correct answer

// Safe iteration over arbitrary objects
function safeAssign(target, source) {
  for (const key in source) {
    if (Object.hasOwn(source, key)) {        // replaces source.hasOwnProperty(key)
      target[key] = source[key];
    }
  }
}

// Works on null-prototype objects (Object.create(null))
const record = Object.create(null);
record.name = 'Alice';
Object.hasOwn(record, 'name');         // true
Object.hasOwn(record, 'toString');     // false — not inherited

// TypeScript: narrows the type after the check
function getOwn<T>(obj: T, key: string): unknown {
  return Object.hasOwn(obj as object, key)
    ? (obj as Record<string, unknown>)[key]
    : undefined;
}

// ESLint rule: prefer-object-has-own — enforces this pattern automatically
```
Tradeoff: `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` is strictly superior to `obj.hasOwnProperty(key)` — it works on null-prototype objects, cannot be shadowed by a same-name own property, and avoids the `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj, key)` ceremony. The only compatibility concern is environments predating ES2022 (Node 16.9+, Chrome 93+), where `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call` remains the safest fallback. Enable the `prefer-object-has-own` ESLint rule to migrate call sites automatically.

**Pattern 164** — `Atomics` + `SharedArrayBuffer` for Lock-Free Cross-Thread State
```javascript
// Shared memory segment
const sab  = new SharedArrayBuffer(4);   // 4 bytes
const view = new Int32Array(sab);        // typed view

// --- Main thread ---
const worker = new Worker('./worker.js');
worker.postMessage({ sab });

// Wait for worker to signal readiness (blocks the main thread — avoid in UI)
Atomics.wait(view, 0, 0); // wait until index 0 != 0

// --- worker.js ---
self.onmessage = ({ data: { sab } }) => {
  const view = new Int32Array(sab);

  // Atomic counter increment (safe across threads)
  Atomics.add(view, 0, 1);
  Atomics.notify(view, 0);  // wake main thread

  // Compare-and-swap: only update if current value matches expected
  const old = Atomics.compareExchange(view, 0, 1, 42);
  // Sets index 0 to 42 only if it was 1; returns previous value
};

// Atomic operations available:
// Atomics.add/sub/and/or/xor — read-modify-write, returns old value
// Atomics.load/store          — guaranteed atomic read/write
// Atomics.compareExchange     — CAS primitive for lock-free algorithms
// Atomics.wait/notify         — futex-style blocking/waking

// Required: COOP/COEP headers for SharedArrayBuffer in browsers
// Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
// Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp
```
Tradeoff: `SharedArrayBuffer` + `Atomics` enable genuinely shared memory between the main thread and Web Workers, eliminating the serialisation overhead of `postMessage` for large buffers (useful for image processing, WASM interop, audio pipelines). The cost is complexity: lock-free programming requires precise reasoning about memory ordering, and a bug (missing CAS, torn read) produces non-deterministic race conditions that are hard to reproduce. `Atomics.wait()` blocks the calling thread — never call it on the main thread in a browser (use `Atomics.waitAsync()` instead). SharedArrayBuffer requires `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` response headers.

### Community Gotchas

**G102** — `Array.fromAsync` Does Not Clean Up Sync Iterators on Error
Developers assume `Array.fromAsync(syncGenerator())` behaves like `for await...of syncGenerator()` on error — calling the generator's `finally` block — but sync iterables receive no iterator cleanup when `Array.fromAsync` aborts.
Why this matters: A sync generator that wraps a file handle or lock in a `try...finally` block relies on the iterator being closed (`return()` called) to release the resource. `Array.fromAsync` does not call `return()` on sync iterators when a mapping function rejects or when a yielded Promise rejects, leaving the `finally` block unexecuted and the resource leaked. The same generator passed to `for await...of` would trigger cleanup correctly. This asymmetry is spec-defined behaviour, not a bug, but it is not documented prominently.
Fix: Do not wrap resource-managing sync generators in `Array.fromAsync` when those generators contain `finally` blocks. Use `for await...of` with a manual `push` into an array, or convert to an async generator (`async function*`) — async iterables receive full `return()` cleanup from `Array.fromAsync`. Add a linting rule or code review checklist item: any generator with `try...finally` must be consumed by `for...of` / `for await...of`, not by `Array.fromAsync`.

**G103** — `structuredClone` Silently Loses Symbol Keys and Non-Enumerable Properties
Developers use `structuredClone(obj)` expecting a complete deep clone, but Symbol-keyed properties and non-enumerable own properties are silently dropped without any error.
Why this matters: `const sym = Symbol('id'); obj[sym] = 123; structuredClone(obj)[sym]` is `undefined` — the property was not cloned. Objects augmented with Symbols (e.g., React internal fibers, third-party library tags, `Symbol.iterator` overrides) are stripped of that metadata. Equally, `Object.defineProperty(obj, 'version', { value: 2, enumerable: false })` produces a property invisible to `structuredClone`. The clone passes `JSON.stringify`-style equality checks but silently diverges from the original when Symbol-keyed behaviour is accessed later.
Fix: For objects with Symbol keys or non-enumerable properties, use a custom deep-clone function that explicitly copies Symbol keys via `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols()` and non-enumerable properties via `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors()`. Libraries like `klona` and `rfdc` do not handle Symbol keys either — check the library source before relying on it. If you own the class, add a `clone()` method that copies all relevant state explicitly.

**G104** — `Atomics.wait()` Deadlocks the Main Browser Thread
Developers port Node.js or WASM synchronisation code to the browser and call `Atomics.wait()` on the main thread, causing the tab to hang indefinitely.
Why this matters: `Atomics.wait()` is specified to block the calling thread until a notify or timeout occurs. Browsers explicitly forbid it on the main thread — it throws `TypeError: Atomics.wait cannot be called in this context` in Chrome/Firefox — but the code may work in Node.js worker threads and WASM contexts, leading to a "works locally, breaks in browser" scenario. Developers testing in Node.js without a browser test harness ship code that immediately deadlocks the tab in production. Even if not the main thread, a long-lived `Atomics.wait()` inside a Worker starves the Worker's own event loop (importScripts, fetch) until the wait resolves.
Fix: Replace every `Atomics.wait(view, idx, val)` on the main thread or in event-driven Worker code with `await Atomics.waitAsync(view, idx, val)` — the async variant returns a Promise and never blocks. Reserve `Atomics.wait()` exclusively for dedicated compute Workers that do not serve an event loop. Gate usage behind an environment check: `if (typeof WorkerGlobalScope === 'undefined') throw new Error('Atomics.wait only in Workers')`.

**G105** — `using` Disposal Errors Wrap, Not Replace, the Original Error
Developers expect a `try { using r = …; throw bodyError; } catch(e)` to deliver `bodyError` to the catch block, but if `r[Symbol.dispose]()` also throws, the catch block receives a `SuppressedError` wrapping both errors — and the body error is buried at `e.suppressed`.
Why this matters: `SuppressedError.message` is the disposer's error message, not the body error. Code that does `catch(e) { if (e.message.includes('network')) retry() }` silently fails to match when the body threw a network error but the disposer also threw, because the outer message belongs to the disposer. Logging frameworks that record `e.message` + `e.stack` miss the root cause entirely. This error-wrapping behaviour exists to avoid silent swallowing, but the `SuppressedError` type is new and most error monitoring tools (Sentry, Datadog) do not yet unwrap it automatically.
Fix: Catch `SuppressedError` explicitly and log both layers: `if (e instanceof SuppressedError) { log(e.error); log(e.suppressed); }`. Add a utility wrapper that normalises `SuppressedError` into an `AggregateError` for frameworks that understand the latter. In disposers, be defensive — wrap disposal logic in its own `try...catch` and log rather than re-throw unless the disposal failure is truly unrecoverable.

**G106** — `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` vs `Temporal.PlainDateTime` Timezone Confusion
Developers reach for `Temporal.PlainDateTime` when they need a "local" time, not realising that `PlainDateTime` carries no timezone and produces incorrect absolute timestamps when passed to APIs expecting UTC milliseconds.
Why this matters: `Temporal.PlainDateTime.from('2025-11-02T01:30:00').epochMilliseconds` throws `TypeError` — `PlainDateTime` has no `epochMilliseconds` property because without a timezone, the absolute instant is undefined. Converting via `.toZonedDateTime('America/New_York')` at DST fall-back time produces two possible instants (01:30 AM occurs twice), and Temporal defaults to the earlier one — silently yielding the wrong instant for calendaring apps that intend the later occurrence. Developers who branch from `Date`-centric thinking use `PlainDateTime` where `ZonedDateTime` is needed, causing off-by-one-hour errors that only manifest on two days per year.
Fix: Default to `Temporal.ZonedDateTime` for any time that will be converted to an absolute instant or displayed to users in a specific timezone. Use `Temporal.PlainDate` only for date-only values (birthdays, deadlines without time) and `Temporal.PlainTime` for time-of-day values without a calendar context (recurring alarms). When constructing a `ZonedDateTime` during a DST ambiguity, pass `{ disambiguation: 'later' }` to `toZonedDateTime()` to select the intended occurrence explicitly.
