## Cycle 68 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 285** — Jest ESM-Native Testing with `jest.unstable_mockModule()` and Dynamic Import
```js
// jest.config.mjs
export default {
  extensionsToTreatAsEsm: ['.ts'],
  transform: {},                        // No Babel — native ESM
  testEnvironment: 'node',
};

// src/config.mjs
export const BASE_URL = import.meta.env?.VITE_API ?? 'http://localhost:3000';

// src/__tests__/config.test.mjs
import { jest } from '@jest/globals';

// Mock must be registered BEFORE the dynamic import that binds the module
jest.unstable_mockModule('../config.mjs', async () => {
  const real = await jest.importActual('../config.mjs');
  return { ...real, BASE_URL: 'https://test.example.com' };
});

// Dynamic import AFTER registration receives the mocked binding
const { BASE_URL } = await import('../config.mjs');

test('BASE_URL picks up the mocked value', () => {
  expect(BASE_URL).toBe('https://test.example.com');
});

test('BASE_URL is still a string (importActual shape preserved)', () => {
  expect(typeof BASE_URL).toBe('string');
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.unstable_mockModule()` with dynamic `await import()` works correctly for ESM under `--experimental-vm-modules`, but every test file that needs the mock must bind via `await import()` after registration — a top-level static `import` binds before `jest.unstable_mockModule()` runs, silently receiving the real module and making the mock appear to have no effect.

**Pattern 286** — Vitest `vi.mock()` with `vi.fn()` and `vi.mocked()` for Type-Safe ESM Mocks
```ts
// src/payments.ts
export async function chargeCard(amount: number, token: string): Promise<string> {
  const { Stripe } = await import('stripe');
  const stripe = new Stripe(process.env.STRIPE_KEY!);
  const intent = await stripe.paymentIntents.create({ amount, currency: 'usd' });
  return intent.id;
}

// src/__tests__/payments.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';

const mockCreate = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ id: 'pi_test_001' });
vi.mock('stripe', () => ({
  Stripe: vi.fn(() => ({
    paymentIntents: { create: mockCreate },
  })),
}));

import { chargeCard } from '../payments.js';

describe('chargeCard', () => {
  beforeEach(() => vi.clearAllMocks());

  it('returns the payment intent ID on success', async () => {
    const id = await chargeCard(1000, 'tok_visa');
    expect(id).toBe('pi_test_001');
  });

  it('calls paymentIntents.create with the correct amount', async () => {
    await chargeCard(500, 'tok_visa');
    expect(mockCreate).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ amount: 500, currency: 'usd' });
  });

  it('propagates Stripe API errors to callers', async () => {
    mockCreate.mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('card_declined'));
    await expect(chargeCard(9999, 'tok_decline')).rejects.toThrow('card_declined');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Hoisting `vi.mock()` to module top-level via Vite transform makes the factory available before static imports resolve — but `vi.mock()` placed inside a `describe` or `it` block is silently discarded with no warning, returning the real module and causing tests to make real HTTP calls or throw unexpected errors from the actual implementation.

**Pattern 287** — Jest `clearMocks` / `resetMocks` / `restoreMocks` — Choosing the Right Lifecycle Setting
```js
// jest.config.js
module.exports = {
  // clearMocks:   wipes .mock.calls and .mock.instances each test
  // resetMocks:   clearMocks + removes mockReturnValue / mockImplementation
  // restoreMocks: resetMocks + restores jest.spyOn() to its original implementation
  restoreMocks: true,   // safest for suites mixing spyOn with module mocks
};

// __tests__/auth.test.js
import { verifyToken } from '../auth.js';
import * as crypto from '../crypto.js';

test('verifyToken returns true for valid signature', () => {
  const spy = jest.spyOn(crypto, 'hmac').mockReturnValue('valid-sig');
  expect(verifyToken('valid-sig', 'payload')).toBe(true);
  expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalledWith('payload');
  // restoreMocks: true → spy is restored after every test file automatically
});

test('verifyToken calls real crypto.hmac when no spy is active', () => {
  // Only correct when restoreMocks: true is set; otherwise spy from prior test persists
  expect(() => verifyToken('anything', 'payload')).not.toThrow();
});
```
Tradeoff: `restoreMocks: true` eliminates `jest.spyOn()` leakage between test files without any per-test `mockRestore()` call, but it has no effect on mocks created with `jest.fn()` or `jest.mock()` — those require explicit `mockReset()` or `jest.resetModules()` respectively, meaning teams that mix both strategies still need targeted per-strategy cleanup.

**Pattern 288** — Vitest `test.each` Template Literal Tables for Exhaustive Input Coverage
```ts
import { describe, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { formatCurrency } from '../formatCurrency.js';

describe('formatCurrency', () => {
  test.each`
    amount     | locale       | expected
    ${1000}    | ${'en-US'}   | ${'$1,000.00'}
    ${1000}    | ${'de-DE'}   | ${'1.000,00 €'}
    ${0.5}     | ${'en-GB'}   | ${'£0.50'}
    ${-50}     | ${'ja-JP'}   | ${'-¥50'}
    ${1000000} | ${'en-US'}   | ${'$1,000,000.00'}
    ${0}       | ${'en-US'}   | ${'$0.00'}
  `('formatCurrency($amount, $locale) → "$expected"', ({
    amount, locale, expected,
  }: { amount: number; locale: string; expected: string }) => {
    expect(formatCurrency(amount, locale)).toBe(expected);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Tagged template `test.each` tables embed expected values directly in the test title via `$variable` interpolation, making failures immediately human-readable — but cells containing objects or arrays render as `[object Object]` / `[object Array]` in test titles; use the array-of-arrays `test.each([[...]])` form when table cells are non-primitive to retain readable test names.

**Pattern 289** — Jest `advanceTimersByTimeAsync()` for Testing Throttle Functions with Internal `await`
```js
import { throttle } from '../throttle.js';

describe('throttle', () => {
  beforeEach(() => jest.useFakeTimers());
  afterEach(() => jest.useRealTimers());

  test('fires immediately on first call', async () => {
    const fn = jest.fn();
    const throttled = throttle(fn, 500);
    throttled('first');
    expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
    expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalledWith('first');
  });

  test('suppresses calls within the wait window', async () => {
    const fn = jest.fn();
    const throttled = throttle(fn, 500);
    throttled('a');
    throttled('b');
    throttled('c');
    expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  });

  test('allows a second call after the window expires', async () => {
    const fn = jest.fn();
    const throttled = throttle(fn, 500);
    throttled('first');
    await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(500);
    throttled('second');
    expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
    expect(fn).toHaveBeenLastCalledWith('second');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync()` (Jest 29.1+) drains microtasks between each simulated tick so async continuations inside throttle/debounce functions settle correctly — but the synchronous `jest.advanceTimersByTime()` does not flush microtasks, leaving Promise chains unresolved mid-advancement and producing misleading pass/fail results for throttle implementations that use `await` internally.

**Pattern 290** — Node.js `module.register()` for ESM Loader Hook Composition in Zero-Config Test Pipelines
```js
// test-loaders/register.mjs
import { register } from 'node:module';
import { pathToFileURL } from 'node:url';

// Stack loaders: last registered = first applied
register('./path-alias-loader.mjs', pathToFileURL('./'));
register('./ts-strip-loader.mjs',   pathToFileURL('./'));

// test-loaders/ts-strip-loader.mjs
export async function load(url, context, nextLoad) {
  if (!url.endsWith('.ts') && !url.endsWith('.tsx'))
    return nextLoad(url, context);
  const raw = await nextLoad(url, { ...context, format: 'module' });
  const src = typeof raw.source === 'string'
    ? raw.source
    : Buffer.from(raw.source).toString('utf8');
  // Simplified type annotation stripper — use a real transform in production
  const stripped = src
    .replace(/:\s*[A-Za-z<>[\]|&?]+(?=\s*[=,);\n{])/g, '')
    .replace(/<[A-Za-z,\s]+>/g, '');
  return { ...raw, source: stripped };
}

// package.json: "test": "node --import ./test-loaders/register.mjs --test src/**/*.test.ts"
```
Tradeoff: `module.register()` (stable in Node 22+) stacks loader hooks without a config file and composes cleanly with the `--test` flag — but each hook runs synchronously in the module-loading critical path for every `import`; in large test suites the cumulative per-import overhead is measurable, and a pre-compiled artifact (esbuild bundle or `tsc --incremental`) is 5–15x faster for suites with 200+ modules.

**Pattern 291** — Vitest `expect.extend()` with Bidirectional Message Factory for Custom Matchers
```ts
import { expect, test } from 'vitest';
import type { MatcherResult } from '@vitest/expect';

expect.extend({
  toBeWithinRange(received: number, floor: number, ceiling: number): MatcherResult {
    const pass = typeof received === 'number'
      && received >= floor
      && received <= ceiling;
    return {
      pass,
      message: () =>
        pass
          ? `Expected ${received} NOT to be within [${floor}, ${ceiling}]`
          : `Expected ${received} to be within [${floor}, ${ceiling}], but it was outside that range`,
    };
  },
});

declare module 'vitest' {
  interface Assertion<T = any>           { toBeWithinRange(floor: number, ceiling: number): T }
  interface AsymmetricMatchersContaining { toBeWithinRange(floor: number, ceiling: number): void }
}

test('custom range matcher covers positive and negative assertions', () => {
  expect(5).toBeWithinRange(1, 10);
  expect(0).not.toBeWithinRange(1, 10);
  expect(10).toBeWithinRange(10, 10);      // boundary inclusive
  expect(11).not.toBeWithinRange(1, 10);
  expect(expect.toBeWithinRange(0, 100)).toEqual(expect.toBeWithinRange(0, 100));
});
```
Tradeoff: Custom matchers via `expect.extend()` produce domain-specific assertion messages that far outperform generic `expect(x).toBe(y)` diffs for numerical ranges, dates, or business objects — but the `message()` factory must produce correct failure text for BOTH the positive case (`pass: false`) and the `.not` case (`pass: true`); returning a single static string always shows the same text regardless of which direction failed, confusing the debugging experience.

**Pattern 292** — Jest `__esModule: true` in Manual Mocks to Correctly Resolve Default Exports
```js
// src/cache.js
import store from './redis-client.js';   // default export

export async function get(key) {
  return store.get(key);
}

export async function set(key, value, ttl) {
  return store.set(key, value, { EX: ttl });
}

// src/__tests__/cache.test.js
jest.mock('./redis-client.js', () => ({
  __esModule: true,        // Required: marks this as an ES module mock
  default: {
    get: jest.fn(),
    set: jest.fn(),
  },
}));

import store from './redis-client.js';
import { get, set } from '../cache.js';

beforeEach(() => jest.clearAllMocks());

test('get delegates to store.get', async () => {
  store.get.mockResolvedValue('cached-value');
  await expect(get('my-key')).resolves.toBe('cached-value');
  expect(store.get).toHaveBeenCalledWith('my-key');
});

test('set passes TTL as EX option to store.set', async () => {
  store.set.mockResolvedValue('OK');
  await set('my-key', 'data', 300);
  expect(store.set).toHaveBeenCalledWith('my-key', 'data', { EX: 300 });
});
```
Tradeoff: Omitting `__esModule: true` from a default-export mock factory causes Jest (with Babel/ts-jest) to wrap the mock in a CommonJS `{ default: ... }` interop envelope — meaning `store` resolves to `undefined` in the module under test while `store.default.get` holds the actual mock, producing `TypeError: store.get is not a function` with no indication that `__esModule: true` is missing.

**Pattern 293** — Node.js `node:test` Built-in Runner with TAP Output and `mock.fn()` Stubs
```js
// tests/order-service.test.mjs
import { test, describe, mock } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { createOrder } from '../src/order-service.mjs';

describe('createOrder', () => {
  test('assigns a generated ID to the order', async (t) => {
    const stubUUID = mock.fn(() => 'test-uuid-001');
    const order = await createOrder({ item: 'book', qty: 2 }, { generateId: stubUUID });
    assert.strictEqual(order.id, 'test-uuid-001');
    assert.strictEqual(stubUUID.mock.calls.length, 1);
  });

  test('calculates total price correctly', async () => {
    const order = await createOrder({ item: 'pen', qty: 5, unitPrice: 1.20 });
    assert.strictEqual(order.total, 6.00);
  });

  test('sets status to "pending" on creation', async () => {
    const order = await createOrder({ item: 'notebook', qty: 1, unitPrice: 5 });
    assert.strictEqual(order.status, 'pending');
  });

  test('rejects when qty is zero or negative', async () => {
    await assert.rejects(
      createOrder({ item: 'pen', qty: 0, unitPrice: 1 }),
      { message: 'qty must be > 0' }
    );
  });
});
// Run: node --test --test-reporter=tap tests/order-service.test.mjs
```
Tradeoff: `mock.fn()` from `node:test` provides Jest-style call tracking (`.mock.calls`, `.mock.results`) with zero external dependencies, but unlike `jest.fn()` it does not have a global auto-reset mechanism — each `mock.fn()` must be reset manually via `.mock.resetCalls()` in `beforeEach` or by re-creating the stub each test, otherwise call counts accumulate across test cases in the same `describe` block.

**Pattern 294** — Vitest `vi.stubGlobal()` and `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` for Hermetic Global State Tests
```ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';

// src/feature-flags.ts
// export function isFeatureEnabled(flag: string): boolean {
//   return !!(globalThis.__FEATURES__?.[flag] ?? false);
// }

import { isFeatureEnabled } from '../feature-flags.js';

describe('isFeatureEnabled', () => {
  afterEach(() => vi.unstubAllGlobals());

  it('returns true when flag is set to true in globalThis.__FEATURES__', () => {
    vi.stubGlobal('__FEATURES__', { darkMode: true, betaUI: false });
    expect(isFeatureEnabled('darkMode')).toBe(true);
  });

  it('returns false when flag is explicitly set to false', () => {
    vi.stubGlobal('__FEATURES__', { darkMode: false });
    expect(isFeatureEnabled('darkMode')).toBe(false);
  });

  it('returns false when __FEATURES__ is undefined', () => {
    vi.stubGlobal('__FEATURES__', undefined);
    expect(isFeatureEnabled('darkMode')).toBe(false);
  });

  it('returns false for an unknown flag', () => {
    vi.stubGlobal('__FEATURES__', { betaUI: true });
    expect(isFeatureEnabled('unknownFlag')).toBe(false);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.stubGlobal()` with `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` in `afterEach` isolates global state mutations completely between tests, but it cannot override properties defined as `configurable: false` on `globalThis` — attempting to stub a non-configurable property throws `TypeError: Cannot redefine property`; those globals require either a full environment swap via `vitest.environment` or a wrapper function indirection that can be independently mocked.

**Pattern 295** — Jest `toMatchInlineSnapshot()` Paired with External Snapshot for Layered Regression Coverage
```jsx
// src/__tests__/InvoiceRow.test.jsx
import { render } from '@testing-library/react';
import { InvoiceRow } from '../InvoiceRow.jsx';

const INVOICE = {
  id: 'INV-2026-001',
  amount: 1250.00,
  status: 'paid',
  date: '2026-05-14',
};

test('InvoiceRow renders critical fields inline (code-review visible)', () => {
  const { getByTestId } = render(<InvoiceRow invoice={INVOICE} />);
  // Inline snapshot — diff shows in PR if amount format or status label changes
  expect(getByTestId('invoice-id')).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`
    <span
      data-testid="invoice-id"
    >
      INV-2026-001
    </span>
  `);
  expect(getByTestId('invoice-status')).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`
    <span
      class="status-badge status-paid"
      data-testid="invoice-status"
    >
      Paid
    </span>
  `);
});

test('InvoiceRow full tree external snapshot (bulk regression gate)', () => {
  const { container } = render(<InvoiceRow invoice={INVOICE} />);
  expect(container.firstChild).toMatchSnapshot();
});
```
Tradeoff: Combining inline snapshots (for critical semantics visible in PR diffs) with external snapshots (for full-tree regression detection) gives two safety layers, but Jest auto-rewrites inline snapshots into the source file during `--updateSnapshot` — a CI environment with a read-only source mount silently skips the rewrite without error, leaving stale inline snapshots that always pass regardless of actual component output.

**Pattern 296** — Testing `TransformStream` Pipelines with `pipeThrough()` and Async Iteration
```js
// src/transforms/uppercase.js
export function uppercaseTransform() {
  return new TransformStream({
    transform(chunk, controller) {
      controller.enqueue(
        typeof chunk === 'string' ? chunk.toUpperCase() : chunk
      );
    },
  });
}

// src/__tests__/uppercase.test.js
import { uppercaseTransform } from '../transforms/uppercase.js';

async function collectTransformed(chunks) {
  const { readable, writable } = uppercaseTransform();
  const writer = writable.getWriter();
  for (const chunk of chunks) await writer.write(chunk);
  await writer.close();

  const result = [];
  for await (const chunk of readable) result.push(chunk);
  return result;
}

test('uppercaseTransform converts each string chunk', async () => {
  const result = await collectTransformed(['hello', ' ', 'world']);
  expect(result).toEqual(['HELLO', ' ', 'WORLD']);
});

test('uppercaseTransform passes through empty stream', async () => {
  expect(await collectTransformed([])).toEqual([]);
});

test('uppercaseTransform passes non-string chunks unchanged', async () => {
  const buf = new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3]);
  const result = await collectTransformed([buf]);
  expect(result[0]).toBe(buf);    // reference equality — not copied
});
```
Tradeoff: Testing `TransformStream` via `async for...of` on the readable side correctly exercises the full pipeline without exposing internal state, but `pipeThrough()` locks both the source readable and the transform writable — calling `pipeThrough()` on a stream that has already had `getReader()` called throws `TypeError: ReadableStream is already locked`; the helper approach above avoids this by directly acquiring the writer and using `for await...of` on the readable before any pipe call.

**Pattern 297** — Parameterized Async Error-Path Testing with `test.each` and `rejects.toThrow`
```ts
import { describe, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { parseJSON } from '../parseJSON.js';

describe('parseJSON error paths', () => {
  test.each([
    ['{broken',          'Unexpected token'],
    ['undefined',        'Unexpected token'],
    ['{"key": }',        'Unexpected token'],
    ['',                 'input must not be empty'],
    [null as any,        'input must be a string'],
  ])('rejects "%s" with an error matching "%s"', async (input, expectedMsg) => {
    await expect(parseJSON(input)).rejects.toThrow(expectedMsg);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Combining `test.each` with `.rejects.toThrow()` covers all error-path variants in a single declaration, dramatically reducing boilerplate — but `.rejects.toThrow()` matches by substring or regex against `error.message`; if the implementation throws a custom `AppError` subclass with a different `message` format than expected, the assertion silently passes with a partial match even when the wrong error type was thrown; add `.rejects.toBeInstanceOf(AppError)` as an additional assertion when error type matters.

**Pattern 298** — `AbortController` Signal Composition with `AbortSignal.any()` for Multi-Condition Cancellation
```js
// src/fetcher.js
export async function fetchWithCompositeTimeout(url, { timeoutMs, externalSignal } = {}) {
  const timeoutCtrl = new AbortController();
  const timeoutId   = setTimeout(() => timeoutCtrl.abort(), timeoutMs ?? 10_000);

  // AbortSignal.any() resolves as soon as EITHER signal fires
  const combined = AbortSignal.any
    ? AbortSignal.any([timeoutCtrl.signal, externalSignal].filter(Boolean))
    : timeoutCtrl.signal;

  try {
    const res = await fetch(url, { signal: combined });
    clearTimeout(timeoutId);
    return res;
  } catch (err) {
    clearTimeout(timeoutId);
    if (err.name === 'AbortError') throw new Error(`Fetch aborted: ${url}`);
    throw err;
  }
}

// src/__tests__/fetcher.test.js
import { fetchWithCompositeTimeout } from '../fetcher.js';

describe('fetchWithCompositeTimeout', () => {
  beforeEach(() => jest.useFakeTimers());
  afterEach(() => { jest.useRealTimers(); jest.restoreAllMocks(); });

  test('aborts when external signal fires before timeout', async () => {
    const externalCtrl = new AbortController();
    jest.spyOn(globalThis, 'fetch').mockImplementation(
      (_url, { signal }) => new Promise((_r, rej) => {
        signal.addEventListener('abort', () =>
          rej(new DOMException('Aborted', 'AbortError'))
        );
      })
    );
    const p = fetchWithCompositeTimeout('https://api.example.com', {
      timeoutMs: 10_000,
      externalSignal: externalCtrl.signal,
    });
    externalCtrl.abort();
    await expect(p).rejects.toThrow('Fetch aborted');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `AbortSignal.any()` (Chrome 116+, Node 20.3+) enables clean multi-condition abort composition without manual event listener wiring — but it is not available in all environments (notably older Node LTS versions and Safari < 17.4), requiring a runtime feature check (`AbortSignal.any ? ... : fallback`) that reduces test coverage confidence; polyfilling via a utility function that manually forwards abort events is the portable alternative.

**Pattern 299** — Vitest `expect.poll()` for Eventually-Consistent State Without Manual `waitFor` Loops
```ts
import { expect, test, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { startProcessor, getProcessorStatus } from '../processor.js';

afterEach(() => vi.useRealTimers());

test('processor reaches "idle" status within 3 seconds of starting', async () => {
  await startProcessor({ workload: 'light' });

  await expect.poll(
    () => getProcessorStatus(),
    { interval: 100, timeout: 3000 }
  ).toBe('idle');
});

test('processor emits "error" status when workload is invalid', async () => {
  await startProcessor({ workload: 'invalid-type' });

  await expect.poll(
    () => getProcessorStatus(),
    { interval: 50, timeout: 1500 }
  ).toMatch(/error|failed/i);
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.poll()` (Vitest 0.32+) eliminates manual `setInterval`/`waitFor` retry loops and produces a clear timeout message when the condition is never met — but `expect.poll()` measures real wall-clock time even when `vi.useFakeTimers()` is active, so calling `vi.advanceTimersByTime()` does not advance the poll's timeout; always use `expect.poll()` with real timers (or reset to real timers before the poll assertion).

### Community Gotchas

**G147** — `jest.mock()` Factory Closures Are Hoisted — Non-`mock`-Prefixed Variables Capture `undefined`
Why this matters: Developers parameterize a `jest.mock()` factory by capturing a file-scoped variable, expecting the factory to read the value set in a `beforeEach`. Babel's `babel-jest` transform hoists every `jest.mock()` call to the top of the compiled output — before any `let`/`const` initializers run. A pattern like `let apiResponse = { ok: true }; jest.mock('./api', () => ({ fetch: () => apiResponse }))` produces `fetch: () => undefined` for the first invocation, because `apiResponse` is in the temporal dead zone when the factory runs. Tests that reassign `apiResponse` inside `beforeEach` appear to fix the issue (the closure updates at call time), masking the initialization-time bug.
Fix: Prefix the factory's closed-over variable with `mock` (e.g., `let mockApiResponse`) — Babel's `babel-plugin-jest-hoist` whitelists identifiers starting with `mock` inside hoisted factories. Alternatively, capture a `jest.fn()` stub and call `.mockReturnValue(newValue)` in `beforeEach` to avoid the hoisting constraint entirely.

**G148** — Vitest `vi.mock()` Inside `describe` / `it` Is Silently Ignored — Real Module Used Instead
Why this matters: Developers scope a `vi.mock()` inside a `describe` block or conditionally inside an `it`, expecting the mock to apply only to that test context. Vitest's Vite transform hoists all `vi.mock()` declarations to module scope at parse time; any `vi.mock()` outside the file's top lexical level is silently dropped — the real module is imported instead with zero indication that the mock was not registered. Tests then call real APIs, hit real network, or throw `TypeError` from real constructors, and the developer diagnoses a module-resolution bug rather than a misplaced `vi.mock()` call.
Fix: Move all `vi.mock()` calls to the file's top level (same level as `import` declarations). To vary mock behaviour per test, call `vi.mocked(fn).mockReturnValueOnce(...)` or `vi.mocked(fn).mockImplementationOnce(...)` inside the individual `it` block after the module-level factory establishes the mock.

**G149** — `toHaveBeenCalledWith()` Is Deep-Strict — Auto-Generated Payload Fields Fail Assertions
Why this matters: Developers assert `expect(analyticsSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ event: 'click', elementId: 'btn-submit' })` expecting it to pass when the function was actually called with `{ event: 'click', elementId: 'btn-submit', sessionId: 'abc-123', timestamp: 1715689200000 }`. `toHaveBeenCalledWith()` performs a complete deep-strict equality check — not a subset check — so the extra `sessionId` and `timestamp` fields added by the analytics library cause the assertion to fail. The Jest diff output shows the full actual call object, but the additional keys look like "wrong values" at first glance, leading developers to investigate the wrong thing.
Fix: Wrap the expected argument in `expect.objectContaining(...)` to assert only on the fields you own: `expect(analyticsSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.objectContaining({ event: 'click', elementId: 'btn-submit' }))`. Use `expect.any(Number)` for auto-generated numeric fields like timestamps, and `expect.stringMatching(pattern)` for auto-generated string IDs.

**G150** — `mock.timers.enable()` in `node:test` Does Not Fake `Date` Without Explicit `apis` Array
Why this matters: Developers using Node.js 20–21's built-in `mock.timers` API assume that calling `mock.timers.enable()` freezes both timers and `Date`, matching Jest's behaviour where `useFakeTimers()` intercepts `Date` by default. In `node:test`, `mock.timers.enable()` without arguments only intercepts `setTimeout` and `setInterval`. Code that calls `Date.now()` or `new Date()` inside the function under test continues reading real wall-clock time, causing assertions like `expect(event.timestamp).toBe(fakeNow)` to fail with a real timestamp instead of the expected fake one. The failure is intermittent on fast machines where the real elapsed time is within tolerance, but reliably fails on busy CI runners.
Fix: Always list `'Date'` explicitly in the `apis` array and provide a `now` seed: `mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['setTimeout', 'setInterval', 'Date'], now: new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z') })`. Call `mock.timers.reset()` in `afterEach` to restore real time between tests.

**G151** — `@testing-library/user-event` v14 `type()` Is Async — Missing `await` Leaves Input Empty
Why this matters: `@testing-library/user-event` v13 had a synchronous `userEvent.type()`. v14 made it async (`Promise<void>`) to accurately interleave pointer-down, focus, keydown, input, and keyup events as a real browser would. Codebases migrated from v13 that call `userEvent.type(input, 'query')` without `await` and then assert `expect(input).toHaveValue('query')` fail intermittently: the input value is empty or partially filled because the async typing has not completed. JavaScript does not warn about un-awaited `void` Promises, so the failure message is simply "Expected '' to equal 'query'" — indistinguishable from a React state-update timing bug.
Fix: Always `await userEvent.type(input, 'value')` in v14+. Use the official `setup()` pattern: `const user = userEvent.setup()` once per test suite (in `beforeEach`) and `await user.type(...)` per test, which uses a shared event queue for correct cross-event ordering. Add the ESLint rule `testing-library/no-await-sync-events` to catch un-awaited `userEvent` method calls at lint time.

## Cycle 60 — 2026-05-14

### Structured Logging to stdout — Production Node.js Pattern [community]

Unstructured `console.log` in production makes log aggregation, alerting, and root-cause analysis very hard. The practitioner standard is to emit newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) to **stdout only** and let the infrastructure (Kubernetes log collector, Docker log driver, PM2, etc.) route, filter, and aggregate. Never specify the log destination in application code — doing so couples the app to specific infrastructure.

**Pino** is the de-facto standard for high-throughput Node.js logging (5–10× faster than Winston at high volume because it serialises asynchronously and defers formatting to external tools like `pino-pretty`).

```javascript
// ── Install ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// npm install pino

import pino from 'pino';

// Production: emit NDJSON to stdout; let infrastructure route it
const logger = pino({
  level: process.env.LOG_LEVEL ?? 'info',
  // Redact sensitive fields before they hit the log stream
  redact: ['req.headers.authorization', 'user.password', '*.token'],
});

// Structured log — every field is queryable in your log aggregator
logger.info({ userId: 42, action: 'login', ip: '1.2.3.4' }, 'User logged in');
// {"level":30,"time":1715689200000,"userId":42,"action":"login","ip":"1.2.3.4","msg":"User logged in"}

// Log levels map to numeric severity — filterable without grep
logger.trace('Detailed internal trace');        // level 10
logger.debug({ query: 'SELECT *', ms: 3 }, 'DB query');   // 20
logger.info('Server started on port 3000');     // 30
logger.warn({ retries: 3 }, 'Slow third-party API'); // 40
logger.error({ err: error }, 'Payment failed'); // 50
logger.fatal({ err }, 'Unrecoverable crash');   // 60

// Child logger — inherit parent context, add per-request fields
function requestMiddleware(req, res, next) {
  req.log = logger.child({
    requestId: req.headers['x-request-id'] ?? crypto.randomUUID(),
    userId: req.user?.id,
  });
  next();
}

// Deep in a service — use req.log, never the root logger
async function chargePayment(req, amount) {
  req.log.info({ amount }, 'Initiating charge');
  try {
    const result = await stripe.charge({ amount });
    req.log.info({ chargeId: result.id }, 'Charge successful');
    return result;
  } catch (err) {
    // Always log err as a field, not a string: preserves stack trace and properties
    req.log.error({ err, amount }, 'Charge failed');
    throw err;
  }
}
```

**Development:** pipe through `pino-pretty` for human-readable output — keep JSON in production:
```bash
node server.js | pino-pretty   # readable during dev
node server.js                 # raw NDJSON in production → sent to log aggregator
```

**Key rules (nodebestpractices):**
- Always write to `stdout`, not to files — let the process manager/container route it.
- Use child loggers with request context so every log line for a request is automatically correlated.
- Log errors as `{ err }` (an object field) — Pino serialises `.stack`, `.message`, `.name` automatically.
- Redact sensitive fields in the Pino config, not at the call site.
- Set `LOG_LEVEL` via environment variable so different environments get different verbosity without code changes.

### Domain-Based Project Structure (Package by Feature) [community]

Organising by technical layer (`controllers/`, `services/`, `models/`) creates tight coupling across unrelated business domains: a change to `orders` touches the same `services/` directory as a change to `users`, making code review, refactoring, and autonomous team ownership harder. The practitioner standard (from nodebestpractices) is to organise by **business domain** — each domain contains all its own layers.

```
// ── Technical-layer structure (AVOID for large projects) ──────────────
src/
├── controllers/
│   ├── users.controller.js
│   ├── orders.controller.js
│   └── payments.controller.js
├── services/
│   ├── users.service.js
│   ├── orders.service.js
│   └── payments.service.js
└── models/
    ├── user.model.js
    ├── order.model.js
    └── payment.model.js
// Problem: feature work (e.g., adding order discounts) touches 3 separate
// directories, all shared by multiple teams. Merge conflicts are common.

// ── Domain-based structure (PREFERRED for medium–large projects) ────────
src/
├── users/
│   ├── users.router.js        // HTTP route declarations
│   ├── users.controller.js    // Request/response handling
│   ├── users.service.js       // Business logic
│   ├── users.repo.js          // Data access (DB queries)
│   ├── users.model.js         // Schema / validation
│   └── users.test.js          // Collocated tests
├── orders/
│   ├── orders.router.js
│   ├── orders.controller.js
│   ├── orders.service.js
│   ├── orders.repo.js
│   ├── orders.model.js
│   └── orders.test.js
├── payments/
│   └── ...
└── shared/
    ├── db.js                  // Shared DB connection pool
    ├── logger.js              // Shared Pino instance
    └── middleware/
        ├── auth.middleware.js
        └── error.middleware.js
```

```javascript
// ── Entry point: wire domains together without cross-importing ─────────
// app.js
import { usersRouter }    from './users/users.router.js';
import { ordersRouter }   from './orders/orders.router.js';
import { paymentsRouter } from './payments/payments.router.js';
import { errorMiddleware } from './shared/middleware/error.middleware.js';

const app = express();
app.use('/api/users',    usersRouter);
app.use('/api/orders',   ordersRouter);
app.use('/api/payments', paymentsRouter);
app.use(errorMiddleware);

// ── Cross-domain: use events or a service interface, not direct imports ─
// WRONG: orders imports from users directly → creates tight coupling
// import { findUser } from '../users/users.service.js'; // ❌ cross-domain direct import

// RIGHT: expose a minimal interface the order service depends on (DIP)
// orders/orders.service.js
export function createOrderService({ userService, orderRepo, logger }) {
  return {
    async place(userId, items) {
      const user = await userService.findById(userId); // injected, not imported
      if (!user.isActive) throw new AppError('User account is not active');
      const order = await orderRepo.create({ userId, items });
      logger.info({ orderId: order.id, userId }, 'Order placed');
      return order;
    },
  };
}
```

**Why it matters:** domain-based structure makes it possible to assign ownership per team, extract a domain into a microservice later, and contain blast radius — a bug in `orders/` cannot accidentally break `users/` because the code is entirely separate.

---

### Flat Promise Chains Over Nested `.then()` [official]

MDN's official Promises guide explicitly identifies unnecessary nesting as an anti-pattern. Nested `.then()` chains lose the centralized error handling that makes Promises better than callbacks. The fix is to return the next Promise from each `.then()` handler and keep the chain flat.

```javascript
// ── ANTI-PATTERN: nested .then() chains ──────────────────────────────
// Looks like "callback hell" — error handling is scattered, indentation grows
doSomething()
  .then(result => {
    return doSomethingElse(result)
      .then(newResult => {           // ← unnecessary nesting
        return doThirdThing(newResult)
          .then(finalResult => {     // ← nesting deepens
            console.log(finalResult);
          })
          .catch(innerErr => {       // ← separate catch per level
            console.error('Third thing failed:', innerErr);
          });
      });
  })
  .catch(outerErr => {               // ← outer catch doesn't cover inner
    console.error('Outer error:', outerErr);
  });

// ── CORRECT: flat chain — one catch covers everything ─────────────────
doSomething()
  .then(result     => doSomethingElse(result))   // return the Promise
  .then(newResult  => doThirdThing(newResult))   // return the Promise
  .then(finalResult => {
    console.log('Final:', finalResult);
  })
  .catch(err => {
    // One catch handles errors from ANY step in the chain
    console.error('Pipeline failed:', err);
  });

// ── EXCEPTION: nesting is valid for optional steps ─────────────────────
// If doSomethingOptional() failure should not abort the whole chain:
doSomethingCritical()
  .then(result =>
    doSomethingOptional(result)           // optional — failure OK
      .catch(err => {
        console.warn('Optional step skipped:', err.message);
        return result; // continue with original result
      })
  )
  .then(result => doSomethingElseRequired(result)) // must succeed
  .catch(err => console.error('Critical failure:', err));

// ── async/await is the modern equivalent of flat chains ───────────────
// Prefer it for new code; the flat chain pattern above is the .then() idiom
async function pipeline() {
  try {
    const result     = await doSomething();
    const newResult  = await doSomethingElse(result);
    const finalResult = await doThirdThing(newResult);
    console.log('Final:', finalResult);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Pipeline failed:', err);
  }
}
```

**Rule of thumb:** if your `.then()` callback returns a new `.then()` call, extract that return into a named function and flatten. Nesting is only justified when a sub-chain's errors should not bubble to the outer chain (optional steps, fallback paths).

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 60

**CG60-1. `console.log` in Production Leaks Sensitive Data and Blocks the Event Loop** [community] — Formatted string concatenation in `console.log` calls is synchronous and CPU-bound. WHY it causes problems: (1) secrets, tokens, and user PII in ad-hoc log strings survive the app's lifetime in plaintext in log files and aggregators; (2) high-throughput services that log on every request find that `console.log` is blocking enough to show up in V8 profiles. Fix: replace all production logging with Pino (or equivalent structured logger); let the log pipeline handle PII redaction centrally via the `redact` option.

**CG60-2. Logging `err.toString()` or `String(err)` Instead of `{ err }` as an Object** [community] — Passing an error to a logger as a string (`logger.error('Failed: ' + err)` or `logger.error(err.message)`) loses the stack trace, the error class name, and any custom properties like `.code` or `.cause`. WHY it causes problems: the log line `"Failed: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined"` tells you what failed but not where — the stack trace that would identify the file and line number is gone. Fix: always pass the error as a structured field: `logger.error({ err }, 'Human-readable context message')` — Pino serialises the full error object including `.stack`.

**CG60-3. Nested `.then()` Callbacks That Create Independent Error Chains** [community] — A `.catch()` at the end of an outer `.then()` chain does not catch errors thrown inside a nested inner `.then()` chain (one that is not returned). WHY it causes problems: the inner chain runs independently — its errors become unhandled rejections that crash the process or fire `window.unhandledrejection`, bypassing all the error handling that looks correct in the outer chain. The outer `.catch()` never fires for the inner failure, and the developer sees a crash coming from "nowhere". Fix: always `return` every Promise from `.then()` callbacks; flatten chains rather than nesting them; use `async/await` where the sequential structure makes the return obligation obvious.

**CG60-4. Domain-Level Singleton Imports Coupling Unrelated Features** [community] — Importing a concrete dependency (database client, HTTP client, external service) at the top level of a domain module and calling it directly makes it impossible to deploy or test that domain independently. WHY it causes problems: spinning up the `orders` service in an isolated test also initialises the DB connection pool, the payment gateway client, and the email service — even if the test only covers order pricing logic. This inflates test startup time, introduces flakiness (network calls in tests), and makes it impossible to deploy `orders` without every dependency being available. Fix: use factory functions that accept dependencies as constructor-style arguments; inject the real implementations at app startup and stubs at test time.

## Cycle 61 — 2026-05-14

### 1. Microtask Starvation — Infinite Promise Chains Starve I/O [official + community]

The event loop drains the entire microtask queue before processing any macrotask (I/O callbacks, `setTimeout`, timers). A loop that continuously queues new microtasks therefore prevents the event loop from ever processing I/O — effectively starving the server under load.

```javascript
// ── DANGER: recursive Promise resolution starves I/O ─────────────────
// Each resolved Promise queues another microtask before the event loop
// can process any I/O events.

// BAD — in a Node.js server, while this loop runs, incoming HTTP requests,
// DB callbacks, and filesystem operations are all blocked.
function infiniteMicrotask() {
  Promise.resolve().then(infiniteMicrotask); // starvation loop
}
infiniteMicrotask(); // server becomes unresponsive

// ── Real-world variant: tight async recursion without real I/O ─────────
async function processItems(items, i = 0) {
  if (i >= items.length) return;
  processSyncItem(items[i]);       // synchronous — no real async I/O
  return processItems(items, i + 1); // each call queues a microtask — starvation
}

// ── Safe: introduce a macrotask checkpoint to yield to I/O ────────────
// Option 1: setImmediate (Node.js) — runs after current I/O callbacks
function processWithMacrotaskYield(items, index = 0) {
  if (index >= items.length) return;
  processSyncItem(items[index]);
  setImmediate(() => processWithMacrotaskYield(items, index + 1));
  // setImmediate gives I/O callbacks a chance to run between iterations
}

// Option 2: scheduler.yield() (browser, Chrome 129+ / Baseline 2025)
async function processChunks(items) {
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    processSyncItem(items[i]);
    if (i % 100 === 0) {
      await scheduler.yield(); // yield to browser scheduler — same priority
    }
  }
}

// Option 3: setTimeout(fn, 0) — guaranteed macrotask boundary (cross-platform)
function tick(items, i = 0) {
  if (i >= items.length) return;
  processSyncItem(items[i]);
  setTimeout(() => tick(items, i + 1), 0);
}
```

**Rule:** `queueMicrotask` and `Promise.resolve().then()` are microtasks — they never yield to I/O. `setImmediate`, `setTimeout(fn, 0)`, and `scheduler.yield()` create macrotask checkpoints where the event loop can process incoming requests, database responses, and file system events.

**Diagnostic:** if a Node.js server becomes unresponsive under load despite low CPU, check for recursive microtask patterns or long synchronous chains between `await` points. Use `node --prof` + `node --prof-process` or `clinic.js` to identify starvation hot spots.

### 2. `import.meta` — Complete Reference for ESM Metadata [official]

`import.meta` is a module-scoped object that provides metadata about the current ES module. Its properties differ between runtimes but the core set is standardised.

```javascript
// ── import.meta.url — always available in ESM ──────────────────────────
// The fully qualified URL of the current module (file:// in Node.js)
console.log(import.meta.url);
// Node.js: 'file:///home/user/project/src/utils.js'
// Browser: 'https://example.com/src/utils.js'

// Construct paths relative to the current file (replaces __dirname in CJS)
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
import { dirname, join } from 'node:path';

const __filename = fileURLToPath(import.meta.url);
const __dirname  = dirname(__filename);
const configPath = join(__dirname, '../../config.json');

// ── import.meta.dirname / import.meta.filename — Node.js 21.2+ ─────────
// Shorthand that avoids the fileURLToPath + dirname dance above
// Available in Node.js 21.2+ (no polyfill needed for modern Node)
console.log(import.meta.dirname);  // '/home/user/project/src'
console.log(import.meta.filename); // '/home/user/project/src/utils.js'

const configDirect = join(import.meta.dirname, '../../config.json');

// ── import.meta.resolve() — resolve a specifier without importing ──────
// Returns the URL a specifier would resolve to, as a string.
// Useful for passing a module path to Worker without executing it.
const workerUrl = import.meta.resolve('./worker.js');
// 'file:///home/user/project/src/worker.js'

const workerUrlFromPackage = import.meta.resolve('some-package/worker');
// resolves through node_modules, respecting package.json exports

const worker = new Worker(workerUrl, { type: 'module' });

// ── import.meta.main — Deno / Bun (Node.js: use process.argv) ──────────
// Deno and Bun provide import.meta.main to detect if the file was the
// script entrypoint (equivalent to Python's __name__ == '__main__')
if (import.meta.main) {
  // Only runs when this file is executed directly, not when imported
  runCLI();
}

// Node.js equivalent (no import.meta.main):
if (process.argv[1] === import.meta.filename) {
  runCLI();
}

// ── import.meta.env — Vite / bundlers ─────────────────────────────────
// Build tools (Vite, Rollup plugins) inject environment variables here
// at build time. Not available in native Node.js runtime.
if (import.meta.env?.PROD) {
  // Production-only code — stripped in dev builds
}
const apiBase = import.meta.env?.VITE_API_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000';

// ── Cross-runtime guard pattern ────────────────────────────────────────
// Some import.meta properties are runtime-specific — guard before use
const moduleDir = import.meta.dirname           // Node.js 21.2+
  ?? (typeof __dirname !== 'undefined' ? __dirname  // CJS fallback
  : null);                                          // Browser / Deno
```

**Runtime support matrix:**

| Property | Node.js | Browser | Deno | Bun |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `import.meta.url` | ✅ always | ✅ always | ✅ | ✅ |
| `import.meta.resolve()` | ✅ 20.0+ | ✅ Chrome 105+ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `import.meta.dirname` | ✅ 21.2+ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| `import.meta.filename` | ✅ 21.2+ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| `import.meta.main` | ❌ (use `process.argv`) | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `import.meta.env` | ❌ (bundler-injected) | ❌ native | ✅ (Deno.env) | partial |

### 3. `Promise.race` — First-Settled Wins [official]

`Promise.race(iterable)` resolves or rejects as soon as the first Promise in the iterable settles (either fulfils or rejects). Unlike `Promise.any` (first *fulfillment*), `Promise.race` reflects the first settlement regardless of outcome.

```javascript
// ── Canonical: timeout wrapper with Promise.race ──────────────────────
function withTimeout(promise, ms, label = 'operation') {
  const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(`${label} timed out after ${ms}ms`)), ms)
  );
  return Promise.race([promise, timeout]);
}

const result = await withTimeout(fetchUserData(42), 3000, 'fetchUserData');

// ── Compare: Promise.race vs AbortSignal.timeout ──────────────────────
// AbortSignal.timeout is preferred for fetch — it cancels the network request.
// Promise.race with a timeout does NOT cancel the losing promise; it just
// ignores it. The fetch continues in the background consuming resources.

// Better for fetch:
const response = await fetch('/api/data', { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000) });

// Promise.race is appropriate when you CAN'T cancel the other promise
// (legacy API, non-cancellable operation):
const cached = await withTimeout(legacyLibrary.loadFromDisk(), 500, 'disk');

// ── First response from multiple endpoints ────────────────────────────
// Pick whichever server responds first (assumes servers are idempotent)
async function fetchFromFastest(urls) {
  return Promise.race(
    urls.map(url => fetch(url).then(r => {
      if (!r.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${r.status} from ${url}`);
      return r.json();
    }))
  );
}
// Note: if the fastest server's response is an error, race rejects.
// Use Promise.any() if you want the first *successful* response instead.

// ── Cancellation caveat — Promise.race does not cancel losers ─────────
// The "losing" promises remain in-flight. For fire-and-forget this is fine.
// For expensive operations (network, DB), use AbortController to cancel them.

async function raceTwoWithCleanup(url1, url2) {
  const ac1 = new AbortController();
  const ac2 = new AbortController();
  const p1 = fetch(url1, { signal: ac1.signal }).then(r => r.json()).then(v => ({ v, cancel: ac2 }));
  const p2 = fetch(url2, { signal: ac2.signal }).then(r => r.json()).then(v => ({ v, cancel: ac1 }));
  const { v, cancel } = await Promise.race([p1, p2]);
  cancel.abort(); // cancel the loser
  return v;
}
```

**Decision guide:**

| Goal | Use |
|---|---|
| First result (success or failure) | `Promise.race` |
| First *successful* result | `Promise.any` |
| All results, fail-fast on first error | `Promise.all` |
| All results, never reject | `Promise.allSettled` |
| Named concurrent results | `Promise.allKeyed` (Stage 2.7) |
| Timeout a non-cancellable operation | `Promise.race([op, timeoutPromise])` |
| Timeout a `fetch` | `fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms) })` |

### 4. Closure Loop Pitfall — Three Solutions [official + community]

Creating closures inside loops is one of the most enduring JavaScript gotchas. The root cause is `var`'s function-scoped (not block-scoped) semantics: all closures in the loop share the same `item` binding, which by the time any callback fires holds the final loop value.

```javascript
// ── THE PROBLEM: var creates ONE binding shared by all closures ─────────
function setupHelpBad() {
  const fields = [
    { id: 'email', help: 'Your email address' },
    { id: 'name',  help: 'Your full name'     },
    { id: 'age',   help: 'Must be over 16'    },
  ];
  for (var i = 0; i < fields.length; i++) {
    var item = fields[i]; // ONE var binding — updated each iteration
    document.getElementById(item.id).onfocus = function () {
      showHelp(item.help); // ALWAYS shows "Must be over 16" — the final item
    };
  }
}

// ── SOLUTION 1: use let/const (modern — preferred) ─────────────────────
// 'const' creates a new binding per iteration — closures see their own copy
function setupHelpModern() {
  const fields = [
    { id: 'email', help: 'Your email address' },
    { id: 'name',  help: 'Your full name'     },
    { id: 'age',   help: 'Must be over 16'    },
  ];
  for (const item of fields) {           // new 'item' binding each iteration
    document.getElementById(item.id).onfocus = () => showHelp(item.help);
  }
}

// ── SOLUTION 2: function factory — captures value at call time ──────────
function makeHelpHandler(help) {
  return () => showHelp(help); // 'help' is a new binding in each call frame
}

for (var i = 0; i < fields.length; i++) {
  document.getElementById(fields[i].id).onfocus = makeHelpHandler(fields[i].help);
}

// ── SOLUTION 3: IIFE — creates a new scope per iteration ───────────────
// Historical pattern; use let/const instead in modern code
for (var i = 0; i < fields.length; i++) {
  (function (item) {
    document.getElementById(item.id).onfocus = function () {
      showHelp(item.help);
    };
  })(fields[i]); // calls itself immediately, capturing fields[i] in 'item'
}

// ── The same trap with async callbacks ────────────────────────────────
// setTimeout and async callbacks share the same timing trap:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100); // prints 3, 3, 3 — not 0, 1, 2
}

// Fix with let:
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100); // prints 0, 1, 2
}

// ── Array.forEach avoids the issue — callback receives element by value ─
fields.forEach(item => {
  document.getElementById(item.id).onfocus = () => showHelp(item.help);
  // item is a parameter (new binding per call) — no closure trap
});
```

**Mental model:** `var` is hoisted to the enclosing *function* scope. Inside a loop, every iteration reads and writes the *same* variable. `let` and `const` create a fresh binding for each block iteration — each closure gets its own snapshot.

### 5. Node.js Object Mode Streams — Non-Binary Transform Pipelines [official]

By default, Node.js streams operate in **buffer mode**: data is a `Buffer` or `string`. **Object mode** lifts this restriction — streams can produce and consume arbitrary JavaScript values (objects, arrays, numbers). Object mode transforms are the idiomatic way to build data-processing pipelines in Node.js.

```javascript
import { Transform, Readable, Writable } from 'node:stream';
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';

// ── Object mode Transform — parse CSV rows into objects ──────────────
const csvToObject = new Transform({
  objectMode: true,          // ← enables object mode for both readable and writable side
  readableObjectMode: true,  // alternatively: enable only the readable side
  writableObjectMode: true,  // or only the writable side (mixed mode)

  transform(line, _encoding, callback) {
    // 'line' is whatever the upstream pushed (a string in this example)
    const [name, age, city] = line.split(',');
    if (name && age && city) {
      this.push({ name: name.trim(), age: parseInt(age, 10), city: city.trim() });
    }
    callback(); // no error, no data = filtered out
  },
});

// ── Object mode Readable — emit JS objects lazily ────────────────────
const recordSource = new Readable({
  objectMode: true,
  read() {
    const records = getNextBatch(); // hypothetical data source
    if (!records.length) return this.push(null); // signal end-of-stream
    for (const r of records) this.push(r);
  },
});

// ── Object mode Writable — consume objects ───────────────────────────
const dbWriter = new Writable({
  objectMode: true,
  async write(record, _encoding, callback) {
    try {
      await db.insert('users', record);
      callback(); // signal success
    } catch (err) {
      callback(err); // propagate error through the pipeline
    }
  },
});

// ── Readable.from() — wrap any iterable as an object-mode stream ──────
// Sync iterable
const numStream = Readable.from([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]); // objectMode: true, emits numbers

// Async generator
async function* fetchAllUsers() {
  let page = 1;
  while (true) {
    const { users, hasMore } = await fetch(`/api/users?page=${page}`).then(r => r.json());
    yield* users;
    if (!hasMore) break;
    page++;
  }
}
const userStream = Readable.from(fetchAllUsers()); // streams users lazily

// ── Full pipeline: CSV file → objects → DB ────────────────────────────
import { createInterface } from 'node:readline';
import { createReadStream } from 'node:fs';

async function importCSV(filePath) {
  const rl = createInterface({
    input: createReadStream(filePath),
    crlfDelay: Infinity,
  });
  const lineSource = Readable.from(rl); // objectMode: true (async iterable → Readable)

  await pipeline(
    lineSource,   // each chunk is a string (one CSV row)
    csvToObject,  // Transform: string → { name, age, city }
    dbWriter,     // Writable: { name, age, city } → DB insert
  );
  console.log('Import complete');
}
```

**Key rules:**
- A stream can be in object mode on both sides, or mixed (binary in / object out or vice versa). Use `readableObjectMode` and `writableObjectMode` separately when mixing.
- Object mode streams have no concept of a `highWaterMark` in bytes — the watermark is a **count** of objects (default: 16 objects).
- `pipeline()` (from `node:stream/promises`) correctly handles object mode streams and propagates errors; never use `.pipe()` for production pipelines.
- `Readable.from(asyncIterable)` is the fastest way to bridge any async generator or async iterable into the Node.js stream ecosystem.

---

### 6. `Promise.allSettled` — Exhaustive Concurrent Execution [official]

`Promise.allSettled` always resolves (never rejects) after every promise settles, returning an array of result descriptors. It is the right choice whenever partial failure is acceptable — dashboards, bulk operations, health checks — and when you need to handle both successes and failures from the same call.

```javascript
// ── Basic pattern ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
const results = await Promise.allSettled([
  fetchUser(1),
  fetchPosts(1),
  fetchMetrics(1), // allowed to fail without aborting the rest
]);

// results[0] = { status: 'fulfilled', value: { id: 1, ... } }
// results[1] = { status: 'fulfilled', value: [...] }
// results[2] = { status: 'rejected',  reason: Error('503') }

// ── Idiomatic: partition into successes and failures ──────────────────
const succeeded = results
  .filter(r => r.status === 'fulfilled')
  .map(r => r.value);

const failed = results
  .filter(r => r.status === 'rejected')
  .map(r => r.reason);

// ── Practical: health-check endpoint ─────────────────────────────────
async function checkHealth() {
  const checks = {
    db:    () => db.ping(),
    redis: () => redis.ping(),
    email: () => emailService.ping(),
  };

  const results = await Promise.allSettled(
    Object.entries(checks).map(async ([name, fn]) => {
      const start = performance.now();
      await fn();
      return { name, ms: Math.round(performance.now() - start) };
    })
  );

  const report = Object.fromEntries(
    Object.keys(checks).map((name, i) => [
      name,
      results[i].status === 'fulfilled'
        ? { status: 'ok', ms: results[i].value.ms }
        : { status: 'error', reason: results[i].reason.message },
    ])
  );

  const allOk = results.every(r => r.status === 'fulfilled');
  return { healthy: allOk, checks: report };
}

// ── Bulk mutation with per-item error reporting ───────────────────────
async function batchUpdateUsers(users) {
  const results = await Promise.allSettled(
    users.map(u => db.updateUser(u.id, u.data))
  );
  const errors = results
    .map((r, i) => r.status === 'rejected' ? { user: users[i], error: r.reason } : null)
    .filter(Boolean);
  if (errors.length > 0) {
    logger.warn({ errors }, `${errors.length}/${users.length} updates failed`);
  }
  return { total: users.length, failed: errors.length, errors };
}
```

**When `allSettled` vs `all`:**
- `Promise.all` — all-or-nothing; any rejection aborts the wait and throws. Use when every result is required and a partial outcome is an error condition.
- `Promise.allSettled` — exhaustive; partial failure is handled gracefully. Use when you need all responses regardless of individual success.

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 61

**CG61-1. Infinite Microtask Loops Starving Node.js I/O** [community] — A `while(true)` loop wrapped in `Promise.resolve().then()` (or recursive `async` calls without real async I/O) creates an unbreakable microtask chain. The event loop never reaches macrotask processing — incoming HTTP requests, timers, and filesystem callbacks queue up indefinitely. WHY it causes problems: the server appears "alive" (process running) but completely unresponsive to all incoming traffic, with no obvious error in logs. This is distinct from a CPU-intensive synchronous loop because the stack never grows — each microtask starts fresh, making it invisible to V8's stack-overflow detection. Fix: introduce `setImmediate` or `setTimeout(fn, 0)` at regular intervals to yield macrotask checkpoints; or restructure the algorithm to use real async I/O instead of synthetic Promise chains.

**CG61-2. `import.meta.dirname` Used in Node.js < 21.2** [community] — `import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.filename` were introduced in Node.js 21.2 (backported to Node.js 22 LTS). On earlier versions they are `undefined`, not an error at parse time — leading to silent failures when used for path construction. WHY it causes problems: code that runs fine in development on Node.js 22+ silently breaks in a Docker image still pinned to Node.js 20 LTS, producing `path.join(undefined, 'config.json')` which evaluates to `'undefined/config.json'` — a path that doesn't exist but doesn't throw immediately. Fix: guard with `import.meta.dirname ?? fileURLToPath(new URL('.', import.meta.url))` for compatibility back to Node.js 16, or pin your Docker base image to Node.js 22+.

```javascript
// Cross-version safe __dirname replacement for ESM:
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
const __dirname = import.meta.dirname
  ?? fileURLToPath(new URL('.', import.meta.url));
```

**CG61-3. `Promise.race` Not Cancelling Losing Promises** [community] — When `Promise.race` settles, the "losing" promises remain in-flight and continue to consume network connections, DB connections, and memory. WHY it causes problems: in a pattern that races N parallel requests and takes the first response, all N requests complete even though N-1 results are discarded — multiplying network and server load by N when only 1/N of the work was needed. Fix: use `AbortController` to cancel the losing promises explicitly, or use `AbortSignal.any()` to compose signals so cancellation propagates through all branches.

**CG61-4. Object Mode Streams Silently Corrupting Data When `objectMode` Is Missing** [community] — A Transform that pushes JavaScript objects without `objectMode: true` silently converts them via `.toString()` (producing `'[object Object]'`) or throws `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE` when the `highWaterMark` enforcement tries to compute byte length on a non-Buffer chunk. WHY it causes problems: the error surfaces far downstream — often in the Writable sink rather than at the Transform — making the root cause (missing `objectMode`) non-obvious. Fix: always set `objectMode: true` (or `readableObjectMode`/`writableObjectMode`) when any stream stage produces or consumes non-string, non-Buffer values.

**CG61-5. `Readable.from()` Without `pipeline()` Causes Unbounded Buffering** [community] — `Readable.from(asyncGen)` starts pulling from the generator immediately, regardless of whether the downstream consumer is ready. If the generator yields faster than the consumer processes, chunks buffer in memory without bound when using `.pipe()` instead of `pipeline()`. WHY it causes problems: a `Readable.from(paginateAllRecords())` connected to a slow DB writer via `.pipe()` can buffer millions of records in memory while the pipeline appears to be running normally. Fix: always pipe `Readable.from` through `pipeline()` from `node:stream/promises`; `pipeline` correctly applies backpressure by pausing the readable when the writable's buffer fills.

---

## Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 61 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Recursive `Promise.resolve().then(fn)` loop | Starves the event loop — I/O callbacks never execute | Introduce `setImmediate` / `setTimeout(fn, 0)` as macrotask yield points |
| `import.meta.dirname` on Node.js < 21.2 | Returns `undefined` — silently constructs invalid paths | Guard: `import.meta.dirname ?? fileURLToPath(new URL('.', import.meta.url))` |
| `Promise.race` without cancelling losers | All branches continue running — N× resource consumption for 1/N useful work | Combine with `AbortController` to cancel losing branches explicitly |
| Object-mode Transform without `objectMode: true` | Objects silently stringified to `'[object Object]'` or `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE` thrown downstream | Set `objectMode: true` (or `readableObjectMode`/`writableObjectMode`) on every non-binary stream stage |
| `Readable.from(gen)` piped with `.pipe()` | No backpressure — generator outpaces consumer, unbounded memory growth | Always use `pipeline()` from `node:stream/promises` instead of `.pipe()` |
| `var` in closures inside loops | All closures share one binding — capture final loop value, not per-iteration value | Use `let`/`const`, a factory function, or `Array.forEach` |
| `Promise.race` where first-*success* is the goal | A rejection from the fastest server kills the race even if others succeed | Use `Promise.any` — ignores individual rejections, rejects only if all fail |
